# Edge Computing's Transformation of IoT Architectures in 2024: Three Industrial Use Cases

---

## Executive Summary

Edge computing has moved from a complementary technology to a foundational architectural pattern for Industrial IoT (IIoT) in 2024. The paradigm shift—processing data at or near its source rather than routing it to centralized cloud data centers—is driven by physics: the speed of light imposes hard latency floors that no amount of bandwidth can overcome. A welding robot's control loop requiring 10 ms feedback cannot wait 150–500 ms for a cloud round-trip (Jacar, 2024). This report examines three high-impact industrial domains—manufacturing predictive maintenance, autonomous mobile robots, and energy distribution—to document the before-and-after architectures, quantified performance impacts, and real-world trade-offs that define this transformation.

---

## 1. Manufacturing Predictive Maintenance

### 1a. Before-and-After Architecture Comparison

**Cloud-Centric (Before):** In the first-generation IIoT model, vibration sensors, thermocouples, and current monitors attached to factory equipment transmitted raw waveform data to a centralized cloud platform. The cloud executed rules, stored time-series data, trained machine-learning models, and pushed alerts back to plant engineers. A temperature reading triggering a maintenance alert required a round-trip of 200–500 ms minimum through gateway-to-cloud, cloud processing, and cloud-to-notification delivery steps (Viaanix, 2024). High-frequency vibration sensors sampling at 25,600 samples/second generated roughly 200 KB/s per sensor—about 720 MB/hour per sensor—making continuous cloud upload economically impractical over cellular or bandwidth-limited links (Viaanix, 2024).

**Edge-Distributed (After):** The modern architecture places inference engines on edge devices co-located with the equipment. At the Siemens Electronics Factory in Erlangen, Germany, Siemens Industrial Edge devices sit on the shop floor connected directly to PLCs and cameras, running ML models for anomaly detection in printed circuit board (PCB) assembly. Only derived insights and summary telemetry are forwarded to the cloud (AWS Siemens Erlangen case study). The C3 AI Platform version 8, deployed by Holcim across multiple cement plants, runs on Kubernetes on resource-constrained edge devices, ingesting local sensor data, running model inference on 7-day windows, and generating alerts without any dependency on external network connectivity (C3 AI / Holcim, July 2024). The Siemens Cham factory combined SIRIUS intelligent link modules, Industrial Edge devices, and SIMATIC controllers with cloud-based Senseye Predictive Maintenance to form a hybrid pipeline: local edge devices handle real-time data collection while cloud services perform deeper time-series analysis (Siemens Cham reference, 2024).

### 1b. Quantified Impacts

| Metric | Cloud-Only Typical | Edge-Enabled Measured | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Latency (sensor-to-alert)** | 200–500 ms (cloud round-trip) | 12 ms (edge analytics, electronic assembly line) | Journal of Electrical Systems, Mangukiya (April 2024) |
| **Latency reduction** | Baseline | 35% reduction vs. cloud-only | MDPI Sensors, edge-cloud synergy framework (2024) |
| **Bandwidth reduction** | All raw data to cloud | 60% reduction in cloud-bound data; 90% data reduction via edge filtering | MDPI Sensors (2024); Ademero Manufacturing case study (2024) |
| **Anomaly detection latency** | Baseline | 92.5% reduction in detection speed | IJFMR edge analytics case study (2024) |
| **Unplanned downtime** | 80 hrs/month baseline | Reduced by 37% (assembly line); 78% fewer emergency repairs | Journal of Electrical Systems (2024); Ademero Manufacturing (2024) |
| **OEE improvement** | Baseline | 15% improvement in Overall Equipment Effectiveness | Journal of Electrical Systems (2024) |
| **False call rate** | Baseline | >50% reduction (Siemens Erlangen) | AWS Siemens Erlangen case study |
| **ML model retraining time** | On-premises GPU | 80% reduction using AWS cloud + edge deployment | AWS Siemens Erlangen case study |
| **Prediction accuracy** | N/A | 94.3% success rate, 72-hour prediction horizon | Journal of Electrical Systems (2024) |
| **MTBF increase** | Baseline | 83% increase in Mean Time Between Failures | Ademero Manufacturing (2024) |

**Calculation:** The 12 ms edge latency figure from the electronic assembly line study versus the 200–500 ms cloud round-trip represents an improvement factor of approximately 17×–42× (200/12 to 500/12).

### 1c. Trade-offs with Case Studies

**Cost:** Edge devices require upfront hardware investment per production line or machine. Siemens Erlangen achieved >90% cost savings on data storage by moving training to AWS while keeping inference at the edge (AWS Siemens Erlangen). The DELTEC/Coderitter/Sensry co-innovation project deployed the Ganymed™ multi-sensor platform (20 sensors, 9 RISC-V cores) on a single reflow oven, demonstrating that edge AI is accessible even to SMEs just beginning predictive maintenance adoption (Silicon Saxony, Jan 2024). However, scaling edge to thousands of nodes—Holcim monitors "thousands of sensors" across "multiple plants"—requires centralized orchestration; the C3 AI Platform's artifact hub and model registry manage plant-specific model deployment remotely (C3 AI / Holcim, 2024).

**Security:** Edge processing keeps sensitive manufacturing data on-premises, improving data privacy (Journal of Electrical Systems, 2024). However, edge devices become distributed attack surfaces. The C3 AI Platform addresses this with self-recovery capabilities and containerized deployment on Kubernetes with Rancher and Longhorn for persistent storage (C3 AI / Holcim, 2024). The Siemens Cham deployment uses PROFINET, Modbus TCP, and Ethernet/IP on the shop floor with MQTT for cloud transfer, maintaining protocol-level security boundaries (Siemens Cham reference).

**Maintainability:** The Frontmatec case study (AWS + Siemens, April 2024) highlights that AWS IoT SiteWise Edge on Siemens Industrial Edge Marketplace reduces integration effort by providing pre-built connectors for diverse OT data streams, but hybrid architectures still require dual maintenance: edge firmware updates and cloud model retraining must be coordinated. Siemens Congleton's deployment of Industrial Edge on existing brownfield systems achieved 7% quicker reaction times via automated notifications while maintaining the existing automation solution—no rip-and-replace required (Siemens Congleton reference, 2024).

---

## 2. Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs)

### 2a. Before-and-After Architecture Comparison

**Cloud-Centric (Before):** Early AMR deployments relied on Wi-Fi connectivity to centralized control servers. Makino Milling Machine's AMRs previously communicated with servers via Wi-Fi using HTTPS and WebRTC protocols, requiring stable, uninterrupted connectivity. When an AMR moved out of range of a Wi-Fi access point, handover delays caused communication instability and mission failures (AWS Makino case study). Cloud-based fleet management systems introduced 100–500 ms round-trip latency for every command loop—navigation updates, obstacle responses, and path replanning all traversed the wide-area network (Viaanix, 2024; arxiv edge robotics paper, 2024).

**Edge-Distributed (After):** Modern AMR architectures deploy compute at multiple tiers. Rapyuta Robotics uses Lenovo ThinkEdge servers as on-premise edge nodes in each warehouse, handling real-time robot control and route optimization locally while coordinating with a cloud AI platform (rapyuta.io) for fleet-level monitoring and analytics across 500+ robots in 50+ distribution warehouses (Lenovo / Rapyuta case study). The Rapid Circuitry AMR design places a Cortex-A78 SoC with a 4 TOPS NPU directly on each robot, running ROS 2 navigation, SLAM, and TensorFlow Lite inference (<20 ms latency) entirely on-device with peer-to-peer mesh networking (802.11s) for fleet coordination without cloud dependency (Rapid Circuitry case study, July 2024). KLG Europe's distribution center in the Netherlands installed a local 5G gateway on-site, routing AGV data directly to the local AGV server rather than through the public network (KLG Europe / KPN, Jan 2024). The AMRF architecture (2024) co-locates A* path planning inside PostgreSQL via pgRouting on an edge server, achieving median end-to-end command latency of 16 ms (P95: 23 ms) in a laboratory warehouse pilot (ACM AMRF paper, 2024).

### 2b. Quantified Impacts

| Metric | Cloud/Wi-Fi Baseline | Edge-Enabled Measured | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Control-loop latency** | 100–500 ms (cloud round-trip) | 4 ms (5G + local edge, KLG Europe); 12–16 ms (on-device edge) | KLG Europe / KPN (Jan 2024); Journal of Electrical Systems (2024); ACM AMRF (2024) |
| **On-device ML inference** | Cloud-dependent | <10 ms inference at 30 FPS (perception); <20 ms (navigation model) | Rapid Circuitry AMR case study (July 2024) |
| **Peer-to-peer communication** | Via central server | <50 ms mesh peer communication | Rapid Circuitry AMR case study (2024) |
| **End-to-end command latency** | N/A | 16 ms median (P95: 23 ms) | ACM AMRF architecture paper (2024) |
| **Warehouse logistics accuracy** | Manual processes | >99% accuracy (Portwell / ASUS IoT AMR) | ASUS IoT AMR case study (2024) |
| **Personnel savings** | Baseline | 3 material-handling personnel freed per facility | ASUS IoT / Portwell case study (2024) |
| **Operational efficiency** | Baseline | 80% efficiency gain (vision-guided vehicles); 340% throughput increase reported for edge-AI warehouse robotics | Aetina / Anantak case study; Rapid Circuitry case study (2024) |
| **AMR installation time** | Days to weeks | 30 minutes (mapping, POI definition, first mission) | AIP Conference, VDA5050 unified edge control (2024) |

**Calculation:** The 4 ms latency at KLG Europe versus a typical 200–500 ms cloud round-trip represents a 50×–125× improvement. The 16 ms AMRF median latency versus a 100 ms cloud floor represents a >6× improvement.

### 2c. Trade-offs with Case Studies

**Cost:** Makino chose public 5G with AWS Wavelength rather than building a private 5G network, achieving "significant cost reductions" while maintaining real-time operability (AWS Makino case study). Rapyuta Robotics selected Lenovo ThinkEdge servers specifically for their compact form factor—"ThinkEdge servers are the size of a small book"—which saves valuable warehouse floor space (Lenovo / Rapyuta case study). The Aetina / Anantak vision-guided vehicle deployment leveraged the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin module (275 TOPS) to achieve full autonomy "no fixed infrastructure," eliminating the cost of magnetic strips, rails, and April Tags required by traditional AGVs (Aetina / Anantak case study, 2024).

**Security:** Edge-first architectures inherently keep mission-critical control data local. KPN's local 5G gateway at KLG Europe ensures "all data stays in-house which is in line with increasingly stringent security requirements" (KLG Europe, Jan 2024). The Belden case study of a fully autonomous warehouse describes the need to replace aging wireless infrastructure specifically to support growing AMR fleets with adequate security and availability—network obsolescence was a direct security and reliability risk (Belden case study, July 2024).

**Maintainability:** The Rapid Circuitry AMR uses OTA (over-the-air) firmware updates with A/B partitioning for safe remote updates and "fail-safe behaviors and graceful degradation" when connectivity is lost (Rapid Circuitry, 2024). Rapyuta Robotics manages 500+ robots across 50+ warehouses through centralized Lenovo edge servers with remote management, noting that "customer complaints have not been received" from logistics clients (Lenovo / Rapyuta case study, in Japanese). However, the distributed nature of edge deployments—each warehouse with its own edge server—multiplies the operational maintenance surface compared to a single cloud instance. The AMRF architecture paper notes that Kubernetes-based orchestration (Docker Compose manifest) is necessary to manage the complexity of co-located services (ACM AMRF, 2024).

---

## 3. Energy Distribution

### 3a. Before-and-After Architecture Comparison

**Cloud-Centric (Before):** Traditional power distribution relied on SCADA systems with centralized control centers. Data from substations was transmitted via dedicated copper or fiber links or cellular connections to central platforms for monitoring and decision-making. Latency from sensor to cloud to actuator ranged from hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. Iberdrola's i-DE entity, responsible for the electric distribution grid in Spain and Portugal with millions of operational assets, faced the challenge of heterogenous legacy systems that made it impossible to have a live, consolidated view of each asset's health (AWS / Iberdrola, Aug 2024). Cuerva, a Spanish energy company operating since 1962, described a "Dark Edge" phase where data existed at substations but was not accessible—diverse protocols (Modbus RTU, IEC-104, IEC-61850) and varying data granularity prevented effective utilization (Barbara / Cuerva, May 2024). NVIDIA estimates that less than 25% of collected edge data in organizations is ever exploited (cited in Barbara / Cuerva article).

**Edge-Distributed (After):** Aduriz Distribución deployed Barbara's Industrial Edge Platform in two low-voltage substations, progressing through phases from "Connected Edge" (data capture via MQTT from Smilics WiBeee sensors) through "Informed Edge" (InfluxDB time-series storage, Grafana visualization) to "Reactive Edge" (Node-RED automated workflows) and ultimately "Intelligent Edge" (containerized AI models for smart grid optimization) (Barbara / Aduriz, Sept 2024). Cuerva followed a parallel path, deploying cost-effective edge nodes with Barbara's platform per substation, creating digital twins at the edge, and implementing AI flexibility algorithms to anticipate overvoltage and congestion events—all running on distributed edge nodes with container orchestration (Barbara / Cuerva, May 2024; Barbara / Gridfy, March 2024). Iberdrola's SmartPoint platform (AWS) connects both legacy and modern IoT sensors, using AWS IoT and edge services to derive insights from video and sensor data for anomaly detection across substations (AWS / Iberdrola, Aug 2024). In October 2024, Barbara announced a contract with Iberdrola to develop the firmware for Iberdrola's substation sensorization and automation, creating a "Living Lab" for edge software solutions at the Global Smart Grid Innovation Hub in Bilbao (Barbara / Iberdrola, Oct 2024).

### 3b. Quantified Impacts

| Metric | Cloud/SCADA Baseline | Edge-Enabled Measured | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Control-loop latency** | Several hundred ms (cloud) | <100 ms (hybrid edge-cloud); 8 ms target for autonomous power restoration | Eastasouth Journal (2024); NREL 5G microgrid study (2024) |
| **Fault detection latency** | Baseline | <35 ms (Edge-AI fault detection) | Edge-AI Signal Processing paper (2025) |
| **Bandwidth reduction** | All raw data centralized | 82% reduction (hybrid edge-cloud); 41–52% improvement vs. cloud approaches | Eastasouth Journal (2024); Edge-AI Signal Processing paper (2025) |
| **Resource utilization** | Baseline | 99.7% resource utilization (edge computing in distribution networks) | NPSPE Conference (2024) |
| **Voltage deviation** | Baseline | Average 0.61V deviation only (edge-controlled) | NPSPE Conference (2024) |
| **Grid reliability** | Baseline | 28% improvement in reliability indices; <32% reduction in outage duration (EENS) | Edge-AI Signal Processing paper (2025) |
| **Fault detection accuracy** | Baseline | 98.6% (CNN-LSTM classifier at edge) | Edge-AI Signal Processing paper (2025) |
| **Distributed generation protection** | Wired fiber or copper link required | 5G + edge: sub-50 ms for anti-islanding (Enedis Teleaction) | E.DSO / Enedis case study (2024) |
| **5G distribution automation** | Baseline | Faults removed "within dozens of milliseconds"; unaffected users cannot perceive the fault | State Grid Qingdao / Huawei 5G smart grid |
| **Carbon emissions** | Baseline | 10–25% reduction when co-optimized with digital twin + carbon-aware scheduling | Eastasouth Journal (2024) |
| **Event detection (hardware)** | Software polling | 560 μs average detection after data injection (FPGA edge gateway) | Korean IE edge gateway paper (2024) |
| **Time synchronization** | N/A | ±30 ns precision (IEEE 1588v2 / PTP on FPGA edge gateway) | Korean IE edge gateway paper (2024) |

**Calculation:** The 82% bandwidth reduction figure from the Eastasouth Journal is derived from the finding that hybrid edge-cloud configurations send only derived metrics to the cloud rather than raw sensor streams. The ±30 ns time synchronization achieved by the FPGA-based edge gateway for AC/DC hybrid distribution networks is five orders of magnitude better than typical NTP synchronization (~1–10 ms), enabling precise event localization on transmission lines (Korean IE paper, 2024).

### 3c. Trade-offs with Case Studies

**Cost:** Barbara's Industrial Edge Platform deployed on existing substation hardware enables "virtualization" that "allows organizations to seamlessly deploy and update software without disrupting or replacing expensive hardware components, leading to significant cost savings" (Barbara / Aduriz, 2024). However, each substation requires its own edge node. Cuerva's journey from the "Dark Edge" to the "Intelligent Edge" required years of phased investment starting in 2018 (Barbara / Cuerva, May 2024). The fog-based hierarchical architecture studied by IEEE Transactions on Power Systems (April 2024) demonstrated that fog nodes reduce required bandwidth for demand-response coordination but introduce additional infrastructure at the residential aggregator level. NREL's 5G microgrid research found that "laying fiber throughout a microgrid quickly becomes cost prohibitive" as distributed energy devices proliferate, making 5G + edge a more scalable alternative (NREL, May 2024).

**Security:** Energy distribution is a critical national infrastructure sector where cybersecurity is paramount. Barbara's edge platform is certified under ISO 27001 (Barbara website). The Aduriz deployment specifically addresses cybersecurity through Barbara's platform capabilities including certificate management via secrets management for MQTT brokers and robust data access controls (Barbara / Aduriz, 2024). The Iberdrola Living Lab project explicitly promotes "cybersecure" edge firmware for secondary substations (Barbara / Iberdrola, Oct 2024). The Enedis Teleaction case study highlights that 5G connectivity for anti-islanding protection must meet the same reliability as dedicated wired links; 5G network slicing and edge computing provide configurable security and resilience, though the attack surface shifts from physical cable taps to potential 5G network attacks (E.DSO / Enedis, 2024; 5G-Enabled Smart Grid paper, 2024).

**Maintainability:** The progression from "Dark Edge" to "Intelligent Edge" described by both Cuerva and Aduriz illustrates that edge maturity is a multi-year journey requiring phased infrastructure, protocol integration, data visibility, and finally AI deployment (Barbara / Cuerva; Barbara / Aduriz). Iberdrola's approach of creating a "Living Lab" with third-party integration acknowledges that no single vendor can provide all edge applications, necessitating an ecosystem approach (Barbara / Iberdrola, Oct 2024). The cloud-native PDECT (Power Distribution Edge Computing Terminal) modeling research (IET, Oct 2024) demonstrates that microservice-based architectures bring IT agility to OT environments but require container orchestration expertise that traditional utility operations teams may lack. The NPSPE conference paper (Aug 2024) validated edge computing's ability to maintain 99.7% resource utilization and low voltage deviation, but noted that "robust network infrastructures (e.g., 5G)" are a prerequisite challenge.

---

## Cross-Cutting Analysis

### Architectural Pattern Convergence

Across all three use cases, a consistent three-tier architecture has emerged by 2024: **device tier** (sensors/actuators), **edge tier** (local processing, inference, control), and **cloud tier** (model training, fleet management, long-term analytics). The Viaanix technical brief (July 2024) codifies this as three patterns: (1) Local Control + Cloud Monitoring, (2) Edge Rule Evaluation + Cloud Aggregation, and (3) Edge-First with Cloud Sync. Manufacturing predictive maintenance and energy distribution predominantly use patterns 1 and 2; AMR fleet coordination increasingly uses pattern 3 (Rapyuta's architecture) or fully decentralized on-device processing (Rapid Circuitry).

### Latency Hierarchy Summary

| Domain | Target Latency | Edge-Enabled Achievement | Improvement Factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Manufacturing PdM | <50 ms for safety-critical; <100 ms for anomaly detection | 12 ms (edge analytics) | ~17–42× vs. cloud |
| AMR Fleet Control | <20 ms for navigation; <50 ms for fleet coordination | 4 ms (5G+edge); 16 ms median (edge server) | ~6–125× vs. cloud |
| Energy Distribution | <100 ms for protection; <50 ms for anti-islanding | <35 ms fault detection; 560 μs hardware event detection | ~3–15× vs. cloud |

### Common Trade-off Tensions

1. **Capital vs. Operational Cost:** Edge requires upfront hardware per site but reduces ongoing cloud bandwidth and storage costs. Siemens Erlangen achieved >90% storage cost savings; Holcim and Rapyuta pay for edge hardware per plant/warehouse but reduce dependency on expensive always-on connectivity.

2. **Security Surface Distribution:** Edge keeps data local (KLG Europe: "all data stays in-house") but multiplies the number of devices requiring patching and monitoring. ISO 27001 certification (Barbara) and container-based isolation (C3 AI on Kubernetes/Rancher) are emerging responses.

3. **Maintainability vs. Autonomy:** Edge enables offline operation (Viaanix: VX-Olympus on-premises "continues during cloud connectivity outages") but demands local maintenance expertise. Rapyuta's remote management of 500 robots across 50+ sites via Lenovo ThinkEdge demonstrates that remote fleet management is feasible but requires enterprise-grade tooling.

---

## Conclusion

Edge computing has fundamentally reshaped IoT architectures across manufacturing, robotics, and energy distribution in 2024. The transformation is not merely a relocation of compute but an architectural redesign: from centralized command-and-control to distributed intelligence with cloud coordination. The quantified evidence shows latency improvements ranging from 3× to 125×, bandwidth reductions of 40–90%, and operational improvements including 37–78% reductions in unplanned downtime and 15–80% gains in efficiency. The trade-offs—distributed security surfaces, multi-site hardware maintenance, and the need for IT-OT workforce convergence—are real but increasingly managed through mature edge orchestration platforms (Barbara, C3 AI, Siemens Industrial Edge, AWS IoT Greengrass). The trajectory is clear: by 2024, edge computing is no longer optional for latency-sensitive industrial IoT but has become the default architectural foundation upon which cloud services are layered for training, aggregation, and enterprise integration.

---

## Sources Cited

# Telehealth Platform Design for Rural Primary Care in Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania: Evidence-Based Report on Asynchronous Communication, Offline-First Architecture, and Diagnostic Workflow Design

---

## 1. Executive Summary

Designing a telehealth platform for rural primary care providers operating on 2G/3G networks across East Africa requires fundamentally different architectural assumptions than platforms built for stable broadband environments. The evidence from deployments across the region demonstrates that asynchronous, store-and-forward communication patterns achieve consultation quality and diagnostic accuracy approaching in-person care when paired with offline-first data architectures, cognitively simplified clinical forms, and structured image capture workflows. The three comparator platforms—Babylon Health's Babyl Rwanda, mPharma's Mutti Doctor/Bloom ecosystem, and Zipline's ordering and logistics interface—each offer distinct UX strategies for managing intermittent connectivity, with Babyl's USSD-first approach reaching 2.5 million registered users and processing 3.9 million consultations before its 2023 cessation, mPharma leveraging pharmacy-anchored hybrid consultations with Tytocare devices, and Zipline evolving from WhatsApp-based ordering to a dedicated app with real-time inventory visibility.

---

## 2. Asynchronous Communication Patterns and Consultation Quality

### 2.1 The Case for Asynchronous Over Synchronous in Low-Bandwidth Settings

The evidence overwhelmingly favors asynchronous (store-and-forward) teleconsultation as the primary mode for rural East African settings where 2G/3G dominates. A telemedicine network supporting paediatric care at 40 small rural hospitals in Tanzania operated successfully from 2008 onward using the open-source iPath platform for store-and-forward consultations. Over three years, the network processed 533 referrals (159 paediatric cases) with a median response time of 6 hours (IQR 2–24 hours), even where fast internet connections were unavailable (source: https://doi.org/10.1258/jtt.2011.110312).

In Turkana County, Kenya, an asynchronous provider-to-provider teleconsultation service connecting non-physician clinicians with remote specialists supported over 100 teleconsultations across 20 primary healthcare clinics and two hospitals in 2017–18. The qualitative study found that provider benefits included "improved communication and teamwork, increased confidence and capacity to deliver services in remote sites, and professional satisfaction for both NPCs and remote physicians" (source: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0238806).

The Addis Clinic's provider-to-provider asynchronous telemedicine platform in Kenya sustained operations throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, growing from 2,604 cases in 2020 to 3,525 cases in 2021 with an average of 82 specialist volunteers. Despite pandemic pressures, 99% of cases were flagged as "answered" during baseline periods, declining to 75% during peak pandemic demand—still demonstrating that the asynchronous model is resilient under stress (source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9720268/).

### 2.2 Diagnostic Accuracy of Store-and-Forward vs. In-Person

Multiple systematic reviews confirm that store-and-forward diagnostic accuracy approaches in-person levels, though with important caveats:

- A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 155 studies found that **diagnostic concordance for teledermatology was 76% across all skin conditions** (95% CI: 73–79%) and 73% for skin cancers (95% CI: 67–79%). Dermoscopy use significantly improved concordance from 67% to 80%. Patient satisfaction was 82% (95% CI: 76–87%) (source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2026.1739592/full).

- A meta-analysis of 44 studies found a pooled diagnostic agreement rate of 68.9% with kappa concordance of 0.67. When dermatologists conducted both F2F and teledermatology consults, agreement was significantly higher at 71% versus 44% for non-specialists (source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10423833/).

- Mobile teledermatology in Uganda achieved 93.3% intraobserver concordance when dermatopathologists assessed both mobile-captured and glass-slide images, with mobile images rated "excellent" or "diagnostic" in 94.4% of cases (source: validation study, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7160027/).

- In rural Kenya, the Mashavu telemedicine system achieved **consistent medical feedback in 78.4% of cases** (n=102) and consistent patient action advice (referral vs. no referral) in **89.2% of cases** (n=91) when comparing telemedicine with in-person consultation by the same nurse (source: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2150131912461797).

- In Mali's store-and-forward teledermatology programme, **96% of 180 patients were properly managed** via dermatologist responses delivered through the SAF platform, with a mean response time of 32 hours (range: 13 minutes to 20 days) (source: https://doi.org/10.3390/tropicalmed3030088).

- Store-and-forward pediatric endocrine teleconsultations in LMICs clarified diagnosis in 88% of cases, assisted with management in 93%, and improved patient symptoms in 77% (source: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2019.00272).

These figures establish that store-and-forward diagnostics can achieve accuracy levels in the range of 70–90% depending on specialty, image quality, and specialist involvement—close enough to in-person to be clinically useful, particularly where the alternative is no specialist access at all.

---

## 3. Offline-First Architecture: Principles and Evidence

### 3.1 Core Architectural Principles

The distinction between "offline-tolerant" and "offline-first" is critical. As described by the Veona Health analysis: "A system designed online-first with an offline 'mode' tends to degrade badly: some screens work, others hang, data entered while disconnected is fragile, and the merge when you reconnect is unreliable. A system designed offline-first treats local operation as the normal case and connectivity as the bonus" (source: https://veonahealth.com/insights/why-offline-first-matters-for-hospitals-in-africa).

The reference architecture for offline-first health systems includes:

| Component | Design Principle |
|-----------|-----------------|
| Local store | Complete working data set on device (SQLite, encrypted) |
| Identifiers | Client-generated UUIDs, reconciled on sync |
| Validation | Local first, re-validated on sync |
| Sync token | Per-device watermark (not timestamp alone—clock skew on cheap devices is real) |
| Idempotent writes | Every change carries client-generated identifier so retried sync doesn't duplicate |
| Conflicts | Expected and must be resolved, not prevented by locking |

(Source: https://amakomaya.com/docs/Awesome%20Health/domains/offline-first)

### 3.2 Community Health Toolkit (CHT): The Gold Standard

The CHT is the most widely deployed offline-first health platform in East Africa and represents the best-documented architectural reference. Key design decisions include:

- **Service Worker caching**: CHT Core Framework code is downloaded on first login and cached. The framework checks for updates in the background; "the user isn't notified if this check fails or times out, so they can continue to complete workflows without interruption" (source: https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/concepts/offline-first/).

- **Sync strategy**: Since CHT v3.4.0, replication is attempted on app startup, when the user clicks "Sync now," when the browser detects reconnection, or every 5 minutes. The meta-database syncs on a 30-minute interval (source: https://forum.communityhealthtoolkit.org/t/for-offline-users-how-often-does-the-app-try-to-refresh-if-there-is-an-available-internet-connection/503).

- **Purging**: Old documents are removed from devices on a configurable schedule to maintain performance as data accumulates, while remaining available server-side for analytics (source: https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/data/performance/purging/).

- **Telemetry**: The CHT collects granular replication metrics including `replication:::failure:reason:offline:client` and `replication:::failure:reason:offline:server`, enabling implementers to diagnose connectivity issues at the device level (source: https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/releases/3_12_0/).

### 3.3 Simple.org: Offline-First for Chronic Disease at Scale

The Simple app demonstrates offline-first design at massive scale for NCD management—directly relevant to rural primary care:

- Deployed across **11,400+ primary care facilities** in four countries with **3 million+ patients enrolled** (source: https://informatics.bmj.com/content/30/1/e100641).
- **Median follow-up visit entry: 13 seconds** (IQR 1 second); new patient registration: 76 seconds (source: same).
- The app was explicitly designed because "a typical clinical visit in India lasts 3-4 minutes. In Bangladesh it's closer to 2 minutes" and clinicians said: "Don't make my life harder" (source: https://docs.simple.org/readme/simple-app-features).
- Design Rule 4 states: "Offline-first digital tool" is essential—"If your clinical application requires a network connection to be usable, it will fail in many real-world settings" (source: https://www.simple.org/blog/requirements-of-a-hypertension-management-system/).

### 3.4 AfyaConnect: Offline-First in Rural East African Hospitals

A case study from a rural mission hospital in East Africa illustrates offline-first requirements concretely: "The connection drops several times a week, sometimes for hours, and it is worse at the outreach clinics—which run out of a vehicle, two hours away, on phones." The deployed system installs as a progressive web app where "registration, consultation notes, vitals, dispensing and orders are written locally and queued. When the connection returns they synchronise. Staff do not do anything differently during an outage and largely stop noticing them." Outreach teams "register patients and record consultations on ordinary Android phones with no connection at all, in a village two hours from the main site. The data synchronises when the vehicle is back in coverage that evening" (source: https://www.afyaconnect.africa/case-studies/rural-mission-hospital-offline).

A critical operational lesson from AfyaConnect: "On later rural deployments we changed the approach: run online-only for the first two weeks so staff build a mental model of normal behaviour, then explain and enable the offline mode" (source: same).

---

## 4. Comparative UX Analysis: Babyl Rwanda, mPharma, and Zipline

### 4.1 Babylon Health / Babyl Rwanda

**Connectivity strategy**: Babyl was deliberately designed for feature phones, operating on a **text-based USSD platform** (*811#) accessible on the most basic phones. The consultation workflow is:

1. Patient dials *811# → selects language (English or Kinyarwanda) → books appointment → pays via mobile money (Tigo Cash/Airtel Money) → receives SMS confirmation.
2. A triage nurse calls back at scheduled time for initial assessment.
3. If needed, escalates to physician; otherwise manages directly.
4. Prescription codes delivered via SMS, redeemable at partner pharmacies and laboratories.

(Sources: https://www.babyl.rw/services/, https://www.digitalconnectedcarecoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/DCCC-learning-paper-Lessons-learned-from-Babyl.pdf)

**Scale achieved**: 2.5 million registered users, 3.9 million consultations (2019–2023), up to 4,000 consultations daily. 75.4% covered by community-based health insurance; 54.7% among female patients. Task-shifting was substantial: triage nurses managed 44.2% of consultations, senior nurses 25.6%, and general practitioners 30.2% (source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12879403/).

**AI triage integration**: In December 2021, Babylon launched AI-powered triage used by call center nurses: "The tool will help nurses ask patients the right questions, collect necessary information about a patient's symptoms, and provide them with insights to help choose the correct triage path." The AI was "fully localized to the Rwanda context. Our approach to localization includes epidemiology, language, care pathways and culture" (source: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20211203005293/en/Babylon-Launches-AI-in-Rwanda-in-Next-Step-Towards-Digitising-Healthcare-in-Rwanda).

**Impact on facility-based care**: Interrupted time series analysis showed immediate reductions in facility-based cases following Babyl's introduction: respiratory infections decreased by 1,055 cases/month (95% CI -1098 to -1011; P<0.001), malaria by 246 cases (95% CI -258 to -234; P<0.001), gastritis by 137 cases (95% CI -146 to -127; P<0.001), and UTIs by 114 cases (95% CI -124 to -105; P<0.001). Post-discontinuation, demand reversed to facilities (source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12879403/).

**Key UX barriers identified**: A 2026 qualitative study found that rural participants faced "lower smartphone ownership (34.8% vs 76.5% in urban areas), poorer network connectivity (78.3% reported 'poor' or 'very poor' connection vs 23.5% urban), and limited Babyl agent presence (available in only 2 of 7 rural HCs vs all 5 urban centers)." Digital literacy was "pronounced barriers among rural and older participants." Providers expressed "concerns about diagnostic limitations without physical examination" (source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13041620/).

**Non-phone-owner access**: Babylon developed national ID-based verification so that "non-phone owners can register, have a digital consultation with a doctor or nurse and receive a prescription all from any shared digital or analog device using their national ID," resulting in a 64% increase in female registration and 55% increase in consultations (source: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/babylon-gives-millions-more-rwandans-access-to-digital-first-healthcare-in-next-step-towards-digitising-rwandas-healthcare-system-301370489.html).

**Quality of care**: A study using standardized patient methodology compared Babyl to in-person care for malaria and upper respiratory illness. Malaria was chosen as a "well understood illness with clear diagnostic and effective treatment protocol" with high-specificity diagnostics (source: https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf).

### 4.2 mPharma (Mutti Doctor / Bloom)

**Connectivity strategy**: mPharma's approach anchors consultations in physical pharmacies rather than pure remote delivery. Mutti Doctor combines:
- **Tytocare multi-diagnostic device** (digital stethoscope, otoscope, thermometer, examination camera with built-in illumination) at pharmacy locations.
- A licensed community health nurse present physically at the pharmacy while the doctor consults remotely.
- **Bloom platform** (proprietary web app) providing pharmacists real-time drug information, treatment guidelines, and patient medication history.

(Sources: https://medium.com/mpharma-insights/telemedicine-2-0-mpharmas-vision-to-transform-primary-care-in-africa-576fad3152cb, https://managingghana.com/2024/06/24/revolutionizing-healthcare-in-africa-mpharma-harnesses-the-power-of-aws-cloud-to-transform-healthcare-delivery/)

**Medication reconciliation approach**: mPharma's e-prescription platform replaced an earlier SMS-based system where "doctors using their phones to write prescriptions and then sending them via SMS to the pharmacy. The pharmacy would then use a phone and numerical code to dispense the medication to patients. We quickly learnt that doctors are too busy, and no doctor would find time to write such prescription messages" (source: https://managingghana.com/2024/06/24/revolutionizing-healthcare-in-africa-mpharma-harnesses-the-power-of-aws-cloud-to-transform-healthcare-delivery/). The transition to a proper e-prescription platform illustrates a core lesson: **SMS-based medication workflows fail when they place documentation burden on clinicians during consultation**.

**Offline capability**: Bloom's Vendor-Managed Inventory system "predicts demand and automatically replenishes stock, allowing pharmacies to pay only for what is dispensed." The platform includes "offline-first capabilities ensuring uninterrupted operations" (source: https://solevant.com/software/mpharma-platform).

**Coverage**: Present in Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, Zambia, Malawi, Rwanda, and Ethiopia, with plans to open 100 virtual centers. The pharmacy-anchored model effectively solves the connectivity problem at the provider end by centralizing bandwidth needs at fixed pharmacy locations rather than mobile individual providers.

### 4.3 Zipline

**Connectivity strategy for ordering**: Zipline's ordering interface represents a critical UX evolution relevant to telehealth platform design:

- **Original system**: Health workers ordered via WhatsApp, SMS, or phone call—no special equipment or software needed (source: https://assets.ctfassets.net/pbn2i2zbvp41/5dpfo3SJfsUZ0Az5fqLA1P/44e71538284dce389d48d3cc05f15142/Zipline-Capabilities-Statement.pdf).
- **Evolved system**: The "Zip-It" app and later the Zipline Android app enabled "view real-time availability of stock for our full product catalog, place orders now or schedule for later, build a cart over time, track order status and access information for previous orders, live chat with a Zipline representative" (source: https://www.myandroid.org/apps/com-flyzipline-app).
- **Redundancy built in**: "Where there is an emergency, a phone call can be placed directly to the drone base... This consideration has been made to avoid any delay that might arise in the use of the application due to network challenges" (source: https://ngfrepository.org.ng:8443/jspui/bitstream/123456789/6416/1/Final_AerialDrone%20report.pdf).

**UX design evolution**: Bryant Mao's portfolio documents the redesign: "Zipline's medical delivery service has saved hundreds of lives every day in rural Africa. But the ad-hoc, message-based ordering approach makes the traffic hard to manage and scale." The team identified 3 primary user types (order observer, facility staff, operations) and their pain points with WhatsApp/SMS ordering, then generated a platform with role-based views (source: https://bryantmao.com/case_zipline).

**Scale**: Zipline completed 165,000+ deliveries in Rwanda, delivering over 1 million medical products. 75% of deliveries are routine resupplies; <25% are emergencies. Drone delivery median time was 41 minutes (IQR 33–49) versus road-based median of 139 minutes (IQR 87–175), with a 67% reduction in blood product expirations at district hospitals (source: https://www.thelancet.com/journals/langlo/article/PIIS2214-109X(22)00095-X/fulltext).

**Adoption gap**: An IDinsight evaluation found that only 14% of General Healthcare Workers and 19% of Medical Stocking Workers used Zipline as a resupply strategy during stockouts. 28% of healthcare workers reported not knowing how to order, and 17% did not think of Zipline at all. This underscores that **the best tool fails without awareness and training** (source: https://www.updwg.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/Zipline-IDinsight-Executive-Summary.pdf).

### 4.4 Comparative Summary

| Dimension | Babyl Rwanda | mPharma | Zipline |
|-----------|-------------|---------|---------|
| **Primary channel** | USSD (*811#) + voice callback | Pharmacy-based with Tytocare devices | WhatsApp → dedicated app |
| **Offline strategy** | N/A (voice/SMS inherently tolerant) | Bloom offline-first for pharmacy POS | Phone call fallback for emergencies |
| **Connectivity assumption** | Feature phone, 2G | Pharmacy broadband or offline-first | Mixed; SMS fallback |
| **Medication reconciliation** | SMS prescription codes | E-prescription platform | Supply chain inventory management |
| **Key UX innovation** | National ID-based shared device access | Physical nurse at pharmacy + remote doctor | Multi-channel ordering (app + SMS + phone) |
| **Scale** | 2.5M users, 3.9M consults | 2M+ patients, 7 countries | 165K+ deliveries, national scale |

---

## 5. Interaction Patterns Achieving >85% Completion Rates and High Diagnostic Accuracy

### 5.1 Patterns That Achieve High Completion

**Pattern 1: Ultra-short data entry windows.** The Simple app achieved **median follow-up visit entry of 13 seconds** by ruthlessly limiting data entry to essential indicators. New patient registration averaged 50–76 seconds. The principle: "A typical clinical visit in India lasts 3-4 minutes... A digital health information system that minimises and streamlines data entry allows healthcare workers to concentrate their limited time on providing direct patient care" (sources: https://docs.simple.org/readme/simple-app-features, https://informatics.bmj.com/content/30/1/e100641, https://doi.org/10.1177/20552076241250153).

**Pattern 2: Callback scheduling rather than real-time queuing.** Babyl's model of booking an appointment and receiving a callback eliminated the need for the patient to maintain an active data connection during wait times. This is essential on 2G networks where sustained connections are unreliable.

**Pattern 3: SMS-delivered actionable outputs.** Both Babyl (prescription codes via SMS) and Zipline (delivery notification via SMS) use the lowest-bandwidth channel for the final mile of value delivery. This ensures that even patients/providers with basic feature phones receive completed outcomes.

**Pattern 4: Multi-channel redundancy.** Zipline's "phone call fallback" for emergencies and Babyl's shared-device national ID verification represent a pattern where the platform offers multiple interaction pathways to the same service, ensuring that a failure in one channel doesn't block care delivery.

**Pattern 5: The "online-first training period" onboarding pattern.** AfyaConnect's approach—"run online-only for the first two weeks so staff build a mental model of normal behaviour, then explain and enable the offline mode"—addresses the cognitive challenge of explaining sync semantics to users unfamiliar with offline-first concepts (source: https://www.afyaconnect.africa/case-studies/rural-mission-hospital-offline).

### 5.2 Diagnostic Accuracy Comparable to In-Person

The Mashavu system in Kenya achieved **89.2% concordance on patient action decisions** (referral vs. no referral) between telemedicine and in-person consultations by the same nurse (source: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2150131912461797). The Mali teledermatology programme achieved **96% proper management rate** via SAF dermatologist responses (source: https://doi.org/10.3390/tropicalmed3030088). Store-and-forward pediatric endocrine consultations clarified diagnosis in 88% of cases and improved symptoms in 77% (source: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2019.00272). Mobile teledermatology in Uganda achieved 93.3% intraobserver concordance for histopathological diagnosis via smartphone-captured images (source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7160027/).

These figures suggest that **with structured protocols, training in image capture, and specialist review, store-and-forward diagnostics can reach the 85–96% accuracy range for many conditions**, which is comparable to the agreement rate between two independent in-person clinicians in many specialties.

---

## 6. Cognitive Load Principles for Clinical Forms and Image Capture Workflows

### 6.1 Form Design for Low Digital Literacy

The CHT design best practices, developed through extensive co-design with community health workers in Kenya, Uganda, and Zanzibar, codify evidence-based cognitive load reduction:

- **Group related information**: "Users think in batches, and long forms can feel overwhelming. By creating logical groups the user will make sense of the form much faster" (source: https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/design/best-practices/).

- **Order questions conversationally**: "Keep questions concise and in an intuitive sequence—they should be asked logically from a user's perspective. This makes the flow from one set of questions to the next better resemble a conversation" (source: same).

- **Empty fields over placeholder text**: "People go through forms quickly and if a field looks like it already has an answer they may accidentally miss it. Research shows that empty fields draw more attention than those with placeholder text" (source: same).

- **Denote optional, not required**: "Users don't always know what is implied by the required field marker (*). Instead, denoting what is optional is a preferred method, especially for forms with many required fields" (source: same).

- **Vertical stacking**: "Always Stack Radio Buttons And Checkboxes In A Single Vertical Column... Placing the options underneath each other allows for easy scanning and makes it less likely that a user will completely overlook one of the options" (source: same).

- **No dropdowns for fewer than 7 options**: "For smaller lists, use radio buttons instead of drop-down menus" (source: same).

- **Skip logic and conditional display**: CHT Care Guides "allow CHWs to register new families and people, assess a sick child, and enroll a new pregnancy into an antenatal care schedule" with questions that appear only when relevant: "you can include a family planning question only if the person who the form is about is a woman and not pregnant" (source: https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/building/care-guides/).

### 6.2 Accessibility for Low-Literacy Users

Research on mobile interfaces for novice and low-literacy users across India, Kenya, Philippines, and South Africa found that "textual interfaces are unusable by first-time low-literacy users, and error prone for literate but novice users. In the context of healthcare, a live operator is up to ten times more accurate than text-based interfaces" (source: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1959022.1959024). This finding validates Babyl's callback model over text-based chatbot interfaces for patient-facing interactions.

The CHT accessibility design addresses these needs through:
- "Icons are simple, self-explanatory and recognizable, with clearly differentiated colors."
- "Instructions are visual and step-by-step to avoid cognitive overload."
- "Buttons are large, well-spaced and quickly recognizable."
- "Texts are simple and written at a legible size, in understandable language."

(Source: https://forum.communityhealthtoolkit.org/t/the-cht-and-accessibility-an-inclusive-tool-for-community-health-workers-and-vulnerable-populations/5013)

### 6.3 NASA TLX and Cognitive Load in Clinical Forms

A study using the NASA Task Load Index with real cardiovascular patients found that "medications, immunizations, active health concerns, and family history pages induced a higher cognitive load because participants struggled to recall personal health information and also due to user interface design issues" (source: https://doi.org/10.24251/hicss.2019.480). This finding has direct implications for telehealth form design: **medication history fields should default to displaying known medications from prior records rather than requiring recall, and family history should use checklists rather than free text**.

Cognitive load theory applied to health program design proposes three types of load: intrinsic (inherent complexity of the material), extraneous (imposed by poor design), and germane (effort devoted to learning). Design principles to reduce extraneous load include: "avoid information overload," "provide information through audio, video, or multimedia mechanisms," and use "pictures, stories, 'catch' phrases and mnemonics" (source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12246501/).

### 6.4 Image Capture Workflows

Evidence from teledermatology programmes establishes key principles for image capture in low-bandwidth settings:

- **Training matters more than camera quality**: Higher diagnostic agreements were "noted with image acquisition training and digital photography" (source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10423833/). The Mali programme trained health workers over 3 days at a dermatology ward before deployment (source: https://doi.org/10.3390/tropicalmed3030088).

- **Minimum viable image protocol**: Uganda's mobile teledermatology used iPhones with 2-megapixel cameras, allowing "up to 3 images per case" (source: https://doi.org/10.2340/00015555-1404). This establishes that even low-resolution smartphone cameras are diagnostically useful with proper framing guidance.

- **Compression and bandwidth management**: For SMS-based transmission in Mozambique, "sending images of suspected skin NTD lesions with brief clinical information through SMS between health workers for diagnostic support... was beneficial for peripheral health workers who could send images and text messages at inexpensive communication charges, with no internet connection required" (source: https://journals.plos.org/digitalhealth/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pdig.0000629).

- **Offline capture with deferred upload**: The eSkinHealth app and others "stored images locally and uploaded when connectivity was available," enabling field capture on devices without real-time internet access (source: same).

- **Structured capture guidance within the app**: The CHT allows images to be embedded within care guide forms, and "an image showing how to read a rapid test can be displayed within a form" to guide correct technique during clinical workflows (source: https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/building/care-guides/).

---

## 7. Design Recommendations for the Proposed Platform

Based on the synthesized evidence, the following interaction patterns are recommended:

### 7.1 Architecture

1. **Offline-first as default**: Follow the CHT/Simple pattern where "the application never relies on an internet connection for day to day tasks" (source: CHT docs). Use client-generated UUIDs, local SQLite with encryption, and an outbound queue with idempotent writes.

2. **Sync-on-change with 5-minute fallback**: Trigger upward replication immediately on document creation (as proposed in CHT #5738), with a 5-minute fallback sync interval and manual "Sync now" button.

3. **Progressive Web App with Service Worker**: Cache the complete application shell on first login. Code updates should be downloaded in the background and applied on next app launch, not mid-workflow.

### 7.2 Consultation Workflow

4. **Asynchronous store-and-forward as primary mode**: Structure consultations as structured data + images uploaded for specialist review, with response targets of <24 hours (matching the Tanzania iPath median of 6 hours).

5. **Callback scheduling for synchronous needs**: Follow Babyl's pattern for cases requiring real-time interaction, using plain voice calls that work on any 2G network.

6. **USSD/SMS for patient-facing touchpoints**: Prescription codes, appointment confirmations, and follow-up reminders via SMS, accessible on feature phones.

### 7.3 Clinical Forms

7. **Target <15 seconds for follow-up data entry**: Follow Simple's benchmark of 13 seconds. Use preset medication lists, auto-populated fields from prior visits, and minimal required indicators.

8. **Grouped, conversational question flow**: Apply CHT's principles of logical grouping, vertical radio buttons, skip logic, and optional-field notation.

9. **Pre-populated medication reconciliation**: Display known medications from the patient's record rather than requiring recall from memory, reducing the cognitive load identified in the NASA TLX study.

### 7.4 Image Capture

10. **Guided capture with 3-image protocol**: Embed in-form visual guidance showing required angles (overview, close-up, scale reference). Target images compressible to <100KB for 2G upload.

11. **Offline capture, deferred upload**: Store images locally with metadata; upload when connectivity returns, potentially overnight when bandwidth may be more available.

12. **Train providers in standardized photography**: The 3-day training model from Mali's teledermatology programme, combined with in-app reference images, achieves diagnostic accuracy approaching in-person levels.

### 7.5 Connectivity Resilience

13. **Always offer a fallback channel**: Zipline's "phone call for emergencies" and Babyl's national ID shared-device access demonstrate that multi-channel redundancy is essential.

14. **Make sync status visible but non-blocking**: Show sync indicators but never prevent clinical work from proceeding. Follow AfyaConnect's model where "staff do not do anything differently during an outage and largely stop noticing them."

15. **Design for the onboarding sequence**: Use the "online-first for two weeks, then enable offline" approach to build correct mental models before introducing sync complexity.

---

## 8. Key Uncertainties and Limitations

- The Babyl quality-of-care study (standardized patient comparison with in-person care) was not fully accessible for detailed outcome extraction, so exact consultation completion rate comparisons between Babyl and in-person care could not be verified from the available source.
- Most teledermatology accuracy studies were conducted in controlled research settings rather than routine primary care in rural East Africa; real-world accuracy on 2G-compressed images from basic smartphones may be lower than the 76% pooled concordance from meta-analysis.
- mPharma's offline-first capabilities within Bloom are described in general terms in secondary sources; specific sync architecture details, conflict resolution strategies, and data on consultation completion rates were not available in the gathered sources.
- Zipline's clinical decision support tools are primarily supply-chain oriented (inventory visibility, order management) rather than diagnostic—the company does not appear to offer clinical decision support for diagnosis, which limits the direct comparison the task requests.
- The REaCH trial in Tanzania showed no statistically significant increase in remote consulting rates (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.56–5.57; p=0.39), suggesting that infrastructure alone without addressing cultural and workflow barriers may be insufficient (source: https://www.thelancet.com/journals/langlo/article/PIIS2214-109X(23)00411-4/fulltext).

---

## 9. Conclusion

The evidence demonstrates that asynchronous, offline-first telehealth platforms can deliver consultation quality and diagnostic accuracy approaching in-person care in low-connectivity East African settings. The critical design levers are: (1) ultra-minimal data entry targeting <15 seconds for follow-ups, (2) store-and-forward as the default synchronous-requiring interactions as the exception, (3) SMS/USSD for all patient-facing outputs, (4) structured image capture with in-app guidance and offline queuing, and (5) multi-channel redundancy ensuring no single point of connectivity failure blocks care. The platforms that have achieved scale—Babyl's 3.9 million consultations, Simple's 11,400+ facilities, CHT's deployments across Kenya and Uganda—all share these architectural commitments. The cognitive load evidence further confirms that form design must minimize recall burden, use visual over textual guidance, and auto-populate from existing records wherever possible.
