# John Deere 9RX 540 vs. Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac: Comprehensive Comparison for a 200-Acre Saskatchewan Canola/Wheat Operation

---

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

For a 200-acre precision agriculture operation near Regina, Saskatchewan focused on canola and wheat with heavy tillage and seeding across clay-loam soils at 12–15 mph field speeds, the **Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac delivers a marginal advantage in fuel efficiency and lower ground pressure, while the John Deere 9RX 540 offers superior telematics ecosystem integration, a stronger dealer footprint in the Regina area, and a newer platform design.** Over a 10-year horizon the two tractors are closely matched in total cost of ownership; the final decision hinges primarily on your existing guidance investment (Trimble RTK) and dealer relationship quality. Below, each evaluation criterion is addressed in detail.

---

## 1. MACHINE SPECIFICATIONS COMPARISON

| Specification | John Deere 9RX 540 | Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac |
|---|---|---|
| Engine | JD14 13.6L 6-cyl, HPCR, DOC+SCR (no DPF) | FPT Cursor 13 12.9L 6-cyl, common rail, SCR-only |
| Rated HP | 540 hp (397 kW) | 535 hp (398.9 kW) |
| Max HP | 594 hp (437 kW) | 605 hp (451 kW) |
| PTO Power | 335 hp (249 kW) | 473 hp (352.7 kW) [wheeled] / ~535 hp rated |
| Displacement | 13,548 cc (826 cu in) | 12,880 cc (786 cu in) |
| Transmission | e18 PowerShift (18F/6R), 40 km/h | 16-speed PowerDrive PowerShift (16F/2R) or optional CVXDrive CVT |
| Fuel Tank | 1,514 L (400 US gal) | 1,173 L (310 US gal) |
| DEF Tank | 120 L (31.7 US gal) | 322 L (85 US gal) |
| Base Weight (Narrow UC) | 24,639 kg (54,320 lb) | ~19,892 kg (43,850 lb) [wheeled]; Quadtrac variant ~24,000–25,000 kg |
| Track Configurations | 4-track: 18", 24", 30", 36" widths; 80", 88", 120" spacing | 4 independent oscillating tracks, 30" or 36" Camso |
| Rear Hitch Capacity | 6,804 kg (15,000 lb) standard; 9,072 kg (20,000 lb) optional | 8,900 kg (19,620 lb) |
| Hydraulic Pump | 55 gpm standard; 110 gpm optional (dual) | 42 gpm standard; 57 gpm high-flow; 113 gpm TwinFlow |

*Sources: [TractorData.com](https://www.tractordata.com/farm-tractors/008/2/5/8253-caseih-steiger-540-quadtrac.html); [John Deere CA](https://www.deere.ca/en/tractors/4wd-track-tractors/9rx-540/); [Case IH Steiger Specs](https://www.farmersequip.com/ag-showroom/case-ih/tractors/Steiger-and-Quadtrac/Steiger-7); [tractor-info.com comparison](https://tractor-info.com/tractors/caseih/steiger-540/vs/john-deere/9rx-540)*

---

## 2. FUEL EFFICIENCY PER ACRE AT 12–15 MPH FIELD SPEEDS

### Nebraska Tractor Test Data

**Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac (Nebraska Test 2188, October 2017):**
- PTO maximum power: 541.99 hp at 1,900 rpm; fuel consumption: 27.81 gal/hr (105.27 L/hr); specific: 0.359 lb/hp·hr; efficiency: 19.49 hp·hr/gal
- PTO at rated speed (2,101 rpm): 480.46 hp; consumption: 26.21 gal/hr (99.20 L/hr); specific: 0.381 lb/hp·hr; efficiency: 18.33 hp·hr/gal

*Source: [Nebraska Test 2188 – Case IH Steiger 540 QuadTrac](https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3656&context=tractormuseumlit)*

**Case IH Steiger 540 (wheeled, Nebraska Test 2096, September 2014):**
- Drawbar maximum power: 441.44 hp; fuel consumption: 26.6 gal/hr (100.7 L/hr)
- Drawbar efficiency: 16.59 hp·hr/gal at max power; 15.82 hp·hr/gal at 75% pull
- Case IH claimed these were records at time of publishing, outperforming the John Deere 9560R's 15.64 hp·hr/gal and 14.58 hp·hr/gal respectively

*Source: [TractorData.com tests](https://www.tractordata.com/farm-tractors/008/2/4/8248-caseih-steiger-540-tests.html); [Ohio Ag Net / Case IH press release](https://ocj.com/2015/04/case-ih-steigertractors-break-drawbar-fuel-efficiency-records-in-nebraska-test-results/)*

**John Deere 9RX 540 (Nebraska Test 2252, May 2022):**
- Drawbar operations at 540 engine hp: fuel rate 174.8–189.4 lb/hr (79.3–85.9 kg/hr), equivalent to approximately 24.8–26.9 gal/hr based on fuel weight of 7.047 lb/gal
- PTO stationary operations at 390 engine hp: 124.7–135.1 lb/hr (56.5–61.3 kg/hr)
- The JD14 engine eliminates the DPF entirely, using DOC+SCR only, yielding approximately 3% lower fuel consumption vs. its predecessor

*Source: [Nebraska Test 2252 – John Deere 9RX 540](https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=4395&context=tractormuseumlit)*

### Estimated Field Fuel Consumption

At typical heavy tillage loads (70–85% engine load) running 12–15 mph on Saskatchewan clay-loam:

- **JD 9RX 540:** approximately 23–27 gal/hr (87–102 L/hr) depending on implement draft
- **Case IH 540 Quadtrac:** approximately 24–28 gal/hr (91–106 L/hr) depending on implement draft

The JD14's HPCR system and DPF-free design give the 9RX a slight edge in fuel consumption per engine-hp, roughly 3% better on paper (per [John Deere's own claims](https://www.deere.africa/en/tractors/9-series-tractors/9rx-series-tractors/9rx-540/)), though the Quadtrac's lower weight and four-independent-track traction advantage in clay-loam soil may partially offset this.

### Fuel Cost Estimation (per hectare)

Assumptions: diesel at ~CAD$1.50/L; 200 acres = ~81 hectares; heavy tillage pass consuming ~85% engine load; working width of a large chisel/disc at ~12m; field speed 13 mph (~21 km/h):

- Ground speed: 21,000 m/hr; effective field efficiency ~80% → effective 16,800 m/hr → 16.8 ha/hr (at 12m implement)
- JD 9RX 540 at ~95 L/hr: fuel cost ≈ $142.50/hr → **$8.48/ha** per pass
- Case IH 540 QT at ~100 L/hr: fuel cost ≈ $150.00/hr → **$8.93/ha** per pass

The difference is modest — roughly **$0.45/ha per tillage pass in favour of the 9RX 540**. Over multiple passes per season the savings accumulate but remain within noise given the operational variability of field conditions.

---

## 3. TRACK DURABILITY ON CLAY-LOAM WITH 180+ OPERATIONAL DAYS

### John Deere 9RX Track System

The 9RX uses a two mid-roller design with a 39.5-inch (100.3 cm) diameter drive sprocket — described by Deere as "about 20% larger than the next largest undercarriage design in the industry" ([OEM Off-Highway](https://www.oemoffhighway.com/drivetrains/article/12143964/john-deere-9rx-fourtrack-tractor-design)). Larger components turn more slowly, generating less heat and dissipating it more effectively, which directly extends component life. The two mid-roller design reduces vibration to the cab and avoids the center-roller-under-axle vibration issue found on three-roller systems.

John Deere's undercarriage maintenance guide emphasizes that track life depends heavily on minimizing roading (roading can increase wear up to 15× field wear rates), maintaining correct alignment, and following break-in procedures ([John Deere track maintenance guide](https://www.dandjfarmsupply.com/pdfs/John_Deere_Track_Reference_Guide.pdf)). John Deere PowerGard extended warranty can cover the powertrain for up to 3 years/7,500 hours beyond standard warranty ([JD Maintenance & Reliability](https://www.deere.ca/en/tractors/4wd-track-tractors/maintenance-reliability/)).

Track belt options for the 9RX include Camso AG 3500 (general ag, 1,000+ annual hour usage) and Camso AG 6500 (heavy tillage, ripper, scraper applications with reinforced drive lugs). The 6500 series provides approximately 30% lower cost per operating hour in heavy applications ([Camso brochure](https://camso.co/content/files/products/AG/2401_AG_TrackBrochure2019_JD_8.5x8.5_EN_V4_Web.pdf)).

For Saskatchewan clay-loam at 180+ days operation, track life estimates based on industry guidance:
- **Field-only use:** track belts typically last 3,000–5,000 hours
- **Mixed field/road use:** expect 2,000–3,500 hours
- With Camso 6500 heavy-duty tracks and minimal roading, 4,000+ hours is realistic

### Case IH Quadtrac Track System

The Quadtrac uses four independently-driven oscillating tracks, each with positive drive via toothed engagement with the drive wheel (not friction/tension like JD). This gives the Quadtrac a distinct traction advantage in clay-loam: four independent contact patches and articulated steering that "maintains full power when turning without soil ridging" ([Case IH Quadtrac brochure](https://cdn.asp.events/CLIENT_Haymarke_CB6BD562_5056_B731_4CF17C014C89B355/sites/Cereals-2022/media/libraries/exhibitor-brochures/23496-20c0014cominb_caseih_quadtrac_broschuere_fin_122020_low11.pdf)).

Industry experience with Quadtrac track replacement: midrollers typically need replacing at 4,000–4,500 hours ([PTK midroller article](https://www.ntstiresupply.com/ptk-shared/two-piece-midroller-conversion-kits-for-case-ih-quadtrac-tractors)). One UK arable farm with heavy clay reported needing to replace front tracks at 2,522 hours and rear tracks at 2,890 hours on an earlier-generation machine, though this was attributed partly to an older track compound ([Farmers Weekly](https://www.fwi.co.uk/machinery/avoid-buying-dodgy-used-crawler-tractor)).

Camso offers the AG 3500, AG 6500 (with DuraDrive reinforcement), and a 32"-wide exclusive option for Quadtrac that "keeps the idler wheels centered on the main cables, improving alignment, reducing drive lug side wear, and protecting the idler and midrollers from edge chunking" — extending track life further ([Camso Case IH brochure](https://camso.co/content/files/products/AG/2410_AG_TrackBrochure2024_CASE_8.5x8.5_EN_V4_WEB.pdf)).

### Clay-Loam Specific Concerns

Clay-loam is abrasive when dry, retains moisture creating sticky conditions, and can cause aggressive undercarriage wear. The Quadtrac's positive-drive engagement may experience faster drive lug wear in abrasive clay soils compared to the 9RX's tension/friction drive, but the four-track weight distribution reduces ground pressure per track. The JD 9RX's larger sprocket diameter and two-roller design reduce heat-related failure risk in extended high-hour seasons. Both machines benefit significantly from 30" or 36" track widths in clay-loam for flotation.

**Bottom line:** Both track systems, with Camso 6500 heavy-duty belts, should deliver 3,500–4,500 hours of track life in Saskatchewan clay-loam with disciplined maintenance. The Quadtrac's four-track design distributes wear over 24 mid-rollers vs. fewer on the 9RX, but replacement cost per track is also lower per belt. **The difference is likely within ±10% in total undercarriage cost over 10 years.**

---

## 4. TELEMATICS INTEGRATION WITH TRIMBLE RTK

### John Deere 9RX 540

The 9RX 540 comes standard with the G5 Plus CommandCenter display and integrated StarFire 7500 receiver with optional SF-RTK capability, which "delivers RTK accuracy without the need of a radio" and "up to 73% faster pull-in times" compared to previous models ([JD CA 9RX 540](https://www.deere.ca/en/tractors/4wd-track-tractors/intelligence-productivity/)).

**However, John Deere's guidance ecosystem is proprietary.** The StarFire system operates exclusively within Deere's ecosystem. If you are committed to Trimble RTK, you face a significant integration challenge:

- The 9RX can accommodate aftermarket Trimble guidance via the AutoTrac Controller system, which supports 9R/9RT/9RX Series 2015+ with the 4640 Universal Display or 4240 display ([JD AutoTrac Controller compatibility](https://www.hutcheonandpearce.com.au/agriculture/precision-ag-technology/guidance/autotrac-controller/)).
- Alternatively, Trimble displays (such as the GFX-1260 or NAV-900) can be mounted aftermarket and connected to the tractor's hydraulic steering via Trimble's own steering kit, bypassing the JD display entirely for guidance.
- Data interoperability between JD Operations Center/JDLink and Trimble's Connected Farm/Trimble Ag Software requires manual export/import or third-party middleware — there is no native seamless integration.
- John Deere recently announced a partnership with Trimble (October 2024) for construction equipment grade control, but this does not currently extend to agricultural guidance on the 9RX ([Trimble press release](https://news.trimble.com/2024-10-22-John-Deere,-Trimble-Partner-to-Deliver-Advanced-Technology-Solutions-to-More-Construction-Customers-Worldwide)).

### Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac

The AFS Connect Quadtrac features the AFS Pro 1200 display and AFS Vector Pro receiver, supporting corrections from WAAS up through AFS RTK+ and standard RTK ([Case IH Technology Guide](https://www.windridgeimplements.com/assets/Uploads/Precision-Technology-Product-Guide-05-25-CIH25042501.pdf)).

**Critically, the Case IH AFS Connect system is more open to third-party integration:**
- The AFS Vector Pro receiver accepts standard RTK corrections, meaning your existing Trimble base station can feed corrections directly if they broadcast on standard radio frequencies.
- Case IH offers the AFS Connect portal for two-way data transfer with "third-party partners of their choosing" ([Case IH AFS Connect](https://www.futurefarming.com/tech-in-focus/case-ih-quadtrac-and-steiger-tractors-ease-data-transfer/)).
- A Trimble display can also be installed as the primary guidance controller in the Quadtrac cab, similar to the JD option, with standard ISOBUS Class II compatibility.
- The AFS system uses ISOBUS Class II and AUX-N for implement automation.

**For a Trimble RTK operation, the Case IH Quadtrac offers somewhat easier integration** through its more open correction-signal acceptance and third-party data sharing philosophy, though neither tractor offers a truly seamless, native Trimble integration. You will likely need to either (a) run Trimble guidance as a separate parallel system on either machine, or (b) adopt the manufacturer's proprietary guidance and replace your Trimble investment.

**If you intend to standardize on the tractor manufacturer's guidance ecosystem**, the JD StarFire/SF-RTK system is widely considered best-in-class for accuracy and pull-in time, while Case IH AFS RTK+ is competitive but has a smaller user base in Saskatchewan.

---

## 5. DEALER SERVICE RESPONSE TIMES WITHIN 100 KM OF REGINA

### John Deere — Brandt Tractor

Brandt Group of Companies is headquartered in **Regina, Saskatchewan** — this is their home base. Key facts:
- 56 dealerships across Canada ([Brandt company info](https://www.brandt.ca/Parts-Services))
- "Technicians available for on-site and emergency service **24 hours a day, seven days a week**. A fleet of heavy-duty service trucks covers our entire territory" ([Brandt Field Emergency Service](https://www.brandt.ca/Parts-Services/Equipment-Maintenance/Field-Emergency-Service))
- Parts Onsite cabinets available at customer locations
- "Extensive parts inventory located close to you and available 24 hours / 7 days a week" ([Brandt Parts](https://www.brandt.ca/Parts-Services/Parts))
- John Deere Regional Depot at 455 Park St, Regina, SK — direct parts depot in the city
- John Deere's "Ultimate Uptime" program offers customizable dealer-delivered support including "response time guarantees, operator training, and on-site parts inventory" ([JD Ultimate Uptime PDF](https://www.deere.ca/assets/pdfs/common/products/ultimate-uptime-dkefeuu.pdf))
- JDLink/Connected Support enables remote diagnostics and proactive dealer service

**Brandt is a massive advantage for John Deere in Saskatchewan.** Being headquartered in Regina means the fastest possible parts availability and service response in the province. For a 100 km radius, Brandt has multiple locations with heavy-ag service capabilities.

### Case IH — Young's Equipment

Young's Equipment is the **largest Case IH dealer in Saskatchewan** with nine locations including a Regina headquarters:
- Regina location: 4000 East Victoria Ave, Highway #1 East, Regina, SK S4P3G7
- Hours: Monday–Friday 7:00 AM–6:00 PM; Saturday 8:00 AM–5:00 PM ([Young's Equipment](https://youngs.ca/parts/products))
- After-hours parts: (306) 994-7651
- "Shuttle Express" parts delivery runs daily from their Regina Parts Distribution Centre during growing season — "most parts will arrive within 1 day of ordering" ([Young's Equipment](https://www.youngs.ca/service/service-productivity-plus))
- Additional locations within 100 km: Moose Jaw, Weyburn, Assiniboia, Davidson
- Rocky Mountain Equipment also serves the region for Case IH

Additionally, **Redhead Equipment** operates a Case IH dealership in Regina (Hwy #1 East, (306) 721-2666) ([Redhead Equipment Regina](https://www.equipmentradar.com/redhead-equipment-regina)).

**Both brands have strong dealer representation near Regina.** However, Brandt's headquarters advantage and 24/7 parts availability with field service fleet gives **John Deere a measurable edge in emergency response time**, particularly during peak seeding and harvest when every hour counts.

---

## 6. 10-YEAR TOTAL OWNERSHIP COST INCLUDING SASKATCHEWAN CCA IMPLICATIONS

### Acquisition Cost

Based on current Canadian market pricing:

- **JD 9RX 540 (new, 2025):** approximately CAD $910,000–$960,000 for Signature Edition with dual displays, SF-RTK, 36" tracks, 110 GPM hydraulics, PTO ([AgDealer listings](https://www.agdealer.com/detail/1406438/2025-john-deere-9rx-540); [MachineFinder CA](https://www.machinefinder.com/ww/en-CA/machines/2024-john-deere-9rx-540-tractor-11193418))
- **Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac (new, 2023–2024):** approximately CAD $710,000–$758,000 for AFS Connect with luxury cab, 36" tracks, TwinFlow hydraulics, PTO ([MarketBook listings](https://www.marketbook.qc.ca/annonces/en-vente/case-ih/steiger-540-quadtrac/materiel-agricole/464); [AgDealer 2023 QT](https://www.agdealer.com/detail/1401062/2023-case-ih-steiger-540-quadtrac))

**The Quadtrac is approximately CAD $150,000–$200,000 less expensive at purchase**, representing a significant capital advantage.

### Saskatchewan / Federal CCA Implications

Both tractors are self-propelled equipment falling under **CCA Class 10** (30% declining balance rate) per the CRA's farming CCA guide ([CRA RC4408 Chapter 16](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/forms-publications/publications/rc4408/rc4408-16.html); [CRA RC4060 Chapter 4](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/forms-publications/publications/rc4060/rc4060-06.html)).

Key CCA provisions relevant to this purchase:

1. **Accelerated Investment Incentive Property (AIIP):** For property acquired after November 20, 2018 and before 2025 (becoming RIIP for acquisitions after 2024), the first-year CCA deduction is 1.5× the normal rate with the half-year rule suspended. For Class 10 at 30%, this means **45% deductible in Year 1** ([CRA Accelerated Investment Incentive](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/businesses/topics/sole-proprietorships-partnerships/report-business-income-expenses/claiming-capital-cost-allowance/accelerated-investment-incentive.html)).

2. **Immediate Expensing for CCPCs:** If your operation is incorporated as a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC), the immediate expensing provision (available for property acquired before Jan 1, 2025 for corporations, or before Jan 1, 2025 for unincorporated — per [Western Producer](https://www.producer.com/opinion/equipment-immediate-expensing-to-end-for-corporations/)) allowed **100% deduction in Year 1** up to $1.5M of eligible equipment. This provision has expired for new acquisitions in 2025+ for corporations but the RIIP successor provides similar accelerated treatment.

3. **Saskatchewan has no provincial CCA overlay** — Saskatchewan follows the federal CCA rules. Provincial tax savings are simply the provincial marginal rate applied to the federal CCA deduction.

### CCA Tax Shield Calculation (illustrative)

Assuming purchase in 2025, CCPC structure, combined federal/SK marginal rate of ~27% (small business rate):

**JD 9RX 540 at $940,000:**
- Year 1 CCA (AIIP/RIIP, 45%): $423,000 → tax shield ≈ $114,210
- Year 2 CCA (30% of remaining $517,000): $155,100 → tax shield ≈ $41,877
- Cumulative 2-year tax shield: ~$156,087

**Case IH 540 QT at $735,000:**
- Year 1 CCA (45%): $330,750 → tax shield ≈ $89,303
- Year 2 CCA (30% of remaining $404,250): $121,275 → tax shield ≈ $32,744
- Cumulative 2-year tax shield: ~$122,047

**The JD 9RX generates ~$34,000 more in Year 1 tax shield due to its higher purchase price**, but this does not offset the ~$200,000 capital outlay difference. After tax shields, the net after-tax cost differential remains approximately **$166,000 in favour of the Quadtrac.**

### 10-Year Cost Model

| Cost Component | JD 9RX 540 | Case IH 540 QT | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Purchase price (CAD) | $940,000 | $735,000 | ~$205K difference |
| Fuel (10 yr, ~800 hrs/yr, $1.50/L) | $1,080,000 | $1,128,000 | ~3% JD advantage |
| Track replacement (2× in 10 yr) | $120,000 | $130,000 | 4 belts @ ~$15K–$16K each |
| Undercarriage maintenance | $60,000 | $70,000 | Rollers, idlers, sprockets |
| Scheduled maintenance (8,000 hrs) | $120,000 | $120,000 | ~$15/hr |
| Extended warranty / PowerGard | $40,000 | $35,000 | JD PowerGard 3yr/7,500hr |
| Insurance | $94,000 | $73,500 | ~1% of value/yr |
| Residual value (10 yr, ~20% of MSRP) | -$188,000 | -$147,000 | JD retains better resale in SK |
| **Net 10-Year Cost** | **$2,066,000** | **$2,044,500** | **~$21K difference** |
| **Cost per hectare worked** (8,100 ha total over 10 yr, assuming 81 ha × ~100 operating days equivalent work) | **$255/ha** | **$252/ha** | Within margin of error |

*Note: 200 acres = ~81 hectares. At ~800 operational hours/year with various implements covering ~1,000 ha of effective work per year (multiple passes), total hectares worked over 10 years ≈ 10,000 ha. Recalculated: $206.60/ha vs. $204.45/ha for the two machines respectively.*

The 10-year total cost of ownership is **remarkably close — within 1–2%** — once fuel efficiency, maintenance, and resale are factored in. The Quadtrac's lower purchase price is largely offset by the 9RX's better fuel economy and stronger resale in the Saskatchewan market (Brandt's dominance sustains JD residual values).

---

## 7. UPTIME AND OVERALL RECOMMENDATION

### Uptime Factors

| Factor | JD 9RX 540 | Case IH 540 QT | Advantage |
|---|---|---|---|
| No DPF (no regeneration downtime) | Yes — DOC+SCR only | Yes — SCR-only | Tie |
| Dealer proximity to Regina | Brandt HQ in Regina, 24/7 service | Young's 9 SK locations, Shuttle Express | **JD (slight)** |
| Remote diagnostics | JDLink + Connected Support with dealer | AFS Connect with remote screen sharing | **JD** |
| Extended warranty options | PowerGard to 10,500 hrs total | CNH extended coverage | **JD (slight)** |
| Engine reliability | JD14 all-new design, hydraulic valve lash | FPT Cursor 13, proven 71,000+ engines in NA | **Case IH (proven track record)** |
| Track system simplicity | 2 mid-rollers per side, fewer moving parts | 6 mid-rollers per track (24 total), more complex | **JD** |
| Operator comfort (fatigue = uptime) | New cab, but Quadtrac reported smoother ride | Oscillating tracks = 70% vibration reduction | **Case IH** |
| Cold start capability | 12V starting | 24V starting (better for SK winters) | **Case IH (slight)** |

### Final Verdict

**For your specific 200-acre operation near Regina on clay-loam soils:**

The **John Deere 9RX 540** delivers the best combination of dealer support proximity, connected service capability, fuel efficiency, and long-term uptime assurance for Saskatchewan conditions. Brandt's Regina-headquartered 24/7 service network, JDLink remote diagnostics, and the DPF-free JD14 engine design minimize the risk of costly downtime during critical 180+ day operating windows. The integrated StarFire 7500 with SF-RTK is best-in-class for precision guidance accuracy, though it requires migrating away from your existing Trimble RTK investment — the single largest friction point.

The **Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac** is the better pure value proposition: ~$150,000–$200,000 lower acquisition cost, a proven FPT engine platform with 71,000+ units and 36 million operating hours in North America ([Case IH brochure](https://assets.cnhindustrial.com/caseih/NAFTA/NAFTAASSETS/Products/Tractors/Steiger-Series/Brochures/Steiger%20Series%20Tractors_brochure_01-18_CIH1707105_pages.pdf)), marginally better traction in soft clay-loam conditions due to four independent tracks and lower ground pressure, and easier integration with your existing Trimble RTK system through the open AFS Vector Pro receiver architecture. Young's Equipment and Redhead Equipment provide solid coverage within 100 km of Regina.

**Recommendation:** If your Trimble RTK investment is substantial and you are not prepared to migrate to a proprietary ecosystem, **choose the Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac.** The capital savings (~$150K–$200K), proven engine durability, Trimble compatibility, and comparable total cost of ownership make it the financially rational choice. Reinvest a portion of the capital savings into premium Camso 6500 tracks and an extended CNH warranty package.

If you are willing to migrate your guidance infrastructure to the tractor manufacturer's ecosystem and prioritize maximum uptime through dealer support depth and remote diagnostics, **choose the John Deere 9RX 540.** The Brandt service network in Saskatchewan is simply unmatched, and the long-term uptime advantage in a 180+ day operational window may be worth more than the price differential over a decade.

---

# Trust-Building Mechanisms for Gig Economy Platforms in Argentina, Colombia, and Brazil

## A UX Research Brief for Latin American Market Expansion

---

## 1. THE TRUST LANDSCAPE: WHY IT MATTERS MORE HERE

Latin America's gig economy operates against a backdrop of deep informality. Approximately 60% of workers in the region are considered informal, relying on short-term gigs found through word-of-mouth in a low-technology ecosystem shaped by economic fragility (MIT Solve / Chambeando). In a survey of 128 people in Lima, 87% reported hiring home-services workers based on personal recommendations from family, friends, or neighbors; 34% cited "recommendations" as the single most important hiring factor (MIT Solve, solve.mit.edu/solutions/69287).

This reality means that any platform entering these markets is not merely competing against other apps—it is competing against deeply entrenched relational trust networks built on WhatsApp groups, Facebook posts, and neighborhood word-of-mouth. The trust problem is not a missing feature; it is the central product challenge.

**Key macro data points:**
- Platform economy registration across the region: ~16% of the population registered, ~9.4% actually providing services through platforms (Alvarez et al., 2020, cited in Fairwork/UCM study).
- As of 2025, nearly 60% of Latin American adults now have access to a bank account, but only 15% have savings accounts or formal loans (BIS, bis.org/speeches/sp250910).
- 45% of Latin Americans did not have a bank account as recently as 2020; ~80% lacked a credit card (IDB, Accelerating Digital Payments).

---

## 2. RATING SYSTEMS: FROM STAR SCALES TO COLOR-BASED REPUTATION

### 2.1 Mercado Libre's Color-Based Reputation (Dominant Across All Three Markets)

Mercado Libre—Latin America's largest marketplace with 667 million monthly visits, four times Amazon's regional traffic—uses a **color-coded reputation system** (red → orange → yellow → green) rather than simple star ratings. This is the region's most influential trust mechanism and shapes user expectations across all three countries.

**How it works:**
- Sellers are measured on three metrics: **orders with complaints**, **delayed handling time**, and **canceled orders**.
- Thresholds differ by country. For example, complaint thresholds to maintain green status: ≤1% in Argentina and Brazil, ≤2.5% in Colombia and Chile (Mercado Libre Seller Help Center, global-selling.mercadolibre.com/help/como-funciona-la-reputacion_16622).
- Sellers achieving green with high volume earn the **MercadoLíder** badge, which dramatically increases search visibility.
- The system recalculates every 60 days (or entire history if fewer than 40 fulfilled orders).

**Trust-sales relationship:** A data-driven study of the platform found that trust was the **most important predictor of sales**, followed by purchase intention and price, but the trust-sales relationship was **statistically inconsistent across nations**—meaning the same reputation signals carry different weights in different Latin American countries (arxiv 1911.01280, "The Consistency of Trust-Sales Relationship in Latin American E-commerce").

**Fake review perception:** A 2024 study of 326 Mercado Libre Colombia buyers found that **perception of fake reviews negatively affects trust in the rating system**, while high-quality reviews positively influence all forms of trust (trust in reviews, marketplace, and rating system). Customer experience is directly mediated by trust in the rating system (Peña-García et al., Frontiers in Communication, doi.org/10.3389/fcomm.2024.1460321). This is especially relevant in Colombia, where the market is still developing review literacy.

### 2.2 Home-Services Platforms: Two-Way Ratings and Verified Reviews

Argentina's emerging home-services platforms (Tegu, Muovi, ROL) have adopted variations tailored to local trust norms:

- **Tegu (Córdoba/Buenos Aires):** Uses "reseñas reales de doble vía" (real two-way reviews)—both client and worker review each other. Identity is verified via DNI + selfie. The platform explicitly states: "Identidad verificada, pago directo sin comisiones y una reputación que el profesional se lleva" (tegu.ar/nosotros). No commission; workers pay a flat fee per lead won.

- **Muovi:** Requires reviews be linked to a completed job: "Cada reseña está vinculada a un trabajo finalizado. Solo los clientes que contrataron pueden calificar" (muovi.com.ar). This solves the free-rider problem of unverified reviews.

- **ROL:** Digitalizes the informal recommendation behavior—78% of users prefer hiring based on family/friend recommendations, so the app translates that behavior into verified public ratings (Infobae, April 2025).

### 2.3 Design Implications for Rating Systems

Research on rating system design (arxiv 1810.13028) demonstrates that **positive-skewed verbal rating scales with descriptive phrases** reduce rating inflation and are more informative. For Latin American markets, where word-of-mouth is the trust baseline, rating systems should:

1. **Anchor ratings to transaction completion** (not browse or contact) to match the mental model of "this person actually did the work."
2. **Use color or badge systems** (as Mercado Libre does) rather than numeric scales alone—these are culturally legible.
3. **Implement two-way ratings** to mirror the reciprocal trust dynamics of informal recommendation networks.
4. **Weight ratings by recency** (Mercado Libre uses 60-day rolling windows) to reflect the dynamic, reputation-sensitive nature of informal work.

---

## 3. IDENTITY VERIFICATION: NATIONAL ID SYSTEMS AND BIOMETRIC LAYERS

### 3.1 Country-Level Digital Identity Infrastructure

Each country has a different maturity of national digital identity, which directly shapes what platforms can build on:

**Brazil – Most Advanced:**
- **gov.br** platform has **164+ million users** registered (out of 213 million population). Uses Silver and Gold identity levels with QR-code biometric login, OpenID/OIDC standards (OECD G20 Digital Identity Collection; identityecosystem.solutions).
- The new **CIN/RG National Identity Card** uses blockchain backend (b-Cadastros/Serpro) and operates across all states (identityecosystem.solutions).
- Brazil's federated identity system with a central identity provider and identity broker is among the most sophisticated globally.

**Argentina – Moderate:**
- The **DNI (Documento Nacional de Identidad)** is available in the **Mi Argentina** app with the same legal validity as the physical card (except for voting and non-MERCOSUR travel) (Shufti Pro, docless identity guide).
- Buenos Aires' **QuarkID** is recognized as a UN Digital Public Good (identityecosystem.solutions).
- **World ID** (Worldcoin) achieved 500,000+ Orb verifications in Argentina—over 1% of the population—with nearly 16,000 verifications in a single day in late December 2023 (world.org/blog, January 2024). This signals strong citizen appetite for digital proof-of-identity.

**Colombia – Developing:**
- The **Registraduría Nacional del Estado Civil** maintains the unique identification register with mandatory registration and biometric data. A digital version is available via mobile app (Greater Internet Freedom report).
- RappiPay partnered with the Registraduría to implement **facial biometric verification** that contrasts the user's face against Registraduría data in 1-2 seconds, replacing manual cédula photo verification (Portafolio, July 2023). The CEO stated the platform had only 3 fraud cases per month using this approach.

### 3.2 Platform-Level Verification Practices

**Rappi (operates in all three countries)** provides the most instructive case study:

1. **Onboarding:** Valid government ID + biometric photo capture + background check via Truora (criminal records, national and international databases).
2. **Continuous authentication:** Every time a courier logs in or delivers an order, **2 selfies** are taken and compared against the original registration photo via facial recognition.
3. **Fraud prevention:** Limited selfie attempts; failure to match results in **permanent account block**. Unblocking requires manual review.
4. **Scale:** Over 3.8 million validations conducted from 2019-2023; 65,000+ users validated per month; fraud rate at onboarding was as high as 60% monthly before automated verification, reduced by **99%** with Truora integration (truora.com/en/success-stories/rappi).

**The black-market account problem:** In Colombia, a shadow market for fake Rappi profiles emerged, with accounts sold for up to $160 on Facebook, driven by urban unemployment that spiked to ~25% (Reuters, September 2020). This reveals a critical UX consideration: verification systems must balance **low friction for legitimate users** against **high friction for fraudulent ones**, and the system must be resilient to account-sharing and renting.

**DolarApp (fintech, Mexico → Argentina → Colombia):** Uses Jumio Go for fully automated ID verification. Users photograph their government-issued ID + take a corroborating selfie. AI determines document authenticity and matches the selfie in seconds. The platform credits Jumio's acceptance of **3,500+ ID subtypes** as critical for the LATAM market (jumio.com/case-study-dolarapp).

### 3.3 Design Implications for Identity Verification

1. **Layer verification progressively.** Don't gate the entire experience behind a wall of verification. Argentina's Tegu model—basic DNI + selfie for initial access, additional background checks and matrícula verification for specific service categories—is a strong pattern.
2. **Leverage national ID infrastructure.** Brazil's gov.br integration is the gold standard. For Argentina, the Mi Argentina DNI is a viable foundation. For Colombia, Registraduría facial biometric matching is the strongest available layer.
3. **Implement continuous re-verification** (Rappi's login selfie model) to counter account-sharing, which is a persistent problem in high-unemployment markets.
4. **Make the verified badge highly visible.** All three home-services platforms (Tegu, Muovi, ROL) prominently display "identidad verificada" as a trust signal—the badge itself is a product feature.

---

## 4. PAYMENT ESCROW AND DIGITAL PAYMENTS: THE CRITICAL TRUST LAYER

### 4.1 Payment Infrastructure by Country

**Brazil – Pix has transformed the landscape:**
- Launched November 2020, Pix now has **~160 million users** (75% of the population) processing nearly **80 billion transactions** in 2025, totaling over R$35 trillion (BCB Pix Report 2023-2025; Citi case study).
- Pix accounts for **40% of e-commerce volume** in Brazil and is projected to surpass credit cards as the leading online payment method by end of 2025 (Reuters/Ebanx, September 2024).
- **88% of users trust Pix's security and privacy** (Zoop/PiniOn survey, May 2025).
- QR codes now initiate 46% of Pix transactions, surpassing Pix keys (41%) for the first time (BCB data, April 2025).
- Pix is **free for individuals**, instant (seconds), and available 24/7/365—making it the obvious payment rail for gig platforms in Brazil.

**Argentina – Inflation-driven instability:**
- Payment infrastructure centers on **CVU (Clave Virtual Uniforme)** for fintech wallets, dynamic CVU, and interoperable QR (Conomy HQ).
- **Mercado Pago** dominates as the region's largest fintech wallet. Its **Split Payments 1:1** solution automatically divides transaction money between marketplace, platform, and seller across Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru, and Uruguay (docs02.mercadopago.com.co).
- Argentina's persistent inflation (which exceeded 200% annually in 2023) creates unique trust challenges: workers want immediate payment to avoid currency erosion, while escrow delays become more costly. This favors instant disbursement models.
- Only ~2% of banked Brazilians don't use Pix, but Argentina's equivalent payment rails are more fragmented and less trusted.

**Colombia – Mobile wallets gaining ground:**
- Key payment methods: **PSE** (bank transfer), **Nequi** (mobile wallet), **Daviplata**, **Bancolombia**, and **Bre-B** (Conomy HQ).
- RappiPay functions as a major digital wallet ecosystem alongside the traditional banking infrastructure.
- The SIC (Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio) has ordered Rappi to meet quality and transparency standards for the products and services offered on its platform, with fines up to 1,300 million pesos for non-compliance (Swiss Info/EFE, May 2024).

### 4.2 Escrow Models in Practice

**The emerging escrow model for LATAM freelancers:**

**Aliado Pay (Argentina):** A thesis project at Universidad de San Andrés describes Aliado Pay as "la primera solución de escrow flexible enfocada en acuerdos freelance cerrados por fuera de plataformas de intermediación." Key features:
- Acts as a neutral third party protecting client money until delivery is confirmed.
- Incorporates digital contracts, dispute system, and portable reputation.
- Target: freelancers in design, programming, marketing, writing—and their clients at startups, SMEs, and agencies (repositorio.udesa.edu.ar).

**SafeDeal (LATAM-wide):** An escrow infrastructure provider targeting the entire region:
- 5-step flow: Buyer creates deal → funds move to escrow → delivery confirmed → funds released.
- **3% transaction fee**, **72-hour dispute window**.
- Seller doesn't need an account—invited via email or WhatsApp link.
- Disputes trigger **AI-assisted mediation** (getsafedeal.com).
- The pitch: "Commerce in LATAM still runs on informal trust. Millions of daily transactions still depend on direct transfers, screenshots, and verbal commitments."

**Cuchara (Uruguay):** A home-services marketplace modeled as a case study:
- **Payment held for 72 hours** after job completion or until customer confirms.
- 15% platform commission deducted from the held payment.
- Disputes above UYU 10,000 require a **second approver**.
- Decision panel shows held amount and calculates pro payout in real time (oceanlab.in/case-studies/cuchara).

**Workana (freelance platform, all three countries):** Uses a standard escrow model: "Hire by project or per hour. Make your payment securely: it will remain in escrow until the freelancer has delivered everything agreed upon" (workana.com).

### 4.3 Design Implications for Payment and Escrow

1. **For Brazil:** Pix integration is non-negotiable. Its instant settlement, zero cost for individuals, and near-universal adoption make it the default. Escrow can be built on top by holding Pix receipts conditionally.
2. **For Argentina:** Instant disbursement is critical given inflation. Consider offering workers the option to receive payment immediately upon confirmation rather than in batch cycles. Mercado Pago's split-payment infrastructure is the most practical integration point.
3. **For Colombia:** Support PSE, Nequi, and Daviplata alongside card payments. The RappiPay ecosystem is a model for embedding financial services within the gig platform.
4. **For escrow across all three markets:** The 72-hour hold-until-confirmed model (Cuchara, SafeDeal) balances buyer protection with seller cash-flow needs. Offer WhatsApp-link invitations so sellers don't need pre-existing accounts—this lowers adoption friction for informal workers.
5. **Installment payments are expected.** Rebill data confirms that in LATAM, "installment payments are common, facilitating access to your services" (rebill.com). Even for services, offering cuotas (installments) via local cards can significantly increase conversion.

---

## 5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION: FROM INFORMAL MEDIATION TO AI-ASSISTED SYSTEMS

### 5.1 Country-Specific Regulatory Frameworks

**Argentina:**
- **COPREC** (Servicio de Conciliación Previa en las Relaciones de Consumo) was the primary consumer dispute mechanism, created in 2014. However, the national government **dissolved COPREC in February 2025** via Decree 55/2025, calling it a "bureratic" stage that "duplicated tasks" with other agencies and had "low efficiency levels" (argentina.gob.ar, February 2025). The replacement system is still being established.
- Before dissolution, COPREC handled marketplace disputes. A notable case involved Mercado Libre being fined for failing to attend a conciliation hearing over a product that was marked as "delivered" but never received by the buyer (Liga del Consorcista).
- **Implication:** Argentina's regulatory environment for consumer disputes is in flux. Platforms need robust internal dispute resolution because external regulatory backstops are weakening.

**Colombia:**
- **SICFacilita** is the Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio's online dispute resolution platform, launched in 2022. In 2023, it received **46,991 complaints**, achieving a **54% resolution rate** (25,551 cases). E-commerce disputes accounted for 12.6% of complaints, with a **67% agreement rate**—the highest among all sectors (SIC, portafolio.co, February 2024).
- The SIC ordered Rappi in May 2024 to comply with quality, delivery time, and warranty standards, with fines of up to 1,300 million pesos for non-compliance.
- Rappi's **Defensoría al Repartidor (DAR)** was launched in October 2023 as an "impartial third party" mediator between Rappi and its 150,000+ Colombian couriers. However, delivery workers across five cities told *Rest of World* they were skeptical—employees "are paid by the company" and the initiative was deemed "performative and redundant" by Fairwork Colombia (restofworld.org, January 2024).

**Brazil:**
- **PROCON** (Programa de Proteção e Defesa do Consumidor) operates at the state level as the primary consumer protection enforcement body.
- Mercado Libre's mediation system handles platform disputes internally, with mediation rates tracked as a KPI and impacting seller reputation scores.

### 5.2 Platform-Level Dispute Resolution Patterns

**Mercado Libre (all three countries):**
- Internal mediation system with explicit thresholds for "mediations" as a reputation metric.
- Country-specific complaint thresholds for green status: ≤0.5% in Mexico/Argentina, ≤1% in Brazil, ≤1.5% in Colombia/Chile/Uruguay (Mercado Libre seller documentation).
- Sellers in red reputation face operational blocks.

**Rappi (all three countries):**
- Continuous facial re-verification addresses identity-based disputes at the infrastructure level.
- UNIDAPP (the platform workers' union) agreed to "remit information relevant to combat fraud" as part of its 2024 agreement with Rappi (Colombian Ministry of Labor, February 2024).

**Cuchara (Uruguay model applicable regionally):**
- Disputes desk with the held payment always visible to the decision-maker.
- Dual-approval threshold for high-value disputes.
- All 24 demo jobs in the prototype open their own record with timeline, agreement, chat, and payment tabs (oceanlab.in).

**Solu (LATAM-wide CX provider):**
- Manages formal complaints, returns, marketplace mediations, and cases with regulatory bodies (COPREC, PROCON, Profeco) across the region.
- 90% resolution within 24 business hours SLA; ~95% first-contact resolution.
- Agent autonomy matrix with 5 monetary levels and pre-set caps, so most cases resolve without escalation (wearesolu.com).

### 5.3 Design Implications for Dispute Resolution

1. **Build the dispute interface around the payment hold.** The Cuchara model—where the disputes desk always shows the held amount—is psychologically powerful. When the money is visible, resolution feels concrete rather than abstract.
2. **Use conversational channels.** Over 400 million Latin Americans use WhatsApp. The MIT Solve "Reclamante" project demonstrates that AI-powered complaint resolution via WhatsApp removes friction that prevents 99% of citizens from filing formal complaints (solve.mit.edu/solutions/100706). Meet users where they already communicate.
3. **Set country-specific resolution expectations.** Colombia's SICFacilita resolves 54% of complaints; Argentina's COPREC has been dissolved. Platform-internal resolution must compensate for varying external regulatory reliability.
4. **Avoid performative mediation bodies.** Rappi's DAR experience shows that if the mediator is perceived as company-aligned, trust actually decreases. If you build an ombudsman function, it must have demonstrable independence.
5. **Tier disputes by value.** The dual-approval model (Cuchara's UYU 10,000 threshold) scales dispute resolution resources efficiently while providing human oversight for high-stakes cases.

---

## 6. HOW PRIOR TRUST EXPERIENCES SHAPE PLATFORM ADOPTION

### 6.1 The WhatsApp Trust Paradigm

The single most important finding for UX design is that **Latin Americans' prior trust experiences are overwhelmingly relational, not institutional.** This has profound implications:

- In Brazil, **69% of informal commerce** happens via WhatsApp groups. The app functions as "a digital bazaar where everyone passes through, with no fee to participate" (O Globo, June 2020, citing anthropologist Juliano Spyer). Among lower-income Brazilians, WhatsApp—called "Zap"—is so dominant for buying and selling that interviewees "almost scoffed at the question about using Zap for purchases, as if it were too obvious" (NUMA/ESPM research).
- In Colombia, a study of WhatsApp-based commerce among migrant entrepreneurs found that the platform reproduced existing social trust networks digitally—vendors sold primarily to friends, family, and school connections (Scielo, 2022).
- A study in Chile found that **51% of consumers feel totally secure** buying via WhatsApp, 42% feel somewhat secure, and only 7% feel insecure (ANDA Chile study). WhatsApp was used by **83% of Chilean consumers** for purchasing purposes.

**Implication:** Your platform is not replacing an absence of trust systems—it is replacing WhatsApp-based trust systems that already work well for users. The adoption challenge is showing users that your platform's trust mechanisms are **superior to or complementary to** their existing WhatsApp networks, not that you solve a problem they don't perceive.

### 6.2 The Disposition-to-Trust Model in Colombia

A study of 233 Colombian collaborative consumption users found that the **disposition to trust** (a personality-level trait) influences trust in the intermediary platform, which in turn influences trust in the service provider, which drives purchase intentions. Critically, **disposition to trust does NOT directly influence purchase intentions**—it must be mediated by platform and provider trust (EconStor, doi 10.1080/23311975.2023.2287789). This means:

- Users who already trust easily (high disposition) will adopt faster, but only if the platform itself is perceived as trustworthy.
- Users who are skeptical (low disposition) can still be converted if the platform provides strong institutional trust signals.

### 6.3 The Cross-Platform Reputation Portability Gap

A 2025 study proposes a **Labor Credit Scoring (LCS)** model that turns worker reputation into a transferable asset across platforms, using alternative data (certifications, behavior data) to enable credible assessments without formal records (Research Square, doi 10.21203/rs.3.rs-7198891/v1). This addresses a core pain point: informal workers who build reputation on one platform lose it when they move to another. The model was field-tested in Thailand and analyzed across Brazil and Mexico.

**For UX:** Portable reputation is an emerging expectation. Platforms that allow workers to import or reference reputation from other platforms (or from their informal WhatsApp client base) will lower onboarding friction significantly.

### 6.4 Two-Way Rating as Social Contract

Research on Uber's two-way rating system in São Paulo found unexpected uses: riders used driver ratings as proxies for safety, and drivers used rider ratings to decide whether to accept rides—essentially **the rating system became a substitute for the institutional trust mechanisms** (police, courts) that riders and drivers felt were unreliable (AIS Electronic Library, confirm2017). In the Colombian ridesharing context, drivers created Facebook and WhatsApp communities that served as alternative "platforms" with their own peer governance models, explicitly to compensate for low earnings and low trust on multinational platforms like Uber (Frontiers in Human Dynamics, 2021).

---

## 7. SYNTHESIS: CROSS-MARKET DESIGN FRAMEWORK

| Dimension | Argentina | Colombia | Brazil |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary trust model** | Relational (WhatsApp + neighborhood networks) | Relational + institutional (SICFacilita provides regulatory backbone) | Relational (WhatsApp "Zap" dominance) + advanced digital ID |
| **Rating system preference** | Color-based badges (Mercado Libre precedent); two-way reviews for services | Verified-transaction-only reviews; color-coded reputation | Star ratings with verified purchase anchoring; MercadoLíder badges |
| **Identity verification** | DNI via Mi Argentina app (legal equivalent of physical card); selfie + DNI matching | Registraduría facial biometric (1-2 sec matching); cédula-based onboarding | gov.br Gold/Silver levels; CPF-linked biometric boarding; most mature infrastructure |
| **Payment rail** | CVU / Mercado Pago / interoperable QR; instant disbursement critical due to inflation | PSE / Nequi / Daviplata / Bancolombia; RappiPay ecosystem | Pix (75% population adoption, 40% of e-commerce); QR codes surpassing keys |
| **Escrow expectation** | Low escrow familiarity; workers expect direct payment; opportunity to introduce | Moderate; Mercado Libre has normalized escrow for goods; services still cash-heavy | Higher tolerance for held payments (Mercado Libre precedent); Pix enables instant conditional release |
| **Dispute resolution** | COPREC dissolved (Feb 2025); platform-internal resolution essential | SICFacilita (54% resolution rate); regulatory actively overseeing platforms | PROCON state-level enforcement; Mercado Libre internal mediation |
| **Key adoption barrier** | Inflation eroding trust in holding payments; preference for immediacy | Account-sharing fraud; migrant worker exclusion from formal ID | Fear of Pix scams growing (2% trust decline YoY); digital divide in rural areas |

---

## 8. KEY RECOMMENDATIONS FOR UX DESIGN

1. **Digitize word-of-mouth, don't replace it.** ROL's insight that 78% of users hire via friend/family recommendations and Tegu's "small communities of families, friends, and neighbors" model show the winning pattern. Let users see which workers their social network has used, not just aggregate strangers' ratings.

2. **Verification badges are product features, not onboarding steps.** Display "identidad verificada" as prominently as a service listing. In markets where 60% of workers are informal, the verified badge is the primary value proposition for clients.

3. **Design payment flows for inflation and unbankedness.** In Argentina, offer same-day disbursement. In Brazil, Pix-native instant settlement. In Colombia, support Nequi and Daviplata alongside PSE. For unbanked workers, integrate with digital wallet partners (Nippy, Mercado Pago) rather than requiring traditional bank accounts.

4. **Build escrow as a trust-building ritual, not just a payment mechanism.** The 72-hour hold with visual countdown (Cuchara model) creates a shared experience of accountability. Make the held amount visible to both parties at all times.

5. **Use WhatsApp as a dispute channel, not just a marketing channel.** AI-assisted complaint generation via WhatsApp (Reclamante model) meets users in the medium they already trust most. Send dispute status updates via WhatsApp, not email.

6. **Implement country-specific reputation thresholds.** Mercado Libre already does this (1% complaint threshold in Argentina vs. 2.5% in Colombia). Calibrate your reputation system to local market norms rather than applying a single global standard.

7. **Protect against account-sharing from day one.** Rappi's experience with the $160 black-market account trade in Colombia shows this is not an edge case—it's an industry-wide vulnerability. Continuous biometric re-verification at login is the minimum viable defense.

8. **Make reputation portable.** Allow workers to reference external credentials, prior platform history, or client testimonials from their informal practice. This bridges the gap between the informal trust they've already built and the formal trust the platform requires.

---

**Sources cited throughout this report include:** MIT Solve (solve.mit.edu), ILO (ilo.org), Frontiers in Communication (frontiersin.org), Mercado Libre Seller Documentation (global-selling.mercadolibre.com), Reuters, IDB (publications.iadb.org), BIS (bis.org), World Bank, Jumio (jumio.com), Truora (truora.com), SafeDeal (getsafedeal.com), Rest of World (restofworld.org), Tegu (tegu.ar), Muovi (muovi.com.ar), Infobae, Banco Central do Brasil, EconStor, arxiv, AIS Electronic Library, and Conomy HQ.

# DSM-5 (2013) vs. ICD-11 (2019) Autism Diagnosis Criteria: A Comparative Analysis with Focus on Sensory Processing Differences

---

## (A) Side-by-Side Criteria Comparison Table

| Dimension | DSM-5 (APA, 2013) | ICD-11 (WHO, 2019) |
|---|---|---|
| **Core Social-Communication Criteria** | All three sub-domains required (A1–A3): (A1) deficits in social-emotional reciprocity; (A2) deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviors; (A3) deficits in developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships. All three must be met currently or by history. (CDC, https://www.cdc.gov/autism/hcp/diagnosis/index.html) | "Persistent deficits in initiating and sustaining social communication and reciprocal social interactions" listed as required Essential Feature, but **no mandatory sub-domains** specified. Seven illustrative manifestation areas are listed (e.g., understanding of social cues, social awareness, peer relationships) with further possibilities. Up to 19 different manifestations are described. (Kamp-Becker 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/) |
| **Sensory Processing Mention/Weighting** | Criterion **B4** — one of four RRBI sub-types: "Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g., apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement)." Requires **≥2 of 4** B-criteria to be met; sensory is one option among four. (CDC, https://www.cdc.gov/autism/hcp/diagnosis/index.html) | Sensory features are listed among **16 possible features** within the restricted/repetitive domain: "Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input includes adverse response to specific sounds, textures, or visual patterns." No mandatory number of B-domain features is required; any combination from the examples suffices. ICD-11 is less prescriptive than DSM-5. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/; Pabau ICD-11 guide, https://pabau.com/diagnostic-codes/icd-11-6a02-autism-spectrum-disorder-diagnosis-coding-guide/) |
| **Severity Specifiers** | Three severity levels (1–3) for **each** core domain independently: Level 1 = "requiring support"; Level 2 = "requiring substantial support"; Level 3 = "requiring very substantial support." (CDC, https://www.cdc.gov/autism/hcp/diagnosis/index.html) | ICD-11 retains a **multi-categorical system with 8 subcategories** differentiating by intellectual ability and language level (e.g., "with disorder of intellectual development and with impaired functional language," "without disorder of intellectual development and with mild or no impairment of functional language"). No severity levels per se. (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8531066/) |
| **Age/Onset Requirements** | Criterion C: "Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life)." No strict age cutoff. (CDC, https://www.cdc.gov/autism/hcp/diagnosis/index.html) | "Onset of the disorder occurs during the developmental period, typically in early childhood, but symptoms may not become fully manifest until later, when social demands exceed limited capacities." ICD-11 explicitly acknowledges that some individuals "start to experience distress, impairment and overt social challenges once societal demands increase (e.g., during adolescence or adulthood)." (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/) |
| **Functional Impairment Threshold** | Criterion D: "Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning." Criterion E: Not better explained by ID or GDD. (CDC, https://www.cdc.gov/autism/hcp/diagnosis/index.html) | "Deficits are sufficiently severe to cause impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning." ICD-11 adds that deficits are "usually a pervasive feature of the individual's functioning observable in all settings, although they may vary according to social, educational, or other context." Broader impairment domains listed (includes "personal" and "family"). (WHO CDDR, https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/dcf73611-9e0f-4d5c-85f6-85a58b0da6de/content) |

**Key sensory processing difference:** In DSM-5, sensory processing (B4) is one of four possible B-domain features, of which ≥2 are required. In ICD-11, sensory features are listed among a broader, non-numerically-constrained set of possible RRB features. Both treat sensory processing as part of the restricted/repetitive domain rather than as a standalone criterion, but DSM-5's more prescriptive structure means a person whose only RRB feature is sensory would still need to show at least one additional RRB to qualify—potentially excluding sensory-predominant presentations. ICD-11's less rigid operationalization may capture such presentations more readily but at the expense of diagnostic precision (Kamp-Becker 2024).

---

## (B) Evidence Synthesis: Peer-Reviewed Studies Comparing DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 Criteria

### Study 1 (Systematic Review/Meta-analysis)
**Kulage et al. (2019) — "How has DSM-5 Affected Autism Diagnosis? A 5-Year Follow-Up Systematic Literature Review and Meta-analysis"**
- **Source:** *Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders*. DOI: 10.1007/s10803-019-03967-5 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10803-019-03967-5)
- **Design:** Systematic review and meta-analysis of 24 studies examining diagnostic concordance between DSM-IV/DSM-IV-TR and DSM-5.
- **Key findings:** A 35% reduction (DSM-IV) and 37% reduction (DSM-IV-TR) in the number of individuals with an ASD diagnosis who would meet DSM-5 criteria. PDD-NOS was least likely to qualify (26% and 47% for DSM-IV-TR and DSM-IV respectively), followed by Asperger syndrome (55% and 19%), and autistic disorder (80% and 87%).
- **Sensory relevance:** The increased threshold in DSM-5 (requiring ≥3 social + ≥2 RRB features vs. DSM-IV's triad model) directly affected identification of individuals with fewer observable RRB features, including those whose primary differences were sensory.
- **GRADE quality:** Moderate (systematic review with observational study data; consistent direction of findings across studies but heterogeneity in methods).

### Study 2 (Meta-analysis)
**Bitsika & Sharpley (2016) — "A Meta-analysis of DSM-5 Autism Diagnoses in Relation to DSM-IV and DSM-IV-TR"**
- **Source:** *Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders*, 3, 119–124. DOI: 10.1007/s40489-016-0070-4 (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-016-0070-4)
- **Design:** Meta-analysis incorporating all 24 available studies on DSM-IV/DSM-IV-TR to DSM-5 concordance.
- **Key findings:** Confirmed a 35–37% reduction in ASD diagnoses moving from DSM-IV/DSM-IV-TR to DSM-5. PDD-NOS and Asperger syndrome populations were most affected.
- **GRADE quality:** Moderate.

### Study 3 (Primary Empirical Study)
**Wilson et al. (2013) — "Comparison of ICD-10R, DSM-IV-TR and DSM-5 in an adult autism spectrum disorder diagnostic clinic"**
- **Source:** *Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders*, 43(11), 2515–2525. DOI: 10.1007/s10803-013-1799-6 (https://researchinformation.umcutrecht.nl/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/)
- **Design:** Cross-sectional clinical comparison; n = 150 intellectually able adults assessed with all three systems.
- **Key findings:** Of those diagnosed with ASD using ICD-10R, only **56% met DSM-5 ASD criteria**. A further 19% met DSM-5 (draft) criteria for Social Communication Disorder. Of those diagnosed with Autistic Disorder/Asperger Syndrome on DSM-IV-TR, 78% met DSM-5 ASD criteria. Sensitivity of DSM-5 was significantly increased by reducing the number of required criteria or by rating "uncertain" criteria as "present," without sacrificing specificity.
- **GRADE quality:** Moderate (single-site, well-defined sample, but cross-sectional design).

### Study 4 (Primary Empirical Study)
**Kalra et al. (2021) — "Comparison of the diagnostic criteria for ASD using DSM and ICD: A study from North India"**
- **Source:** *J. Indian Assoc. Child Adolesc. Ment. Health*, 17(1), 25–47. DOI: 10.1177/0973134220210103 (https://doi.org/10.1177/0973134220210103)
- **Design:** Cross-sectional diagnostic concordance study; n = 100 children aged 2.5–16 years assessed using DSM-5, DSM-IV-TR, and ICD-10 (DCR-10).
- **Key findings:** DSM-5 ASD showed Cohen's κ = 0.846 with DSM-IV-TR and κ = 0.874 with ICD-10 (DCR-10) for childhood autism/autistic disorder. Agreement dropped to κ = 0.699 (DSM-5 vs. DSM-IV-TR ASD) and κ = 0.703 (DSM-5 vs. ICD-10 DCR-10 ASD) when broader ASD categories were compared. DSM-5 specificity was 1.0 and 0.961 compared with DSM-IV-TR ASD and ICD-10 DCR-10 ASD respectively. Children with atypical autism/PDD-NOS were most likely to lose diagnosis.
- **GRADE quality:** Low-to-moderate (single-site Indian sample; good interrater procedures but limited generalizability).

### Study 5 (Perspective / Critical Review)
**Kamp-Becker (2024) — "Autism spectrum disorder in ICD-11—a critical reflection of its possible impact on clinical practice and research"**
- **Source:** *Molecular Psychiatry*. DOI: 10.1038/s41380-023-02354-y (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/)
- **Design:** Narrative critical perspective comparing ICD-11 and DSM-5 conceptualizations.
- **Key findings:** ICD-11 allows "a high variety in symptom combinations" at the "expense of precision." The RRB domain in ICD-11 lists 16 possible features with no minimum number required, creating risk of "non-falsifiable diagnoses" and "a large danger of false positive diagnoses." Sensory features are subsumed within this broad, flexible structure. The author argues ICD-11 moves ASD "away from an observable, behavioral, and neurodevelopmental disorder to a disorder of inner experience that can hardly be measured objectively."
- **GRADE quality:** Very low (expert opinion/perspective), but raises important clinical validity concerns shared by other commentators.

---

## (C) Clinical Guideline Positions

### World Health Organization (WHO)
WHO developed and endorses ICD-11, which came into effect January 1, 2022, following approval by the 72nd World Health Assembly in May 2019 (https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/classification/icd/icd11/a72_29-en_icd-11-adoption.pdf). WHO published Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements (CDDR) for mental, behavioural, and neurodevelopmental disorders including ASD (6A02). WHO "requests all Member States to follow their commitment to move on to ICD-11" (https://www.who.int/news/item/11-02-2022-icd-11-2022-release). As of 2024, 35+ countries were using ICD-11 with 50+ countries conducting or expanding pilots (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICD-11). WHO considers sensory processing features as part of the RRB domain in ASD (ICD-11 CDDR).

### American Psychiatric Association (APA)
APA publishes the DSM-5 (2013) and DSM-5-TR (2022), which remain the standard diagnostic reference in the United States. The DSM-5-TR added elements related to culture, sex/gender, and co-occurring conditions. The APA has not issued formal guidance on adopting ICD-11 criteria for clinical diagnosis, as ICD-10-CM remains the US billing standard. Sensory processing (B4) was introduced as a new criterion in DSM-5, representing a significant change from DSM-IV (where sensory features were only listed as associated features). (https://www.cdc.gov/autism/hcp/diagnosis/index.html)

### American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)
The AAP's 2020 clinical report "Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder" references DSM-5 criteria, noting: "The DSM-5 includes sensory symptoms in the diagnostic criteria for ASD. The DSM-5 does not include sensory processing disorder as a discrete diagnosis." The AAP recommends use of tools such as the Short Sensory Profile to quantify sensory differences and notes that "sensory symptoms may be more evident at younger ages and may define subtypes of the disorder." The AAP does not reference ICD-11 criteria directly in its autism guidance. (https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/145/1/e20193447/36917/Identification-Evaluation-and-Management-of)

### National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
NICE guidelines (CG128 for under 19s; CG142 for adults) state that "an autism diagnosis should be based on criteria listed in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM-5) or the International Classification of Diseases 11th Revision (ICD-11)." In March 2022, NICE updated references from ICD-10 to ICD-11 following the NHS adoption (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Update-information). NICE notes sensory processing differences as part of the "core characteristics" of autism and references "altered sensory sensitivity, sensory processing difficulties and emotional regulation difficulties" in its adult guidance (CG142). The 2021 surveillance review noted ICD-11 adoption would be monitored for impact on guidelines. (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Context; https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK554918/)

---

## (D) Advocacy Organization Positions

### Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN)
ASAN actively lobbied the DSM-5 Neurodevelopmental Disorders Workgroup from 2009–2012, achieving "significant partial successes in protecting access to diagnosis, addressing disparities in diagnosis for marginalized groups, and blocking harmful proposals" (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-13-8437-0_13). ASAN supported the unified ASD diagnosis (eliminating separate Asperger/PDD-NOS categories) but expressed concern that DSM-5 criteria were "likely still too narrow" and that the severity scale was "problematic." ASAN advocated for inclusion of sensory features and motor/movement differences as diagnostic criteria. In a 2023 statement, ASAN confirmed it "stands by its position on the DSM-5 from 10 years ago" and remains "in support of the unified diagnosis" (https://www.thetransmitter.org/spectrum/debate-remains-over-changes-in-dsm-5-a-decade-on/). ASAN has not issued a formal comparison of DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 neurodiversity-affirming qualities, but its advocacy for broader, less restrictive criteria and against deficits-based framing aligns with the ICD-11's more flexible approach, though ASAN's primary engagement has been with the DSM system. ASAN's joint statement with the Autism Society of America emphasized that "contrary to assertions that ASD is over diagnosed, evidence suggests that the opposite is the case—namely, that racial and ethnic minorities, women and girls, adults and individuals from rural and low-income communities face challenges in accessing diagnosis." (https://autisticadvocacy.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/06/DSM-5_Policy_Brief_ASAN_final.pdf)

### National Autistic Society (NAS, UK)
NAS presents both DSM-5 and ICD-11 as valid frameworks, noting that "many people (including most autistic people) do not consider autism to be a disorder, and autism is not a disease" (https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment). NAS consistently reframes RRBIs positively as "self-soothing or self-regulating behaviours, and focused and dedicated interests" and explicitly includes sensory differences as part of the "core characteristics" needed for diagnosis. NAS acknowledges that both manuals "reference the core characteristics of autism" and does not formally endorse one manual over the other. However, NAS's language and framing throughout its guidance materials aligns with neurodiversity-affirming practice, emphasizing difference rather than deficit.

### Autism Speaks
Autism Speaks presents DSM-5 as the primary US diagnostic reference, describing the criteria in detail on its website (https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5). It highlights the addition of sensory issues as one of "six major changes" in DSM-5: "The addition of sensory issues as a symptom under the restricted/repetitive behavior category. This includes hyper- or hypo-reactivity to stimuli (lights, sounds, tastes, touch, etc.) or unusual interests in stimuli (staring at lights, spinning objects, etc.)." (https://www.autismspeaks.org/dsm-5-and-autism-frequently-asked-questions). Autism Speaks has not issued a formal position comparing the neurodiversity-affirming qualities of DSM-5 vs. ICD-11. Note: Autism Speaks has historically been criticized by ASAN and other autistic-led organizations for not centering autistic voices and for a more medicalized/deficit-based framing of autism.

---

## (E) Diagnostic Safety Risks

### Under-Diagnosis with DSM-5
The most robust evidence concerns DSM-5's narrowing effect. The Kulage et al. (2019) and Bitsika & Sharpley (2016) meta-analyses both found a **35–37% reduction** in individuals meeting criteria compared to DSM-IV/DSM-IV-TR, primarily affecting those previously diagnosed with PDD-NOS or Asperger syndrome. Wilson et al. (2013) found only 56% of ICD-10R-diagnosed adults met DSM-5 criteria, with 19% potentially redirected to Social Communication Disorder—a diagnosis with fewer service entitlements. This is particularly relevant for sensory-focused presentations: under DSM-5, an individual whose primary RRB feature is sensory (B4) must demonstrate at least one additional RRB, potentially missing those with sensory-dominant profiles.

### Under-Diagnosis in Women and Girls
Multiple sources document that current diagnostic frameworks systematically under-identify autistic women and girls due to camouflaging/masking, socially normative restricted interests, and diagnostic tools validated primarily on male samples (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10926859/; https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8604819/). Females may present with sensory processing differences and restricted interests that "align with socially acceptable topics" but still cause significant impairment, yet these are "frequently overlooked during diagnostic evaluations" (https://www.mdpi.com/2076-328X/15/8/1073). This is a risk under both DSM-5 and ICD-11, but DSM-5's more rigid B-criteria structure may exacerbate it by requiring specific behavioral exemplars rather than allowing clinical judgment about atypical sensory profiles.

### Over-Diagnosis Risk with ICD-11
Kamp-Becker (2024) argues that ICD-11's less prescriptive criteria create "a large danger of false positive diagnoses, of further increased prevalence rates, limitations of access to ASD-specific services and of increasing the non-specificity of treatments." The lack of mandatory sub-criteria and the inclusion of 19 social-communication manifestations and 16 RRB features with no minimum number required could make differential diagnosis between ASD and other conditions (anxiety, ADHD, personality disorders) more difficult. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/)

### Sensory-Focused Presentation Risks
Under DSM-5, the requirement of ≥2 of 4 B-domain features means that a person presenting primarily with sensory differences (B4) who does not meet at least one additional RRB criterion (stereotyped movements, insistence on sameness, or fixated interests) would not receive an ASD diagnosis. This could result in missed diagnoses for individuals—particularly women and girls—whose RRB presentation is dominated by sensory features. ICD-11's non-numerical approach to RRB features may better capture such presentations but at the cost of reduced diagnostic specificity.

---

## (F) Reimbursement and Coding Summary

### United States
- **Current coding:** The US uses **ICD-10-CM** (not ICD-11) for all HIPAA-covered billing transactions. The primary billing code for autism is **F84.0** ("Autistic disorder"), which has become the de facto standard code for all DSM-5 ASD diagnoses despite reflecting an older classification framework. Related codes include F84.2 (Rett syndrome), F84.3 (Other childhood disintegrative disorder), F84.5 (Asperger syndrome), and F84.9 (Pervasive developmental disorder, unspecified) (https://pabau.com/diagnostic-codes/icd-10-code-for-autistic-disorder/; https://www.medcloudmd.com/post/icd-10-f84-0-autism-billing-documentation-guide-2026).
- **ICD-11 transition:** There is **no confirmed US transition date** for ICD-11 adoption. The US has not yet announced when ICD-11 will replace ICD-10-CM. Per a 2023 JAMA Health Forum article, implementation "will require a minimum of 4 to 5 years" (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2807690). CMS continues to update ICD-10-CM annually (the October 2026 update was the most recent at time of research).
- **Crosswalk:** WHO's official crosswalk maps ICD-10 F84.0 to ICD-11 **6A02.Z** ("Autism spectrum disorder, unspecified") as an equivalent code (https://autoicdapi.com/icd10-to-icd11/F84.0). ICD-11 offers more granular subcategories (e.g., 6A02.0 with ID and impaired language; 6A02.1 with ID and unimpaired language; 6A02.2 without ID and with impaired language; etc.).
- **Coverage implications:** US payers and state autism insurance mandates typically specify coverage based on a qualifying ASD diagnosis by a licensed clinician using DSM-5 criteria; coverage does not currently reference ICD-11. A transition to ICD-11 coding would not change the underlying clinical criteria used (clinicians would continue to apply DSM-5 or ICD-11 diagnostic criteria), but would change the billing codes submitted.

### European Union / International
- The NHS in England adopted ICD-11 in **March 2022** (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Update-information). NICE guidelines were updated accordingly.
- As of 2024, **14 countries were actively using ICD-11** and 50+ countries were conducting or expanding implementation pilots (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICD-11; https://www.who.int/news/item/11-02-2022-icd-11-2022-release).
- In countries that have adopted ICD-11, autism diagnoses are coded under **6A02** with post-coordination options for specifying intellectual and language features. This allows more granular capture than ICD-10's F84 codes.
- Reimbursement implications vary by country. ICD-11's improved granularity and digital tools are designed to "support accurate resource allocation and cost management" (https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/classification-of-diseases), but migration requires extensive system updates; only 23.5% of ICD-10-CM codes map to a single ICD-11 stem code (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2807690).

---

## Summary of Key Findings

1. **Sensory processing** is newly elevated to a diagnostic criterion in both systems (B4 in DSM-5; listed feature in ICD-11's RRB domain), representing a major advance from DSM-IV/ICD-10 where it was only an associated feature. Both manuals place sensory features within the RRB domain rather than as a standalone criterion.

2. **DSM-5 is more prescriptive** (requiring ≥3 A + ≥2 B features with specific sub-domains); **ICD-11 is more flexible** (listing examples without mandatory numeration). This creates a trade-off: DSM-5 risks under-identification (35–37% reduction from DSM-IV), while ICD-11 risks over-identification and reduced specificity.

3. **Sensory-predominant presentations** may be particularly vulnerable to under-diagnosis under DSM-5, which requires at least one additional RRB beyond sensory features.

4. **No head-to-head diagnostic accuracy study comparing ICD-11 directly to DSM-5** for autism has been published as of the evidence gathered; the comparison data available concerns DSM-5 vs. DSM-IV/ICD-10 transitions.

5. **The US has no ICD-11 transition timeline**; billing continues under ICD-10-CM (F84.0). Several EU countries have adopted ICD-11. The practical clinical criteria used by diagnosticians (DSM-5 or ICD-11) are distinct from the billing codes submitted.

6. **Advocacy organizations** broadly support the unified ASD diagnosis and the inclusion of sensory features. ASAN favors broader criteria and has engaged primarily with the DSM process. The NAS acknowledges both manuals equally. Autism Speaks uses DSM-5 as its primary reference.
