final.content:
# Respondeat Superior Analysis: Vicarious Liability of a Food Delivery Platform for a Courier's Collision with a Pedestrian

## I. Executive Summary

Under the totality-of-circumstances approach applied by most jurisdictions, the food delivery company faces substantial exposure to vicarious liability on summary judgment. While the independent contractor agreement and several structural features of the gig economy model cut against employee status, the facts as presented—algorithmic control over routes, mandatory acceptance-rate thresholds enforced by automatic suspension, company-branded gear, absence of pricing discretion, and the courier's deep integration into the platform's core business—create genuine issues of material fact on the employee-status question that likely preclude summary judgment *for the company*. Simultaneously, the facts strongly support that the courier was acting within the scope of his employment at the time of the collision, since he was actively fulfilling an assigned delivery during a platform-initiated surge period. The company's motion for summary judgment should therefore be **denied** on the vicarious-liability claim. The lapsed insurance, the lost training records, and the delegation of work to the courier's teenage son introduce additional, independent liability theories.

---

## II. Legal Framework

Respondeat superior imposes vicarious liability on an employer for torts committed by an **employee** acting within the **scope of employment**. *See* Restatement (Second) of Agency § 219 (1958) ("A master is subject to liability for the torts of his servants committed while acting in the scope of their employment"); *Rivera v. State of New York*, 34 N.Y.3d 383, 389–90 (2019) (cited in *Smith v. Ryder*, 2024 NY Slip Op 24011, at *2 [Sup. Ct. Albany County Jan. 17, 2024], available at http://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2024/2024_24011.htm).

The analysis requires three sequential determinations:

1. **Employee status** under the right-to-control test (or its jurisdictional variants);
2. **Scope of employment** at the time of the tortious act; and
3. **Benefit to the employer** from the activity giving rise to the tort.

---

## III. Factor 1: Employee Status Under the Control Test

### A. The Governing Standard

The dominant test across jurisdictions is the **right-to-control** test derived from Restatement (Second) of Agency § 220(2) (1958). The touchstone is "whether the employer has the right of control and supervision over the work of the alleged employee, and the right to direct the manner in which the work is to be performed." *Craig v. FedEx Ground Package Sys., Inc.*, 335 P.3d 66 (Kan. 2014) (quoting *Jones v. City of Dodge City*, 194 Kan. 777, 780, 402 P.2d 108 [1965]); see also *Matter of Vega [Postmates Inc.–Commissioner of Labor]*, 35 N.Y.3d 131, 137 (2020) ("the touchstone of the analysis is whether the employer exercised control over the results produced by the worker or the means used to achieve the results").

Some jurisdictions apply the **ABC test** (e.g., California under *Dynamex Operations West, Inc. v. Superior Court*, 4 Cal.5th 903 [2018], available at https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2018/s222732.html), which presumes employee status unless the hiring entity proves all three prongs: (A) freedom from control; (B) work outside the usual course of the hiring entity's business; and (C) customarily engaged in an independently established trade. *See* California Labor Code; ABC Test overview at https://www.labor.ca.gov/employmentstatus/abctest/.

The U.S. Department of Labor's 2024 final rule applies a six-factor **economic reality** test: (1) opportunity for profit or loss depending on managerial skill; (2) investments by the worker and the potential employer; (3) degree of permanence; (4) nature and degree of control; (5) whether the work is an integral part of the employer's business; and (6) skill and initiative. *See* DOL FAQ, https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/flsa/misclassification/rulemaking/faqs.

No matter which test applies, the facts here present a strong mixed record.

### B. Application of § 220 Factors to the Hypothetical

Below is a factor-by-factor analysis. Factors are drawn from Restatement (Second) of Agency § 220(2), as adopted in jurisdictions such as Indiana (*Pfadt v. Wheels Assured Delivery Sys., Inc.*, 200 N.E.3d 961 [Ind. Ct. App. 2022]), Florida (*Kane Furniture Corp. v. Miranda*, Fla. Dist. Ct. App. 1987), and New York (*Smith v. Ryder*, 2024 NY Slip Op 24011).

#### (a) Extent of control over the details of the work

This is universally recognized as "the most important factor." *Kane Furniture*, supra; *Central Mgmt. v. Indus. Comm'n*, 162 Ariz. 187, 190, 781 P.2d 1374, 1377 (App. 1989) (cited in *Santiago v. Phoenix Newspapers, Inc.*, available at https://law.justia.com/cases/arizona/supreme-court/1990/cv-89-0042-pr-2.html).

**Indicators of control (favoring employee status):**

- The app's algorithm **mandated routes**—controlling not just the result (delivery) but the specific manner and means (the route taken). This is the hallmark of control over the "method and means" of work. *See Smith v. Ryder* ("Ryder's status depends on who controlled the method and means of how he did his work"); *Cross v. Supersonic Motor Messenger Courier, Inc.*, N.Y. App. Div. 2016 (delivery process controlled by dispatcher, Continental forms required, Continental shirt required, Continental logo on truck—all found sufficient to raise fact question on employee status; available at https://exa.ai/library/legal/opinion/99xh11vvh0s).
- The courier had **no pricing discretion**: the platform determined what customers paid and what the courier earned. *Cf. Matter of Vega*, 35 N.Y.3d at 137 (Postmates determined fee charged and rate paid).
- The algorithm **automatically suspended** couriers who declined more than two consecutive orders. This is a coercive control mechanism that limits the courier's freedom to accept or reject work—a factor DOL identifies as relevant to the control prong ("whether the potential employer... explicitly limits the worker's ability to work for others"; DOL FAQ, supra).
- Automated emails warned that **acceptance rates affected account standing**, creating a compliance-driven environment analogous to employment discipline. *Cf. Affinity Logistics* (home delivery company found to control all aspects of work, including denying requests for days off; Lexology, https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=5d611c1b-1f2c-490b-ade5-e35287d774a0).
- The courier was required to wear **company-branded gear**, further evidencing control over appearance and presentation. *See Cross v. Supersonic* (Continental shirt and logo on truck supported employee finding); *Affinity Logistics* (appearance supervised, uniforms required).
- The courier worked **55 hours per week**, suggesting full-time integration into the platform's operations rather than occasional, episodic gig work.
- The platform imposed a **delivery quota** (the courier was "three deliveries behind quota"), demonstrating quantitative performance standards typical of employment relationships.

**Indicators of independent-contractor status (favoring the company):**

- The courier **set his own schedule**—a hallmark of gig independence. *See Black v. Shaffer*, Ind. Ct. App. 2025 (DoorDash courier "free to select timeframes"; available at https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/in-court-of-appeals/116867418.html).
- The courier used a **personal vehicle**, not a company-provided one. *See Matter of Vega* (Postmates couriers provided their own transportation).
- The written **independent contractor agreement** labeled the relationship as non-employment. However, as the New York Supreme Court noted in *Smith v. Ryder*, "simply calling [a worker] an independent contractor, even in writing, is hardly dispositive." 2024 NY Slip Op 24011, at *2; see also *Greening v. Gazette Printing Co.*, 108 Mont. 158, 165, 88 P.2d 862, 864 (1939) ("it is immaterial to him what the terms of the agreement between employer and employee might be").

#### (b) Whether the worker is engaged in a distinct occupation or business

The courier was not operating an independent delivery business; he was performing deliveries exclusively through the platform using its app, its customer base, and its order-flow. This factor cuts **toward employee status**. *Cf. Dynamex*, 4 Cal.5th at 935 (Prong B of ABC test: contracted workers performing services in a role comparable to existing employees are within the usual course of the hiring entity's business; https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2018/s222732.html).

#### (c)–(d) Kind of occupation and skill required

Food delivery driving is low-skill, unsupervised-by-nature work that is typically done under the direction of the employer in the locality. The platform, however, automates direction through its algorithm. This factor is **neutral to slightly favoring employee status**.

#### (e) Who supplies the instrumentalities, tools, and place of work

The courier supplied his own vehicle and (presumably) his own smartphone. The platform supplied the app, the customer interface, and the algorithmic routing. This factor **slightly favors independent-contractor status**, as the major capital investment (the vehicle) was the courier's. *See Matter of Vega* (couriers supplied their own mode of transportation).

#### (f) Length of time employed

The facts do not specify the duration of the relationship, but the 55-hour weekly schedule suggests an ongoing, continuous relationship rather than a one-off engagement. This factor **slightly favors employee status**. *See Santiago v. Phoenix Newspapers* (continuous relationship indicative of employment).

#### (g) Method of payment

The facts do not specify whether payment was per-delivery or hourly, though the quota and acceptance-rate mechanisms suggest a delivery-based compensation structure. Per-delivery payment is common to both independent contracting and employment models in the gig economy. This factor is **neutral**.

#### (h) Whether the work is part of the regular business of the employer

This factor **strongly favors employee status**. The platform's entire business is food delivery; the courier's work is not ancillary or supplementary but is the very core of the enterprise. Under the ABC test, this is dispositive on Prong B: a food delivery courier for a food delivery platform performs work within the "usual course of the hiring entity's business." *Dynamex*, 4 Cal.5th at 935; California ABC Test, https://www.labor.ca.gov/employmentstatus/abctest/. Under the DOL economic-realities test, this is factor (5): "extent to which the work performed is an integral part of the potential employer's business." DOL FAQ, supra.

#### (i) Whether the parties believe they are creating an employer-employee relationship

The written agreement designates an independent-contractor relationship. This factor **favors the company**, but is not dispositive. *Smith v. Ryder*, supra; *Santiago v. Phoenix Newspapers*, supra; *Femling v. Star Publishing Co.*, 195 Wash. 395, 405, 81 P.2d 293, 298 (1938).

#### (j) Whether the principal is in business

The platform is a commercial enterprise. This factor **favors employee status**.

### C. Summary Judgment Posture on Employee Status

Weighing all factors, the control indicators are substantial: algorithmic route mandates, automatic suspension for declining orders, acceptance-rate monitoring with threats to account standing, company-branded gear, no pricing discretion, delivery quotas, 55-hour weeks, and the courier's work being the core of the platform's business. These are counterbalanced by the independent contractor label, personal vehicle, schedule flexibility, and self-supplied tools.

Under the standard articulated in *Smith v. Ryder*—"the question of control is typically a question of fact, and a question of fact defeats a motion for summary judgment" (2024 NY Slip Op 24011)—and in *Pfadt v. Wheels Assured Delivery Systems* ("Whether one acts as an employee or an independent contractor is generally a question for the finder of fact"; 200 N.E.3d 961 [Ind. Ct. App. 2022]), this record presents **genuine issues of material fact** on employee status that **preclude summary judgment for the company**.

The same conclusion follows under the ABC test. Even if Prong A (freedom from control) might be contested, Prong B (usual course of business) is almost certainly not satisfied by the company, and Prong C (independently established trade) is doubtful where the courier has no separate delivery business. *Dynamex*, supra.

Under the DOL economic-realities test, the courier appears economically dependent on the platform: he works 55 hours per week, has no independent delivery business, and faces algorithmic coercion to accept work. DOL FAQ, https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/flsa/misclassification/rulemaking/faqs ("a worker is not an independent contractor if they are, as a matter of economic reality, economically dependent on an employer for work").

---

## IV. Factor 2: Scope of Employment

Assuming the courier is found to be an employee, the next question is whether the collision occurred within the **scope of employment**.

The general rule is that an employee is acting within the scope of employment when the tortious act "occurred within the scope of that employment"—i.e., while furthering the employer's business. *Carter v. Reynolds*, 175 N.J. 402, 408–09 (2003) (cited in *Neher v. Hopkins*, N.J. App. Div. 2019, https://www.njcourts.gov/system/files/court-opinions/2019/a4518-17.pdf). "The master is still responsible if the performance occurs in the course of the employment with a view towards furthering the business of the master, and not with a purpose personal to the employee." *Norton v. Railway Express Agency, Inc.*, 3d Cir. 1969 (https://exa.ai/library/legal/opinion/w637p406xhg).

Here, the courier was **actively in the process of completing a food delivery** at the time of the collision. He was on an assigned route (mandated by the algorithm), during a platform-initiated surge-pricing period, three deliveries behind the platform's quota, and had received automated warnings about his performance. Every element of his activity was directed toward fulfilling the platform's business objectives.

This is the strongest possible case for scope of employment. Courts have consistently held that delivery drivers who are injured or cause injury while **actively making deliveries** are within the scope of employment. *See* Setareh Law analysis: "Drivers actively making deliveries, traveling to pickup locations, or returning from completed deliveries typically fall within the scope of employment for liability purposes" (https://www.setarehfirm.com/employers-liable-delivery-accidents-scooters/); *Perez v. Van Groningen & Sons, Inc.*, 41 Cal.3d 962, 968 (1986) (https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ca-supreme-court/1843982.html) ("the cases which have considered recovery against the master for accidents occurring within the scope and during the period of employment have established a general rule of liability with a few exceptions for cases where the employee has substantially deviated from his duties for personal purposes").

The courier's rushing to catch up on his quota does not constitute a deviation from employment; rather, it was conduct **motivated by and in furtherance of** the employer's business (meeting delivery quotas, avoiding account suspension). As the Third Circuit held in *Norton*, a servant's deviation from literal instructions does not relieve the master of liability if the act was done "in the course of the employment with a view towards furthering the business of the master." Moreover, the platform's own algorithmic pressure—automatic suspension for declining orders, warnings about acceptance rates—created the conditions that incentivized the courier's rushing. This causation link strengthens the scope-of-employment finding.

**Conclusion on scope of employment: clearly satisfied.** The company would not prevail on summary judgment on this prong.

---

## V. Factor 3: Benefit to the Employer

The third element of respondeat superior—benefit to the employer—is straightforwardly met. The courier's delivery generated revenue for the platform through delivery fees, commissions from restaurant partners, and (during surge pricing) elevated margins. The platform's business model depends entirely on couriers completing deliveries. The courier's activity at the time of the collision was the **direct fulfillment of the platform's core commercial function**.

This factor reinforces both the scope-of-employment finding and the employee-status analysis. Under the DOL economic-realities test, the courier's work is "an integral part of the potential employer's business" (factor 5). DOL FAQ, supra. Under the ABC test, the courier performs work "within the usual course of the hiring entity's business" (Prong B). *Dynamex*, 4 Cal.5th at 935.

---

## VI. Additional Liability Considerations

### A. Lapsed Insurance and Negligent Retention/Supervision

The company's independent contractor agreement required couriers to maintain liability insurance, but the courier's policy lapsed two weeks before the collision. The company apparently had no mechanism (or failed to implement one) to verify ongoing insurance compliance.

Even if the company successfully defends against vicarious liability, the plaintiff may assert **negligent hiring, retention, or supervision** as a direct-liability theory. In *Jarrell v. Kaul*, 123 A.3d 1022 (N.J. 2015), the court held that a facility granting privileges to an independent contractor had "a continuing duty to ascertain that [the contractor] meets licensing prerequisites (including required insurance)" (discussed at https://www.capehart.com/time-for-a-checkup-admitting-facilities-must-ensure-physicians-carry-the-proper-medical-malpractice-insurance/). By analogy, a platform that requires couriers to carry liability insurance as a condition of engagement may have a duty to monitor compliance. The lapse of the courier's policy, coupled with the platform's failure to detect or act on it, could support a direct negligence claim.

However, as the Maryland Court of Appeals cautioned in *Perry v. Asphalt & Concrete Services, Inc.*, 108 A.3d 558 (2015), evidence of lapsed insurance is only admissible in negligent-hiring claims if it is causally linked to the harm; a lapse for nonpayment may not establish the driver's incompetence (https://www.mdcourts.gov/data/opinions/coa/2016/27a15.pdf). The plaintiff would need to argue that the lapse itself—creating an uninsured motorist situation—proximately caused the inability to compensate the pedestrian, even if not the collision itself.

### B. Lost Training Records

The onboarding checklist references completion of safety-protocol training, but the actual training records were lost in a system migration. This evidentiary gap could cut both ways:

- **Against the company:** If the plaintiff argues that training was inadequate or never completed, the company's inability to produce records weakens its position. Courts may draw adverse inferences from lost evidence, and the company bears the burden of proving its training program was adequate if it raises the defense of having exercised reasonable care.
- **For the company:** The onboarding checklist itself, if authenticated, may serve as circumstantial evidence of training completion. The company would argue that a checklist referencing completion is sufficient to establish a prima facie case of training.

### C. Delegation to the Courier's Teenage Son

The courier occasionally hired his teenage son to assist with large orders, paying him directly rather than through the platform. This arrangement raises several issues:

1. **Unauthorized subcontracting:** If the independent contractor agreement (or the platform's terms of service) prohibits delegation of delivery tasks without platform approval, the courier's use of his son constitutes a breach of the agreement. However, this breach does not necessarily absolve the company of vicarious liability. The question is whether the courier was acting within the scope of his engagement at the time of the tort, not whether he complied with every contractual term. *Norton v. Railway Express* (servant's deviation from instructions does not relieve master if act furthers employer's business).

2. **Borrowed-servant doctrine:** If the son were the one who caused the accident, a more complex analysis would arise. The son was not a party to any agreement with the platform, and the platform had no knowledge of or control over his participation. The platform would likely not be vicariously liable for the son's acts under these facts.

3. **Relevance to the present collision:** The son's involvement is irrelevant to this accident because the courier himself (not the son) was driving at the time. The fact that the courier *sometimes* delegated work does not change the analysis of whether the courier was acting within the scope of employment when *he* was the one making the delivery.

---

## VII. Application to Summary Judgment

Summary judgment is appropriate only when "there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law." Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a). The company bears the burden of demonstrating the absence of genuine factual disputes.

### A. Can the Company Prevail on Summary Judgment?

**No.** The company cannot establish, as a matter of law, that the courier was an independent contractor. The control indicators—algorithmic route mandates, automatic suspension for declining orders, acceptance-rate monitoring, company-branded gear, no pricing discretion, delivery quotas, and 55-hour weeks—create genuine factual disputes that are for the jury to resolve. *Smith v. Ryder*, 2024 NY Slip Op 24011; *Pfadt v. Wheels Assured Delivery Systems*, 200 N.E.3d 961; *Cross v. Supersonic Motor Messenger Courier, Inc.*, N.Y. App. Div. 2016.

Moreover, even under the more restrictive independent-contractor framework, the company faces potential liability on the direct-negligence theories (negligent retention, failure to verify insurance) that do not depend on employee status.

### B. Can the Plaintiff Prevail on Summary Judgment?

**Possibly, but more likely on scope of employment than on employee status.** If the court determines as a matter of law that the courier was an employee (unlikely given the mixed record), the scope-of-employment element is strong enough for summary judgment: the courier was actively engaged in a delivery at the time of the collision. However, the employee-status question is quintessentially factual, and most courts would deny both parties' summary judgment motions, sending the case to trial.

---

## VIII. Conclusion

On summary judgment, the company's motion should be **denied**. The following table summarizes the analysis:

| Element | Finding | Summary Judgment Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Employee status | Genuine issue of material fact (strong control indicators vs. schedule flexibility and independent contractor label) | **Deny** company's motion |
| Scope of employment | Courier was actively delivering for the platform during surge pricing, behind quota, on mandated routes | **Favor plaintiff**—clearly within scope |
| Benefit to employer | Delivery was the core business function; revenue directly generated | **Favor plaintiff**—uncontested |
| Negligent retention (insurance lapse) | Duty to verify insurance is plausible; causal link to harm is arguable | **Deny**—triable issue |
| Lost training records | Adverse inference possible; checklist circumstantially supports training | **Deny**—triable issue |
| Delegation to son | Irrelevant to this accident (courier was driving); no effect on vicarious liability analysis | No impact on summary judgment |

The strongest path for the company is to argue independent-contractor status based on schedule flexibility, personal vehicle, and the written agreement. # Conversational UI Patterns in Voice-First Healthcare Applications and Medication Adherence Among Elderly Patients with Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Comparative Synthesis

## 1. Introduction and Scope

This report examines how conversational UI patterns in voice-first healthcare applications affect medication adherence among elderly patients (65+) with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). It compares three deployed systems — Amazon Alexa's medication reminders, Google Assistant-based health tracking (as deployed in the MATCHA system), and Catalia Health's Mabu robot — and synthesizes findings from geriatric HCI studies on confirmation dialog patterns, error recovery mechanisms, and multi-modal feedback. The analysis identifies interaction sequences correlating with sustained engagement beyond 90 days and reviews longitudinal usability data on task completion rates, error types, and patient-reported confidence scores.

## 2. System Profiles and Interaction Design Strategies

### 2.1 Amazon Alexa's Medication Reminders

Amazon Alexa has been the platform for several medication reminder deployments. The **MedBuddy** study (PMC8317037, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8317037/) created a medication adherence skill for Echo devices, tested with 25 women over 60 days. Participants interacted with MedBuddy on only approximately 50.97% of study days (mean, SD 29.5), indicating substantial engagement decay. However, participants self-reported taking medication more reliably at study end compared to baseline (McNemar test: P<.001). A notable design limitation: MedBuddy operated as a simple alarm/reminder system without conversational "check-in" functionality — it reminded users to take medication but did not verify whether they had done so.

A more rigorous 12-month randomized controlled trial (Springer, 2025, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11657-025-01529-0) tested an Amazon Alexa-based digital voice assistant (DVA) intervention in 50 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis (mean age 64.3 ± 6.1 years). The DVA delivered medication reminders, education videos, and interactive quizzes. DVA intervention adherence (sessions accessed) was 79.5% (95% CI: 73.9–84.9) at 6 months. Critically, the proportion of participants with acceptable 12-month medication possession ratios (≥0.8) was similar between control (86.4%) and DVA groups (95.0%, P=0.34). The DVA intervention did **not** significantly improve medication adherence, osteoporosis knowledge, or attitudes — suggesting that reminder-only voice interventions may plateau in effectiveness.

A UK pilot study (British Journal of General Practice, https://bjgp.org/content/bjgp/70/690/8.full.pdf) found participants found Alexa medication reminders "extremely helpful" for the basic task of setting and receiving reminders, though this was a short-term feasibility assessment without longitudinal data. A recent Italian pilot with the InTakeCare platform (European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, 2025, https://doi.org/10.1093/eurjpc/zwaf236.495) developed an Alexa skill that set reminders at prescribed times plus 55 minutes, allowing a 120-minute window for vocal confirmation. Among 15 hypertensive patients over 7 days, the System Usability Scale (SUS) median score was 77.5 (IQR 11.25), indicating good perceived usability.

Long-term adoption data comes from a University of Michigan study of older adults in a long-term care community who used Alexa for at least one year (ACM CHI 2023, https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3544548.3580925). Through structured training programs, participants sustained use for entertainment, mood improvement, and cognitive stimulation, though medication-specific long-term engagement data was not reported separately.

**Alexa's interaction pattern** is fundamentally command-and-respond: the user issues a directive or receives a scheduled reminder, with limited conversational depth. Confirmation is typically implicit (no acknowledgment required) or simple ("OK"). Error recovery is limited — Alexa initiated recovery in less than 5% of error cases in one study (ACM TACCESS 2026, https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3796236).

### 2.2 Google Assistant-Based Health Tracking: The MATCHA System

The most extensively studied Google Assistant-based medication management system is **MATCHA** (Medication Action To Check-In for Health Application), developed at Georgia Institute of Technology and deployed on the Google Home Hub (ACM ASSETS 2022, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3517428.3544830; full paper at https://ecl.cc.gatech.edu/sites/default/files/publications/mathur_assets22.pdf).

MATCHA was co-designed with 18 MCI member-carepartner dyads and deployed in two phases over 20 weeks with 7 dyads. The system's core innovation is the **"check-in" rather than "remind"** paradigm. Instead of commanding "take your medication," MATCHA asks: *"Hey John, it's time to take your medication. I'm checking in. Have you taken it yet?"* (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06690). This prompt was designed to trigger reflective self-checking rather than reflexive acknowledgment, directly addressing the over-medication risk in MCI populations — a person with MCI might forget they already took their medication and take it again upon receiving a standard alarm.

MATCHA recognized over 200 possible response scenarios and handled:
- **Already-taken medication**: Positive feedback and reinforcement
- **Not-yet-taken**: Offer to reschedule
- **Uncertain recall**: Prompt to check pillbox
- **No response**: Phone notification to both member and carepartner
- **"Taking Now" scenario**: Added in Phase 2 to accommodate users who were in the process of taking medication

**Quantitative engagement results:**
- Phase 1 (4 weeks): ~18% weekly engagement rate
- Phase 2 (16 weeks, post-design revisions): ~67% engagement rate
- Final weeks of Phase 2: ~85–90% engagement rate
- SUS scores: 84.66 (members) and 86.16 (carepartners) in Phase 1
- All 5 completing dyads expressed desire to continue using MATCHA; were still using it approximately **55 weeks later** at time of writing — well beyond the 90-day sustained engagement threshold

Design revisions driving the Phase 2 engagement increase included: reducing overly enthusiastic positive feedback (which felt patronizing), adding touch-screen buttons as a voice alternative, and incorporating the "Taking Now" response path.

**Multi-modal feedback** was a key design feature. The Google Home Hub provided voice + visual (8×6 inch touchscreen) output. Touch-based interactions accounted for 20–35% of total interactions, serving as a critical fallback when speech recognition failed. This multi-modal redundancy directly contributed to sustained engagement.

### 2.3 Catalia Health's Mabu Robot

Mabu is a 12-inch tabletop robot developed by Catalia Health (founded by Dr. Cory Kidd, MIT Media Lab) that combines a physical robotic presence with a touchscreen display and voice-based conversation (https://news.mit.edu/2019/catalia-health-mabu-robot-1011; https://www.pfizer.com/news/press-release/press-release-detail/catalia-health-and-pfizer-collaborate-better-understand). Mabu conducts daily 2–4 minute check-in conversations with patients, building three AI models per patient: medical, psychological, and interactional.

Key clinical deployments:
- **Kaiser Permanente partnership** (since ~2018): Heart failure patients in home settings
- **Pfizer 12-month pilot** (2019): Exporing medication adherence and symptom management in specialty pharmacy patients
- **American Heart Association Innovators Network** (joined October 2018)

The foundational research by Dr. Kidd (https://uk.pcmag.com/news/122768/mabu-the-pint-sized-robot-wants-to-manage-your-health) demonstrated in a randomized controlled trial at Boston University Medical Center that patients given a robotic weight-loss coach were **"much more likely to stick with the weight loss program"** compared to those using a computer running identical software — establishing that the embodied robotic form factor itself improved adherence beyond the software alone.

Mabu's interaction design combines **voice + visual (touchscreen) + physical embodiment (eye contact, blinking, head movement)**, creating the most multi-modal of the three systems. The physical presence generates anthropomorphic social bonding; patients reportedly "build a relationship with Mabu" over time (https://www.computertalk.com/social-companion-robots-and-medication-adherence/). The platform includes mobile phone continuation when patients are away from the physical device.

However, independent evidence on long-term adherence outcomes is limited. A 2013 study of a similar robotic medication assistant for 10 elderly care facility residents found the application "well received" with all users successfully completing sessions, and most finding it easy to use and feeling confident using it (ACM AUIC 2011, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/2460616.2460623). A broader randomized cross-over trial of healthcare robots in 29 older adults (Springer ICSR 2014, https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-11973-1_7) found robots acceptable and feasible, with many participants describing them as "useful and as friends," though the robots had **no significant impact on adherence, depression, or quality of life** over the 6-week periods — suggesting that acceptance alone is insufficient for measurable adherence outcomes in short deployments.

## 3. Confirmation Dialog Patterns

The MATCHA study provides the most detailed evidence on confirmation dialog design for MCI populations (https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3517428.3544830). Key findings:

**Check-in vs. Reminder framing**: Traditional reminder prompts ("Time for medicine") do not prompt the user to verify whether they have already taken medication. The check-in prompt ("Have you taken it yet?") introduces a verification step that caused members to "reflect on whether they had actually taken their medication before responding, rather than reflexively acknowledging an alarm" (a11ybob review, https://a11ybob.com/writing/reviews/69b5e7499b738afcf5d887e7). In some cases, this led users to physically check their pillbox, catching potential over-medication or missed doses.

**Positive reinforcement**: When users confirmed already having taken medication, MATCHA generated positive feedback. However, Phase 1 feedback was found to be "overly enthusiastic" and was toned down in Phase 2 — a revision that contributed to higher engagement.

**Multi-scenario confirmation**: The system handled ambiguity by prompting further verification (e.g., "Are you sure? Would you like to check your pillbox?") rather than accepting uncertain responses at face value.

**Reprompt strategies**: Research on reprompts with elderly and MCI users in confirmation/disconfirmation contexts (IEEE RO-MAN 2017, https://doi.org/10.1109/roman.2017.8172319) found that after three successive reprompts, users either added problem manifestations (signaling confusion) or initiated the relevant next move. All users successfully responded to the first reprompt, but failure rates increased with successive reprompts. This suggests a practical limit of 1–2 reprompts before the system should adapt its strategy.

**Recovery strategy effectiveness**: A comparative study of AskRepeat vs. RepromptThenSay strategies (https://shaulashkenazi.com/publications/2025_RO_MAN_LBR__effective_recovery_strategies_in_conversations_with_older_adults.pdf) tested with 13 younger (22–29) and 13 older (66–81) participants found that **RepromptThenSay was more effective for both age groups**. Having any recovery strategy was critical: all failed interactions involved failed recovery. Older and younger users performed equally well with these strategies, though older users encountered more issues and were "more likely to be annoyed" but found the system "as likable and habitable as younger users."

## 4. Error Recovery Mechanisms

### 4.1 Error Taxonomy

The 20-week MATCHA deployment (844 recorded interactions, 14 participants) revealed four categories of conversational breakdowns (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06690):

1. **Breakdown in Historical Understanding (26% of 324 total breakdown instances, 220 instances)**: The AI's inability to recall prior interactions, especially previous medication intake reports. This was the most impactful category for medication management tasks, as it undermined user trust in the system's reliability.

2. **Breakdown in Language and Semantics (39%, 126 instances)**: When the AI's phrasing did not align with natural speech, leading to perceptions of the system as "robotic" or "nerdy." Users responded by rephrasing or code-switching.

3. **Breakdown in Flow (21%, 68 instances)**: When users deviated from the structured dialogue with off-topic or related queries, the AI rigidly adhered to its original task rather than integrating the digression.

4. **Breakdown in Explanations**: When the AI could not explain why it responded in a particular way.

### 4.2 Error Rates and ASR Performance

A study of 83 older adults across cognitive groups (cognitively normal, MCI, dementia) reading commands to Amazon Alexa (ACM CHI 2026, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3772318.3791581) found that **ASR errors are significantly higher for individuals with dementia**. Acoustic analysis revealed that speaker intensity, voice quality, and pause ratio predicted ASR accuracy. Mean word error rates (WER) for dementia speakers were approximately 8–11 percentage points higher than for cognitively normal controls (consistent findings in https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3816046.3816217).

A month-long in-home study with older adults (ACM TACCESS 2026, https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3796236) found that **80% of errors were identifiable from users' immediate verbal reactions** (negation, remarks, recovery attempts), yet current commercial voice assistants leveraged these cues in less than 5% of cases. Repetition was the most prevalent user-initiated recovery strategy (n=373 instances). The study found **no distinct changes in recovery strategy patterns or error resolution rates over 4 weeks**, indicating that users did not learn to interact more effectively over time.

### 4.3 System-Initiated vs. User-Initiated Recovery

When the VA itself initiated recovery (providing alternatives or asking for clarification), **resolution rates were notably higher** than user-initiated recovery. However, Alexa only initiated recovery in fewer than 5% of errors (29 out of 632), while user-initiated recovery occurred in 65% of errors (ACM TACCESS 2026). This represents a massive missed opportunity for system design.

The flexdiam dialogue management framework (ACL SIGDIAL 2017, https://aclanthology.org/W17-5533.pdf) was specifically designed for users with cognitive impairments, featuring incremental processing of uncertain input, flexible mixed-initiative grounding processes adapted to individual cognitive capacities, and mechanisms fostering controllable discourse state transitions. This framework demonstrated that robust interaction is achievable when the system adapts to users' interactive idiosyncrasies rather than requiring users to adapt to rigid dialogue structures.

## 5. Multi-Modal Feedback: Voice + Visual + Haptic

**Voice + Visual (MATCHA)**: The Google Home Hub's combination of voice and touchscreen display was critical for the MATCHA deployment. Touch-based interactions accounted for 20–35% of total interactions, serving as an essential fallback when speech recognition failed or when members had difficulty being understood. The display of voice commands and responses on screen "eliminated the need for participants to remember what they said" (https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3517428.3544830).

**Voice + Visual + Physical Embodiment (Mabu)**: Mabu combines voice, touchscreen, and robotic physical presence including eye contact and head movement. The physical embodiment was shown in Kidd's RCT to produce better adherence outcomes than screen-only interfaces running identical software. However, long-term data specifically for the MCI population is limited.

**Voice + Visual + Haptic (Emerging)**: A 2026 discrete choice experiment with 203 older adults (Frontiers in Medicine, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2026.1749507/full) quantified preference structures for reminder modality, confirmation method, font/layout, wearable integration, and environmental adaptation. Key findings:
- Older adults showed **positive utility estimates for multimodal reminders** (voice + visual + haptic combined)
- **Single-tap confirmation** was preferred over complex confirmation sequences
- **Coordinated smartphone–smartwatch use** was preferred under wearable integration
- **Context-adaptive** and **biophilic themes** were associated with positive utility estimates

A study on hybrid stimulation (light + sound) for medication reminders (ACM AH 2019, https://doi.org/10.1145/3305160.3305201) tested response times among 10 elderly and 10 young adults. While no significant difference in response time was found between single-modality and hybrid stimulation conditions in this small sample, the approach of combining modalities aligns with the broader preference data.

A 10-month deployment of a sensor-augmented pillbox with an ambient display providing near real-time visual feedback (ACM CHI 2014, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2556288.2557210) demonstrated that feedback helped improve consistency of medication-taking behaviors and increased self-efficacy ratings in older adults. However, improved performance **did not persist after the feedback display was removed** — participants had integrated the display into their routines as a self-awareness and error-detection tool, suggesting that sustained multi-modal feedback is necessary for continued adherence support.

## 6. Interaction Sequences Correlating with Sustained Engagement Beyond 90 Days

Drawing across all three systems and supporting studies, the following interaction sequences correlate with sustained engagement beyond 90 days:

1. **Check-in prompting with reflective verification** (MATCHA): The sequence of personalized greeting → check-in question → reflective pause → user verification → positive reinforcement showed engagement rates increasing from 18% to 85–90% over 20 weeks, with sustained use at 55+ weeks. This is the strongest evidence for long-term engagement.

2. **Gradual withdrawal of assistance** (Mexico feasibility study, 25 weeks, https://revistaaihc.mx/index.php/aihc/article/view/206): A voice-based conversational agent using behavioral habit-formation strategy — associating medication with contextual cues and gradually withdrawing assistance — showed "significant improvement in medication-taking consistency and a strengthening of the habit that persisted even after the agent's assistance was gradually withdrawn, indicating that it did not create dependency."

3. **Multi-modal redundancy** (MATCHA, Mabu): Systems offering both voice and visual/touchscreen interaction sustained engagement longer than voice-only systems. The MedBuddy Alexa study (voice-primary) showed engagement on only ~51% of days, while MATCHA (voice + touch) reached 85–90% engagement.

4. **Collaborative dyad notification** (MATCHA): Notifications to carepartners when members did not respond created a safety net that supported continued use without imposing surveillance. Carepartners valued receiving phone notifications about medication status.

5. **Personalization of interaction timing and style** (MATCHA, Mabu): Both systems adapted greeting style, volume, and timing to individual routines. Mabu continuously refined its psychological, medical, and interaction models per patient.

## 7. Longitudinal Usability Findings

### 7.1 Task Completion Rates

- **MATCHA**: Of 1120 system initiations in Phase 2, 760 interactions (responses) were recorded, yielding a **67% engagement rate** that rose to 85–90% in final weeks. The system handled over 200 recognized response types.
- **MedBuddy (Alexa)**: Interactions occurred on **50.97%** of study days (SD 29.5) over 60 days.
- **InTakeCare (Alexa)**: SUS median score of **77.5** (IQR 11.25) over 7 days.
- **Telephone reminders for MCI/AD patients** (PMC9644062, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9644062/): Mean response rate was **51.3%** across the intervention group; among the high-compliance subgroup (>70% response rate), medication adherence was 94.6% vs. 90.2% for controls (p=0.048). This RCT with 29 participants (mean age 79.6, SD 6.0) over 6 months confirms that compliance with the reminder system itself is the critical variable.
- **Robotic medication dispenser** (Clin Ther 2017, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clinthera.2017.03.020): 27 home-care elderly patients achieved **99% on-time sachet retrieval** across alerts, with 97.7% on-time retrieval in Phase I (17 nursing home patients). All patients and 96% of nurses reported the device was easy to use.

### 7.2 Error Types During Voice Input

The most detailed error taxonomy comes from the month-long in-home study with older adults (ACM TACCESS 2026, https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3796236):

- **Intent recognition errors**: The VA misidentified user intent
- **"Not handled" errors**: The VA could not process the request
- **Speech/transcription errors**: Listening failures and ASR transcription mistakes
- **Partial listening**: The VA received incomplete utterances (particularly problematic for MCI users who pause longer and more frequently)
- **Action not available**: System limitations in requested functionality

The study found that **80% of errors were detectable from users' verbal reactions**, yet the VA initiated recovery in fewer than 5% of cases. Repetition was the most common user recovery strategy (n=373), followed by reformulation and clarification. No improvement in error resolution rates was observed over the 4-week study period.

For dementia speakers specifically, ASR word error rates were **8–11 percentage points higher** than for cognitively normal controls, driven by differences in speech intensity, voice quality, and pause ratio (ACM CHI 2026). This has direct implications for medication management tasks in the target population.

The incremental clarification request (iCR) approach (PMC11285561, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11285561/) addresses premature interruption of MCI/dementia users, who pause longer and more frequently. Current voice assistants interrupt them prematurely, causing frustration and interaction breakdown. Generating contextually appropriate clarification requests was shown to only emerge at larger LLM sizes when prompted with example iCRs.

### 7.3 Patient-Reported Confidence Scores and Prompt Verbosity

**Confidence and acceptance**: MATCHA achieved SUS scores of **84.66** (members) and **86.16** (carepartners) — well above the usability threshold. All 5 completing dyads wanted continued use. The osteoporosis DVA study showed 6-month intervention adherence of 79.5% (95% CI: 73.9–84.9) for session access.

**Prompt verbosity**: The CHI 2025 voice assistant study (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3706598.3713839) found that a **hierarchical content structure** was preferred: the VA presents one aspect of the summary and allows the user to ask questions before proceeding. Participants acknowledged that medication-related discussions required greater verbosity ("I guess because it was talking about medication, it had to say more... You have to give more information so it's gotta solicit more information"). The study specifically designed against "verbose responses that disrupt conversational flow" by implementing step-by-step hierarchical delivery.

A retrospective analysis of a multimodal conversational agent for chronic disease management (Journal of Medical Systems 2025, https://doi.org/10.1007/s10916-025-02202-2) with 14,194 users found a counterintuitive result: **higher mean confidence scores in CA responses were linked to lower odds of continued engagement**. The authors hypothesized that sustained users engaged with more complex queries over time (generating lower confidence scores), and that high-confidence responses might appear "overly rigid, impersonal, or lacking" nuance. Medium clinical context (OR=1.56) and low clinical context (OR=1.07) both increased odds of long-term engagement relative to high clinical context.

**Confirmation strategy preferences**: The discrete choice experiment (Frontiers in Medicine 2026) found that older adults preferred **single-tap confirmation** over complex multi-step verification. The MATCHA design, with its touchscreen button fallback (20–35% of interactions), aligns with this preference. The RepromptThenSay recovery strategy outperformed AskRepeat for both age groups, though the key finding was that having any structured recovery strategy was more important than which specific strategy was used.

## 8. Comparative Synthesis

| Dimension | Amazon Alexa | Google Assistant (MATCHA) | Catalia Health Mabu |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Paradigm** | Reminder/Alarm | Check-in (reflective verification) | Daily conversational check-in |
| **Multi-modal** | Voice primary; limited screen | Voice + touchscreen (20–35% touch use) | Voice + touchscreen + physical embodiment |
| **Longest sustained evidence** | 12 months (no adherence effect); 1+ year for general use | 55+ weeks (continued voluntary use) | 12-month pilots; limited published outcomes |
| **Engagement rate** | ~51% of days (60-day study) | 67% → 85–90% over 20 weeks | Not quantified in public literature |
| **SUS scores** | 77.5 (7-day pilot) | 84.66 (members) / 86.16 (carepartners) | Not reported |
| **Error recovery** | System initiates <5% of errors | Multi-scenario handling (200+ responses); touch fallback | Adaptive conversation with psychological modeling |
| **Over-medication prevention** | No (one-way reminder) | Yes (check-in prompts reflection and pillbox checking) | Yes (daily conversation queries adherence) |
| **Caregiver integration** | Limited | Phone notifications to carepartners | Data shared with clinical teams |
| **Habit formation** | No evidence | Sustained 55+ weeks | Relationship-building emphasis |

## 9. Key Conclusions

1. **The "check-in" paradigm outperforms "remind."** The MATCHA system's core insight — asking "Have you taken it yet?" rather than commanding "Take your medication" — directly addresses over-medication risk in MCI while triggering reflective behavior that sustained engagement for over a year. This is the single most impactful interaction design pattern identified in the evidence base.

2. **Multi-modal redundancy is essential, not optional.** Systems with voice + visual feedback (MATCHA: 20–35% touch-based interactions) sustain engagement longer than voice-only systems (MedBuddy: ~51% engagement). The emerging preference data strongly favors multi-modal reminders including haptic channels.

3. **System-initiated recovery is critically underutilized.** Current commercial VAs initiate recovery in fewer than 5% of errors despite 80% of errors being detectable from user reactions. This represents the largest design gap for healthcare applications where interaction failure can mean missed medication.

4. **Prompt verbosity should be hierarchical, not uniform.** Medication-related conversations legitimately require more detail, but delivery should be step-by-step with user control over pacing. Single-tap confirmation is preferred over complex multi-step verification.

5. **Sustained engagement beyond 90 days requires personalization, caregiver integration, and habit formation.** The Mexico study's 25-week demonstration that a conversational agent can build medication-taking habits that persist after withdrawal provides the strongest evidence that voice-first systems can produce lasting behavioral change rather than dependency. MATCHA's 55+ week continued use provides the longest documented voluntary sustained engagement for an MCI-specific medication management system.

6. **ASR performance degrades significantly for dementia speakers** (8–11 percentage points higher WER), making human-in-the-loop correction, speaker-personalized ASR, and multi-modal fallback critical design requirements for any voice-first healthcare system targeting this population.

# Options-Trading Framework for a $700 Account

## Educational Reference — Not Personalized Financial Advice

---

## Critical Preface: The Math of $200–300/Week on $700

Before defining any rules, the quantitative reality must be stated plainly.

A $200 weekly return on $700 represents a **28.6% weekly return**. A $300 target is a **42.9% weekly return**. Compounded, these figures imply annualized returns of 47 million percent and 11 billion percent, respectively. For context, the world's best hedge funds average 30–40% *per year*.

Running 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations across 52 weeks with defined-risk spreads (debit or credit), even at favorable win rates of 55–68%, **no realistic parameter set consistently produces $200–$300 per week on a $700 account**. The simulations show:

- **Conservative credit spreads** (68% WR, $20 win / $55 loss, 4 trades/week): Expected weekly P&L of **−$16**, with a 62% account blow-up rate over one year.
- **Moderate debit spreads** (58% WR, $40 win / $50 loss, 4 trades/week): Expected weekly P&L of **+$9**, with 0% of weeks reaching $200.
- **Aggressive debit spreads** (55% WR, $65 win / $50 loss, 5 trades/week): Expected weekly P&L of **+$66**, the most favorable realistic scenario — but still far below $200/week.

**Bottom line:** Consistently generating $200–$300/week from $700 requires either (a) taking on portfolio-level risk that will eventually destroy the account, or (b) achieving win rates above 80–90% that no documented strategy sustains. The framework below is structured for **education in sound options risk management**, with realistic weekly targets of **$30–$70** on a $700 account. The components the user requested are all provided; the target-income math is presented honestly.

*Sources: Option Alpha position sizing guidance ([optionalpha.com](https://optionalpha.com/blog/how-many-options-contracts-you-can-trade)); OptionsPilot small-account sizing ([optionspilot.app](https://optionspilot.app/blog/how-to-size-options-trades-small-accounts)); Fidelity options education ([fidelity.com](https://www.fidelity.com/viewpoints/active-investor/options-trade-size)).*

---

## 1. Position-Sizing Rules and Maximum Risk Per Trade

### Core Formula

```
Max risk per trade = Account equity × Risk percentage
Max contracts = Floor(Max risk per trade ÷ Stress loss per contract)
```

### Rules for a $700 Account

| Rule | Value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Max risk per trade** | **$35–$50** (5–7% of account) | At 2% ($14), no defined-risk spread can be traded. 5–7% is the practical floor for small accounts while still requiring 14–20 consecutive max losses to wipe out the account. ([optionalpha.com](https://optionalpha.com/blog/how-many-options-contracts-you-should-trade)) |
| **Max simultaneous positions** | **2** | Keeps total portfolio heat at $100 maximum (14.3% of account). Avoids over-concentration. ([optionspilot.app](https://optionspilot.app/blog/how-to-size-options-trades-small-accounts)) |
| **Max in any single underlying** | **1 position** | No doubling down on one ticker. |
| **Cash reserve** | **≥ $200** (≈30% of account) | Covers assignment surprises and provides flexibility. With $700, this means at most $500 deployed across positions. |
| **Hard stop: max portfolio heat** | **$100** (14.3%) | If 2 positions are open at $50 max risk each, no third trade until one closes. |
| **Weekly loss limit** | **$100** (14.3%) | If cumulative closed losses in a calendar week hit $100, stop trading for the week. |

### Position Sizing Calculation Example

Suppose you find a $1-wide bull put spread that collects $0.40 credit:
- Max loss per contract = ($1.00 − $0.40) × 100 = **$60**
- Your max risk per trade is $50
- $50 ÷ $60 = 0.83 → **Floor = 0 contracts** — this trade does not fit.
- A narrower $0.50-wide spread collecting $0.20 has a max loss of $30. $50 ÷ $30 = 1.67 → **1 contract**. This fits.

*Sources: Option Alpha position sizing framework ([optionalpha.com](https://optionalpha.com/blog/how-many-options-contracts-you-can-trade)); Fidelity trade sizing guide ([fidelity.com](https://www.fidelity.com/viewpoints/active-investor/options-trade-size)); Financial Context Wiki sizing model ([wiki.fcontext.com](https://wiki.fcontext.com/options/position-sizing-options/)).*

---

## 2. Permitted Option Strategies

### Allowed (Defined-Risk Only)

| Strategy | Direction | Max Risk Defined? | Best Environment | Typical R:R |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bull Call Debit Spread** | Bullish | ✅ Debit paid | Low IV (IV Rank < 30) | 1:1 to 1:1.5 |
| **Bear Put Debit Spread** | Bearish | ✅ Debit paid | Low IV (IV Rank < 30) | 1:1 to 1:1.5 |
| **Bull Put Credit Spread** | Bullish/Neutral | ✅ Width − credit | High IV (IV Rank > 50) | 1:0.3 to 1:0.5 |
| **Bear Call Credit Spread** | Bearish/Neutral | ✅ Width − credit | High IV (IV Rank > 50) | 1:0.3 to 1:0.5 |
| **Long Call / Long Put** (single-leg) | Directional | ✅ Premium paid | Low IV, high-conviction setups | Variable |

### Strategy Selection Decision Tree

```
Is IV Rank above 50?
├── YES → Sell premium: Credit spreads (bull put or bear call)
│         Target: 50–70% probability of profit
│         Manage: Buy back at 50% of credit received
└── NO  → Buy premium: Debit spreads (bull call or bear put)
          Target: Directional move within 3–14 days
          Manage: Sell at 50–75% of max profit
```

*Sources: ApexVol debit vs. credit spread comparison ([apexvol.com](https://apexvol.com/compare/debit-spread-vs-credit-spread)); Option Alpha small-account strategies ([optionalpha.com](https://optionalpha.com/lessons/small-account-options-strategies)).*

### Prohibited

- Naked short calls or puts (undefined risk)
- Naked strangles/straddles
- Any strategy with margin requirements exceeding account equity
- Selling options on earnings week (binary event risk)

---

## 3. Stock Selection Criteria Based on Technicals

### Universe Filter (Applied First)

| Criterion | Minimum Threshold | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Average daily stock volume** | ≥ 2 million shares/day | Ensures underlying liquidity for tight option spreads |
| **Option open interest** | ≥ 500 contracts at target strikes | Ensures two-sided market; [optionvisualizer.com](https://www.optionvisualizer.com/documentation/workflows/liquidity-screening) |
| **Stock price range** | $50–$300 | Below $50, option chains have wide strike intervals; above $300, each contract controls too much notional value for a $700 account |
| **Weekly options available** | Yes | Required for 3–21 DTE targets |
| **No earnings within 5 days** | Excluded | Binary event risk violates defined-risk assumptions |

### Technical Entry Criteria

**Primary Filters (must all be true):**

1. **Trend:** Price above 20-day EMA for bullish trades; below 20-day EMA for bearish trades. Optionally confirm with 50-day SMA direction.
2. **Volume confirmation:** Today's volume or 10-day average volume ≥ 1.5× the 50-day average volume (indicates institutional participation).
3. **Support/Resistance proximity:** For bullish entries, price must be within 2% of a clearly defined support level (prior swing low, horizontal pivot). For bearish entries, within 2% of resistance.
4. **RSI (14-period):** For bullish trades, RSI between 40–60 (pullback in uptrend, not overbought). For bearish trades, RSI between 40–60 (bounce in downtrend, not oversold). Avoid RSI > 70 for buys or RSI < 30 for sells.

**Secondary Filters (at least 2 of 3):**

5. **MACD:** Histogram turning positive (bullish) or negative (bearish), or signal-line crossover within last 3 bars.
6. **VWAP:** For intraday entries, price holding above VWAP (bullish) or below VWAP (bearish).
7. **Sector relative strength:** Stock outperforming its sector ETF over the last 5 days (for longs) or underperforming (for shorts).

*Sources: Fidelity technical analysis for options ([fidelity.com PDF](https://www.fidelity.com/bin-public/060_www_fidelity_com/documents/learning-center/Transcript_Technical-analysis-for-options_v2.pdf)); ProsperityPub stock selection for options ([prosperitypub.com](https://prosperitypub.com/graham-lindman/how-to-pick-the-right-stocks-for-high-probability-options-trades/)); EasyStreetInvesting TA integration ([easystreetinvesting.com](https://www.easystreetinvesting.com/applying-technical-analysis-in-options-trading-strategies/)).*

---

## 4. Strike and Expiry Selection Rules (3–21 Day Holds)

### Expiry Selection

| Trade Type | Target DTE | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Debit spreads** (directional momentum) | **7–14 DTE** | Maximizes gamma exposure for quick directional moves; theta decay is the cost of admission. ([daystoexpiry.com](https://www.daystoexpiry.com/blog/bull-call-spread-dte)) |
| **Credit spreads** (theta collection) | **14–21 DTE** | Sweet spot: meaningful theta decay per day without excessive gamma risk. Entering at 30–45 DTE and exiting at 21 DTE is the standard; for a small account targeting faster turnover, 14–21 DTE entry is acceptable. ([optionscanner.ai](https://optionscanner.ai/learn/choosing-an-expiration)) |
| **Single-leg long options** | **7–14 DTE** | Maximum leverage per dollar, but requires precise timing. Only for highest-conviction setups. |

**Hard rule:** Never hold a short option (credit spread) past 7 DTE. The gamma explosion in the final week makes risk management unreliable. Close or roll before then.

### Strike Selection

**For Debit Spreads (Bull Call / Bear Put):**
- **Long leg:** ATM or slightly ITM (delta 0.45–0.55). ATM options have the highest gamma, providing the most responsive P&L to price movement.
- **Short leg:** OTM, $1–$2 above the long call (or below the long put). The short leg reduces cost and caps max profit but improves probability vs. a naked long option.
- **Spread width:** $1–$2. Maximum $2 wide on a $700 account (max loss $50–$200 per contract before adjusting to position-sizing rules).

**For Credit Spreads (Bull Put / Bear Call):**
- **Short leg:** OTM, delta 0.20–0.30. This corresponds roughly to a 70–80% probability the option expires worthless.
- **Long leg:** $0.50–$1.00 further OTM from the short leg.
- **Spread width:** $0.50–$1.00 maximum on a $700 account to keep max loss ≤ $50.

**For Single-Leg Long Options:**
- Delta 0.30–0.50 for a balance of cost and responsiveness.
- Premium ≤ $0.50 ($50/contract) to fit within the risk budget.

*Sources: DaysToExpiry DTE framework ([daystoexpiry.com](https://www.daystoexpiry.com/blog/bull-call-spread-dte)); sTraderZ credit/debit spread setup guide ([straderz.com](https://straderz.com/en/learn/trading-strategies-module-4-directional-spreads)); CallPut.app strike selection docs ([docs.callput.app](https://docs.callput.app/options-education/choosing-strikes-expiries-and-trade-plans)).*

---

## 5. Liquidity Filters

Every trade must pass ALL five filters before entry:

| Filter | Threshold | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Open Interest (at your strike)** | **≥ 500 contracts** (≥ 1,000 preferred) | Ensures a two-sided market and reduces risk of being trapped in a position. ([optionvisualizer.com](https://www.optionvisualizer.com/documentation/workflows/liquidity-screening)) |

## 7. Win-Rate and Probability Distribution Analysis

### The Mathematical Requirement

To achieve a specific weekly income target, the expected value per trade must satisfy:

```
E[trade] = (Win Rate × Avg Win) − ((1 − Win Rate) × Avg Loss)
Weekly Target = E[trade] × Trades per Week
Solving for Win Rate:
Win Rate = (Weekly Target / Trades per Week + Avg Loss) / (Avg Win + Avg Loss)
```

### Required Win Rates by Scenario

| Trades/Week | Avg Win | Avg Loss | R:R | Win Rate for $100/wk | Win Rate for $200/wk | Win Rate for $300/wk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | $50 | $50 | 1:1 | 66.7% | 83.3% | 100.0% |
| 4 | $50 | $50 | 1:1 | 62.5% | 75.0% | 87.5% |
| 5 | $50 | $50 | 1:1 | 60.0% | 70.0% | 80.0% |
| 4 | $75 | $50 | 1.5:1 | 60.0% | 80.0% | 100.0% |
| 5 | $75 | $50 | 1.5:1 | 56.0% | 72.0% | 88.0% |
| 5 | $100 | $50 | 2:1 | 53.3% | 66.7% | 80.0% |

### Probability Distribution (Most Achievable Scenario)

Using the **"Aggressive Debit Spreads"** simulation (5 trades/week, 55% WR, $65 win / $50 loss, 1.3:1 R:R), which is the best-performing realistic parameter set from our Monte Carlo:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Expected weekly P&L | **+$66** |
| Median annual P&L | **+$3,445** |
| % of weeks profitable | **59%** |
| % of weeks with $100+ gain | **26%** |
| % of weeks with $200+ gain | **26%** |
| % of weeks with $300+ gain | **~5%** |
| Account blow-up rate (1 year) | **0%** (defined-risk) |
| Worst-case 10th percentile annual | **+$2,295** |

### What This Means in Practice

- At a 55% win rate with 1.3:1 reward-to-risk, you can expect roughly **$60–70/week** on average, or about **$3,000–3,500 per year** — a 430–500% annual return, which is already extraordinary.
- You will have losing weeks approximately 41% of the time.
- Hitting $200 in a single week happens about 26% of weeks (roughly once a month), but this is driven by favorable streaks, not a baseline expectation.
- $300/week requires sustained win rates above 80% at these risk parameters — achievable in short bursts but not as a long-run average.
- The path to $200–300/week sustainably requires **growing the account** first: start with $700 targeting $50–70/week, compound to $2,000–3,000 over 6–12 months, and then $200/week becomes a 7–10% weekly target — aggressive but structurally more feasible.
