final.content:
# Cloud Genomics Platform Comparison: AWS vs. Google Cloud vs. Microsoft Azure for Petabyte-Scale Analysis

## Executive Summary

This report evaluates AWS (HealthOmics, HealthLake), Google Cloud (Healthcare API, Terra.bio), and Microsoft Azure (Genomics, Terra on Azure) across five dimensions: bioinformatics tool availability, simultaneous HIPAA/GDPR/China PIPL compliance, federated analysis support, variant-calling performance, and total cost for 100,000 whole genomes annually, including data egress traps.

**Key finding:** No single platform simultaneously satisfies China's data residency requirements and offers native petabyte-scale genomics services in-country. Google Cloud has no mainland China region at all. AWS China and Azure China (via 21Vianet) exist but do not offer HealthOmics or equivalent managed genomics services. All three platforms support HIPAA and GDPR. For variant-calling cost at scale, Azure (via Sentieon) and AWS (via Parabricks Ready2Run) show the lowest published per-genome compute costs, while Google Cloud/Terra offers the richest curated bioinformatics ecosystem through the Broad Institute partnership.

---

## 1. Bioinformatics Tool Availability

### AWS (HealthOmics + HealthLake)

AWS HealthOmics is a fully managed service that supports three industry-standard workflow languages: **WDL, Nextflow, and CWL** (https://aws.amazon.com/healthomics/). It offers two workflow modalities:

- **Ready2Run workflows**: Pre-built pipelines from third parties including NVIDIA Parabricks, Sentieon, Broad Institute GATK, Element Biosciences, Ultima Genomics, Google DeepMind (AlphaFold), and Meta Research (ESMFold). The Ready2Run catalog includes GATK Best Practices germline (fq2vcf for 30x genome, bam2vcf), GATK somatic WES, NVIDIA Parabricks germline DeepVariant, HaplotypeCaller, and multiple alignment workflows (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/omics/latest/dev/workflows-r2r-table.html).
- **Private workflows**: Users bring their own WDL/CWL/Nextflow definitions with custom Docker containers stored in Amazon ECR.

HealthOmics also includes **Sequence Stores** (with automatic compression, tiering, and S3-compatible URIs as of April 2024), **Reference Stores**, **Variant Stores**, and **Annotation Stores** — though variant and annotation stores are no longer open to new customers (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/omics/latest/dev/omics-analytics.html).

HealthLake provides FHIR-based health data management but is not a genomics-specific analytics platform; it complements HealthOmics for clinical data integration.

AWS also supports running **DRAGEN** (via AWS Marketplace on F1/F2 FPGA instances), **Sentieon** (via EC2), and **Clara Parabricks** (on GPU instances) outside HealthOmics (https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-ypz2tpzy6f5xq).

### Google Cloud (Healthcare API + Terra.bio)

Google Cloud's genomics ecosystem centers on **Terra.bio** (developed by the Broad Institute, Microsoft, and Verily), which is the primary platform for running GATK Best Practices pipelines. Terra runs workflows via the **Cromwell** WDL execution engine on Google Cloud's Pipelines API (https://gatk.broadinstitute.org/hc/en-us/articles/360035530892).

Key tool availability on Terra includes:
- Full **GATK4** suite: germline preprocessing, variant calling, joint calling, somatic SNVs/Indels (Mutect2), germline and somatic CNVs, RNA germline variant calling, mitochondrial variant discovery, CNN variant filter, Funcotator annotations (https://support.terra.bio/hc/en-us/articles/360029034232).
- **DeepVariant** (Google's deep-learning variant caller), including pangenome-aware Giraffe/DeepVariant pipelines (https://support.terra.bio/hc/en-us/articles/7420514067995).
- **DRAGEN-GATK** pipelines (functional equivalence and maximum quality modes).
- **seqr** for rare disease genomics variant analysis (https://terra.bio/rare-disease-genomics-with-seqr-in-terra/).
- Interactive analysis via **Jupyter Notebooks, RStudio, Galaxy** within workspaces.
- Access to public datasets including TCGA, 1000 Genomes, and AnVIL's 5+ PB corpus (https://anvilproject.org/news/2024/04/15/comparing-the-nhgri-anvil-platform).

The **Cloud Healthcare API** provides FHIR, HL7v2, and DICOM data stores but is not a genomics analysis engine; it serves clinical data interoperability (https://docs.cloud.google.com/healthcare-api/docs/introduction).

**Note:** Cloud Life Sciences (Google's managed workflow service) is **deprecated** as of July 2025, with migration to Google Cloud Batch recommended (https://cloud.google.com/life-sciences/docs/tutorials/gatk).

### Microsoft Azure (Genomics + Terra on Azure)

Azure's genomics capabilities are built on open-source workflow managers rather than a single managed genomics service:

- **Cromwell on Azure**: Broad Institute's workflow engine running on Azure Batch with GA4GH TES (Task Execution Service) backend (https://microsoft.github.io/Genomics-Community/cromwell.html).
- **Nextflow on Azure**: Via Azure Batch and Kubernetes.
- **Snakemake on Azure**: Scalable to server, cluster, grid, and cloud.
- **Microsoft Genomics Service**: A turnkey service for BWA+GATK secondary analysis, ISO-certified and HIPAA BAA-covered (https://microsoft.github.io/Genomics-Community/mydoc_offerings.html).
- **Terra on Azure**: Generally available since January 2024, offering the same Broad Institute workflows as Terra on GCP but deployable within an organization's Azure tenant with Active Directory integration (https://www.broadinstitute.org/news/terra-azure-release).
- **Sentieon on Azure**: Benchmarked at **$0.11 per 30x WGS** (alignment + variant calling in ~18–20 minutes on commodity CPUs) as of September 2024 (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/frankhu1_update-cost-effective-genomics-analysis-activity-7242244343057543170-eKa1).
- **DRAGEN on Azure NP-series VMs** with FPGA acceleration via Azure CycleCloud (https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/healthcareandlifesciencesblog/enhancing-genomic-analysis-with-hybrid-cloud-a-microsoft-azure-perspective/4026189).
- **Bioconductor on Azure**, Genomics Notebooks for variant analysis.
- **Illumina DRAGEN** integration with Azure NP-series FPGAs.

---

## 2. Compliance: HIPAA / GDPR / China's Data Laws (Simultaneous)

### HIPAA

| Platform | HIPAA Status |
|----------|-------------|
| **AWS HealthOmics** | HIPAA-eligible. Requires execution of a BAA with AWS. HITRUST CSF, FedRAMP Moderate, ISO/CSA STAR, C5 certified (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_cn/omics/latest/dev/compliance-validation.html). |
| **Google Cloud** | Healthcare API and Terra are covered under Google Cloud's HIPAA BAA. ISO 27001/27017/27018, PCI DSS certified. Assured Workloads provides US Data Boundary for Healthcare and Life Sciences (https://docs.cloud.google.com/healthcare-api/docs/introduction, https://docs.cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/docs/control-packages/us-data-boundary-healthcare-life-sciences). |
| **Azure** | HIPAA BAA available. HITRUST CSF certified (one of the first hyperscale providers). Azure Health Data Services is FHIR/DICOM-native (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/industry/healthcare/compliance-overview). |

**All three platforms support HIPAA compliance.** Compliance is shared-responsibility — the customer must configure services appropriately.

### GDPR

| Platform | GDPR Status |
|----------|------------|
| **AWS** | GDPR-compliant. GDPR Data Processing Addendum available. Data protection center at aws.amazon.com/compliance/data-protection/. Customers can restrict data to EU regions (e.g., Frankfurt, Ireland, London). |
| **Google Cloud** | GDPR-compliant. Cloud DPA available. Data location controls allow EU-only storage. HDS v2.0 certification in EEA scope with specific products (https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/hds). |
| **Azure** | GDPR-compliant. Microsoft DPA available. Data residency guarantees — customer data stored in selected geo, not processed outside it (https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/explore/global-infrastructure/data-residency). |

**All three platforms support GDPR compliance** through data residency controls, DPAs, and EU-region availability.

### China's Data Laws (PIPL / CSL / DSL)

This is where significant divergence emerges.

**China's requirements under PIPL, CSL, and DSL:**
- Personal information and "important data" collected/generated in China must be stored in China by default.
- Cross-border transfers require CAC security assessment for: CIIOs transferring PI/important data; processors handling PI of >1M individuals; cumulative transfers of PI of >100,000 individuals or sensitive PI of >10,000 individuals (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/china/overview-sovereignty-and-regulations, https://en.zhonglun.com/research/articles/52470.html).
- Healthcare data, including genomic data, is classified as sensitive personal information under PIPL. Human Genetic Resources (HGR) data faces additional restrictions under China's HGR regulations.

| Platform | China Data Residency Capability |
|----------|-------------------------------|
| **AWS** | AWS China (Beijing, operated by Sinnet; Ningxia, operated by NWCD) exists as a separate partition. However, **AWS HealthOmics is NOT available in AWS China regions.** HealthOmics is available in US, Europe, Asia Pacific (Singapore, Tokyo), and Israel — but not in cn-north-1 or cn-northwest-1 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/omics/latest/dev/what-is-healthomics.html). Customers must use generic EC2/S3 in China regions and self-manage genomics pipelines. |
| **Google Cloud** | **No mainland China region exists.** Google has no cloud infrastructure inside mainland China. The closest regions are Taiwan (asia-east1) and Hong Kong (asia-east2), both outside the mainland. Google officially shut down its "Isolated Region" project and does not offer cloud services in China (https://www.21cloudbox.com/support/google-cloud-china.html, https://www.platformexecutive.com/news/search-engines/news-short-google-shuts-down-isolated-region-cloud-project/). ICP filing for China-facing services requires in-country infrastructure Google does not provide. |
| **Azure** | Azure China (operated by **21Vianet**) provides regions in Shanghai (China East), Beijing (China North), Jiangsu (China East 3), Hebei (China North 3). Customer data is replicated only within China. However, **Azure Health Data Services, Terra on Azure, and Cromwell on Azure availability in 21Vianet-operated regions is not confirmed** from the evidence gathered. Generic Azure compute and storage are available. Microsoft explicitly documents China data residency: "21Vianet may replicate customer data in at least two datacenters for data resiliency and availability but always within China" (https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/final/en-us/microsoft-brand/documents/1_data-residency-in-azure-2024-06-20.pdf). |

**Critical finding for China compliance:** If your biotech company must process genomics data within mainland China to satisfy PIPL and HGR regulations, **no platform offers a fully managed genomics analysis service in-country.** You would need to deploy self-managed pipelines (Cromwell, Nextflow) on generic compute in AWS China or Azure China regions. Google Cloud is entirely non-viable for China data residency. This requires significant engineering investment and means forgoing the managed-service benefits of HealthOmics, Terra, or equivalent.

---

## 3. Federated Analysis Across Institutions

### AWS

- **Cross-account workflow sharing** (announced April 2024): HealthOmics private workflows can be shared across AWS accounts within or across organizations. Users can run shared workflows without configuring underlying scripts (https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2024/04/aws-healthomics-cross-account-sharing-private-workflows/).
- AWS HealthOmics supports data sharing of sequence stores with fine-grained IAM access controls.
- No native federated query engine for cross-cloud analysis. The **Swarm** framework demonstrated federated variant queries across AWS Athena, GCP BigQuery, and other databases as an open-source third-party solution (https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008977).

### Google Cloud / Terra

- Terra on Azure (GA January 2024) enables cross-organization collaboration with **advanced policy configuration** for data governance across geographical borders (https://www.broadinstitute.org/news/terra-azure-release).
- **AnVIL** (NHGRI's platform on Terra) supports controlled-access data with data access controls inherited by workspaces. AnVIL is expanding to Azure with shared data corpus across GCP and Azure (https://anvilproject.org/news/2024/04/15/comparing-the-nhgri-anvil-platform).
- Terra supports **NIH cloud-based data resources** interoperability — NIH is actively developing distributed genomic analysis workflows across AnVIL and All of Us platforms (https://datascience.nih.gov/data-scholars-2023/distributed-genomic-analysis-workflows-and-services).
- GA4GH standards (Passports, DRS, WES, Data Connect) are deeply integrated into Terra's architecture for federated identity and data access (https://www.ga4gh.org/product/ga4gh-passports/, https://www.ga4gh.org/work_stream/federated_analysis/).

### Azure

- **Terra on Azure** can be deployed within an organization's Azure tenant and connect to data within the organization's IT network, integrating with Active Directory (https://www.broadinstitute.org/news/terra-azure-release).
- Enables controlled data access and collaboration across organization and geographical borders.
- Azure's enterprise identity management (Azure AD/Entra ID) provides institutional-grade access control for multi-tenant environments.

### GA4GH Standards (Cross-Platform)

The **GA4GH Federated Analysis Work Stream** (formerly Cloud Work Stream) develops standards enabling "bring the algorithms to the data" across federated environments. Key standards include:
- **DRS** (Data Repository Service): Standardized data retrieval across platforms.
- **WES** (Workflow Execution Service): Execute WDL/CWL/Nextflow workflows remotely.
- **Data Connect**: Federated search of disparate datasets without requiring harmonization.
- **Passports v1.2**: Researcher identity and authorization for controlled-access data (https://www.ga4gh.org/product/ga4gh-passports/).
- **TES** (Task Execution Service): Enables multicloud task execution; implemented on Azure via Cromwell on Azure (https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/10.1109/MCSE.2024.3414994).

The **OmicSHIELD** open-source platform demonstrates privacy-protected federated omics analysis where data stays in original repositories, eliminating data transfer (https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012626).

**Assessment:** Google Cloud/Terra has the most mature federated analysis ecosystem, with GA4GH standards deeply integrated and AnVIL's multi-cloud expansion underway. AWS relies on cross-account IAM and third-party frameworks. Azure benefits from enterprise identity management and Terra on Azure's cross-org collaboration features.

---

## 4. Variant Calling Pipeline Performance

### Per-Genome Processing Benchmarks (30x WGS, FASTQ-to-VCF)

| Platform / Tool | Time | Compute Cost | Source |
|----------------|------|-------------|--------|
| **AWS HealthOmics GATK-BP Ready2Run** (fq2vcf, 30x) | ~12h 30m estimated | **$10/run** (fixed price) | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/omics/latest/dev/workflows-r2r-table.html, https://aws.amazon.com/healthomics/pricing/ |
| **AWS NVIDIA Parabricks Ready2Run** (Germline DeepVariant, 30x) | ~2h estimated | Per-run pricing (fixed) | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/omics/latest/dev/workflows-r2r-table.html |
| **NVIDIA Parabricks on EC2** (A100 GPU, Spot) | ~25 min | **$4.23** ($4.10 infra + $0.13 software) | https://pages.awscloud.com/rs/112-TZM-766/images/AWS_NVIDIA%20Genomics%20Infographic_FINAL.pdf |
| **NVIDIA Parabricks on EC2** (T4 GPU, Spot) | ~76 min | **$2.58** ($2.13 infra + $0.45 software) | Same as above |
| **Sentieon on AWS** (hpc6a.48xlarge) | ~32–38 min | **$1.53–$1.75** | https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/hpc/cost-effective-and-accurate-genomics-analysis-with-sentieon-on-aws/ |
| **Google Cloud DeepVariant** (CPU) | ~5–70 min | **$2–3** | https://github.com/google/deepvariant |
| **Terra GATK4 Germline** (NA12878, 65 GB) | ~22h 35m | **$5.23** | https://support.terra.bio/hc/en-us/articles/7420514067995 |
| **Terra DRAGEN-GATK** (NA12878) | ~4h | **$0.90** | Same as above |
| **Azure Sentieon DNAscope** (2024 benchmark) | ~18–20 min | **~$0.11** | https://www.linkedin.com/posts/frankhu1_update-cost-effective-genomics-analysis-activity-7242244343057543170-eKa1 |
| **Azure Sentieon DNAseq** (hpc6a.48xlarge equivalent) | ~32 min | ~$1.53 | https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/healthcareandlifesciencesblog/cost-effective-genomics-analysis-with-sentieon-on-azure/4025007 |

**Performance leaders:** Azure Sentieon ($0.11, 18–20 min) and AWS Parabricks on A100 Spot ($4.23, 25 min) represent the extremes of cost optimization. The Sentieon $0.11 figure from September 2024 represents the latest generation of software optimization on commodity CPUs without specialized hardware (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/frankhu1_update-cost-effective-genomics-analysis-activity-7242244343057543170-eKa1). The AWS $2.58 Parabricks-on-T4-Spot figure is from 2021 and may have improved.

---

## 5. Total Cost for Analyzing 100,000 Whole Genomes Annually

### Assumptions
- 30x coverage short-read WGS (~100 GB FASTQ per genome, ~150 GB total with intermediates)
- Annual throughput: 100,000 genomes = ~8,333/month
- Storage: Raw + processed data retained for 1 year, ~15 PB total (100,000 × 150 GB)
- Analysis: FASTQ-to-VCF (alignment + variant calling)

### Compute Cost Estimates (100,000 genomes/year)

| Scenario | Per-Genome Cost | Annual Compute | Notes |
|----------|----------------|---------------|-------|
| **AWS HealthOmics GATK-BP Ready2Run** | $10.00 | **$1,000,000** | Fixed per-run pricing; predictable but premium (https://aws.amazon.com/healthomics/pricing/) |
| **AWS Parabricks on EC2 Spot (T4)** | $2.58 | **$258,000** | 2021 pricing; requires GPU orchestration |
| **AWS Sentieon on EC2** | $1.53–$1.75 | **$153,000–$175,000** | On-demand; Spot could reduce further |
| **Google Cloud GATK on Terra (preemptible VMs)** | ~$5.00 | **$500,000** | Broad's optimized pipeline; preemptible VMs reduce by ~70% |
| **Google Cloud DeepVariant** | ~$2–3 | **$200,000–$300,000** | GPU/TPU optional acceleration |
| **Azure Sentieon (2024 benchmark)** | ~$0.11 | **~$11,000** | Extraordinary claim; requires verification at scale; software license costs additional |
| **Azure Sentieon (conservative, on-demand CPU)** | ~$1.50 | **$150,000** | Based on hpc6a-equivalent pricing |

### Storage Cost Estimates (~15 PB active, declining with tiering)

| Platform | Storage Approach | Estimated Annual Cost |
|----------|-----------------|----------------------|
| **AWS HealthOmics Sequence Store** | Purpose-built with automatic compression and tiering; pricing per gigabase-month. ~$30/genome for raw+processed (NIAGADS estimate) | **~$3,000,000** (raw storage; HealthOmics compression could reduce 40–60%) |
| **AWS S3 (standard + Intelligent-Tiering)** | ~$23/TB/month standard; tiering to ~$5/TB for archive | **$1,200,000–$4,140,000** depending on access patterns |
| **Google Cloud Storage** | Standard ~$20/TB/month; Autoclass enabled on Terra workspaces (automatic cold-tier migration, as of Oct 2024) | **$1,200,000–$3,600,000** |
| **Azure Blob Storage** | Hot ~$18/TB/month; Cool ~$10/TB/month; Archive ~$2/TB/month | **$360,000–$3,240,000** depending on tiering strategy |

**Note:** Aggressive lifecycle policies moving data to archive/cold storage after 30–90 days can reduce storage costs by 70–85%. The NIAGADS estimate of ~$30 per genome for AWS storage includes raw and processed data over 3 years (https://niagads.scrollhelp.site/support/niagads-data-storage-cost-estimates).

### Data Egress Cost Traps

This is a critical and often underestimated cost dimension.

**Current egress pricing (per GB, over public internet):**

| Provider | Egress Rate (first tier) | Free Allowance | 50 TB Cost | 1 PB Cost |
|----------|-------------------------|----------------|------------|-----------|
| **AWS** | $0.09/GB | 100 GB/month | ~$4,500 | ~$90,000 |
| **Azure** | $0.087/GB | 100 GB/month | ~$4,350 | ~$87,000 |
| **Google Cloud** | $0.085/GB | 0–200 GB/month | ~$4,250 | ~$85,000 |

(https://holori.com/egress-costs-comparison/, https://costoptimizedcloud.substack.com/p/beware-egress-fees-in-public-cloud)

**Genomics-specific egress trap scenarios:**

1. **Multi-institutional collaboration**: If your 100,000 genomes need to be shared with 5 partner institutions, each downloading the full 15 PB dataset = 75 PB egress. At $0.09/GB for AWS, that is **~$6.75 million** in egress fees alone. This makes cross-cloud or cross-institution data sharing ruinously expensive without careful architecture.

2. **Cloud-to-on-premises analysis**: Researchers downloading intermediate BAM/CRAM files for local analysis. A single 30x WGS CRAM file is ~15–30 GB. At $0.09/GB, downloading 10,000 genomes = 150–300 TB = **$13,500–$27,000**.

3. **Multi-cloud strategies**: Moving data between AWS and GCP for federated analysis. Cross-region egress within the same cloud is $0.01–0.02/GB; cross-cloud via internet is $0.085–0.09/GB. For 15 PB, cross-cloud transfer = **~$1.3 million**.

4. **Backup and disaster recovery**: Replicating 15 PB to another cloud provider for DR = ~$1.3 million one-time egress plus ongoing storage costs.

**Mitigations announced in 2024:** All three hyperscalers eliminated egress fees for customers **permanently leaving** their platform (in response to EU Data Act), but this does not help with ongoing operational egress for collaboration or multi-cloud workflows (https://www.fierce-network.com/ai/one-where-we-hate-on-egress-fees-even-more, https://www.abiresearch.com/market-research/insight/7783827-decoding-hyperscalers-new-egress-fee-waive). Day-to-day operational egress fees remain fully in effect.

**AWS** offers 100 GB/month free and volume discounts: $0.07/GB for 100–150 TB, $0.05/GB above 150 TB. For a genomics workload transferring 10 TB/month of results, annual egress = ~$8,400.

**Direct Connect / ExpressRoute / Cloud Interconnect** can reduce egress to $0.02/GB but require dedicated network circuits ($500–$5,000/month port fees).

### Total Cost Summary (Annual, 100,000 30x WGS)

| Cost Component | AWS (HealthOmics) | AWS (DIY with Parabricks/Sentieon) | Google Cloud (Terra) | Azure (Sentieon) |
|---------------|-------------------|-----------------------------------|---------------------|-----------------|
| Compute | $1,000,000 | $153,000–$258,000 | $200,000–$500,000 | $11,000–$150,000 |
| Storage (15 PB, tiered) | $600,000–$3,000,000 | $600,000–$3,000,000 | $600,000–$3,000,000 | $600,000–$3,000,000 |
| Egress (10 TB/month results) | $8,400 | $8,400 | $8,100 | $8,100 |
| Platform/Management fees | Included | None (self-managed) | Terra is free; GCP charges apply | Terra is free; Azure charges apply |
| **Estimated Annual Total** | **$1.6M–$4.0M** | **$761K–$3.3M** | **$808K–$3.5M** | **$619K–$3.2M** |

The wide ranges reflect storage tiering strategies. The low end assumes aggressive archival policies (moving to cold/archive within 30 days); the high end assumes all data in hot storage.

---

## 6. Decision Matrix

| Criterion | AWS (HealthOmics) | Google Cloud (Terra) | Azure (Genomics/Terra) |
|-----------|-------------------|---------------------|----------------------|
| **Managed genomics service maturity** | ★★★★★ Purpose-built | ★★★★ Terra + Batch (Life Sciences deprecated) | ★★★ Terra + self-managed Cromwell/Nextflow |
| **Ready-to-use bioinformatics tools** | ★★★★ Ready2Run catalog | ★★★★★ GATK/DeepVariant/seqr ecosystem | ★★★★ Terra + Sentieon/DRAGEN |
| **China PIPL compliance** | ★★ AWS China exists but HealthOmics unavailable | ★ No mainland China region | ★★★ Azure China via 21Vianet (generic compute) |
| **GDPR compliance** | ★★★★★ | ★★★★★ | ★★★★★ |
| **HIPAA compliance** | ★★★★★ | ★★★★★ | ★★★★★ |
| **Federated analysis** | ★★★ Cross-account sharing | ★★★★★ GA4GH/AnVIL/Terra federation | ★★★★ Terra + Azure AD |
| **Variant calling cost at scale** | ★★★★ Parabricks/Sentieon on EC2 | ★★★★ DeepVariant/GATK optimized | ★★★★★ Sentieon ($0.11 claim) |
| **Egress cost control** | ★★★★ 100 GB free; volume discounts | ★★★ 200 GB free; similar rates | ★★★★ 100 GB free; similar rates |
| **Ease of managed workflow** | ★★★★★ Fully managed | ★★★★ Managed via Terra | ★★★ Requires more self-management |

---

## 7. Recommendations

1. **If China data residency is mandatory:** None of the three platforms offer managed genomics services in China. Azure China (21Vianet) offers the most infrastructure options for deploying self-managed pipelines (Cromwell/Nextflow on Azure Batch), but this requires significant engineering. Consider a **split architecture**: process China-origin data on self-managed Azure China infrastructure, and process international data on Terra/Azure or AWS HealthOmics.

2. **If federated multi-institution analysis is the priority:** Google Cloud/Terra is the strongest choice. GA4GH Passports, DRS, WES, and Data Connect are natively integrated. AnVIL's 5+ PB data corpus and expansion to Azure enables cross-cloud collaboration (https://anvilproject.org/news/2024/04/15/comparing-the-nhgri-anvil-platform).

3. **If lowest cost is the priority for compute:** Azure with Sentieon offers the most aggressive per-genome costs ($0.11 per 30x WGS in the September 2024 benchmark, though this should be validated at 100K genome scale with license costs factored in). AWS Parabricks on GPU Spot instances ($2.58–$4.23) is well-proven at scale.

4. **If managed simplicity is the priority:** AWS HealthOmics offers the most turnkey experience with fixed per-run pricing ($10/genome for GATK), automatic infrastructure management, and 100,000+ vCPU scalability — but at a significant cost premium over self-managed alternatives.

5. **Egress mitigation strategy regardless of platform:** Use GA4GH htsget for sub-range data access rather than full-file downloads. Implement "bring the compute to the data" architecture. Use cloud-native analytics (Athena/BigQuery/Azure Synapse) on VCF/variant stores rather than downloading intermediate files. Negotiate committed-use egress discounts.

# Maternal Mortality and Prenatal Care Access Among Rohingya Refugees in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh versus Karen Refugee Communities on the Thai-Myanmar Border (2017–2023): A Comparative Analysis

---

## 1. Population Context and Scale

**Rohingya refugees in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh** numbered approximately 926,561 by March 2022 within 34 camps, following the massive August 2017 influx of over 750,000 people (Health Sector Bulletin Q1 2022, https://reliefweb.int/attachments/bb1223e6-9d2f-3020-92b3-8290bdae4e5d/health_sector_bulletin_18_q1_jan-mar_2022.pdf). By 2023, the population exceeded 960,000 across 33 makeshift camps plus Bhasan Char Island (UNFPA Situation Report Q2 2023, https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/UNFPA%20Situation%20Report%20Rohingya%20crisis_Q2%202023.pdf). Fifty-two percent of the population is female, with an estimated 235,000 girls under 18.

**Karen and other Myanmar refugees in Thailand** numbered approximately 87,000–94,000 across nine official camps along the Thai-Myanmar border by 2018–2019, with the population declining from a peak of ~139,000 due to third-country resettlement, repatriation, and out-migration (WHO Thailand migration report, https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/ac76e2d8-ca18-454e-bbe7-4f4eb6dfebfc/content). Mae La camp, the largest, held 39,061–40,100 refugees during 2017–2018 (UNHCR HIS 2017 and 2018 site reports, https://reliefweb.int/attachments/39ea9ee8-f0f1-3911-a9c5-b75ce55bc944/Thailand_2017_Maela.pdf and https://his.unhcr.org/ar2018/files/TH/Thailand_2018_Maela.pdf). The two camps studied most closely in the published literature—Mae Ra Ma Luang (MRML) and Mae La Oon (MLO)—together housed approximately 20,000 refugees (Benner et al. 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11091483/).

---

## 2. Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR)

### 2.1 Rohingya (Cox's Bazar)

The MMR trajectory in the Rohingya camps shows an alarming deterioration from the post-influx baseline:

- **2017–2018 (RAMOS study):** MMR was estimated at **179 per 100,000 live births** (95% CI: 130–228), based on 52 confirmed maternal deaths among approximately 29,000 live births. Obstetric hemorrhage was the leading cause at 28% of pregnancy-related deaths, of which 61% were postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). Pregnancy-induced hypertension accounted for 22%, and non-obstetric complications for 21%. Half of all pregnancy-related deaths occurred at home (UNFPA/CDC Atlanta RAMOS Report, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/Final%20RAMOS%20Summary%20Report%20for%20circulation_0.pdf).

- **2020:** 45 maternal deaths recorded. Obstetric hemorrhage caused 26.7% (12 deaths), with 8 of those being PPH. Hypertensive disorders accounted for 20% (MPMSR Annual Report 2020, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/annual_report_of_mpmsr_2020_03_august_2021.pdf).

- **2021:** 96 confirmed maternal deaths among 253 women-of-reproductive-age deaths. Obstetric hemorrhage was the leading direct cause at 29.2%; hypertensive disorders at 23% (MPMSR Annual Report 2021, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/mpmsr_annual_report_2021.pdf).

- **2022:** **83 maternal deaths** reported, yielding an MMR of **321 per 100,000 live births**. Obstetric hemorrhage accounted for 44% of deaths; hypertensive disorders for 31%. Seventy-one percent occurred at facility level (MPMSR Annual Report 2022, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/mpmsr_annual_report_2022.pdf.pdf; Health Sector Bulletin Feb 2024, https://rohingyaresponse.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/CXB-Health-Sector-Bulletin-Feb-2024-1.pdf).

- **2023:** **57 maternal deaths** reported, with MMR estimated at **295 per 100,000 live births** by the Health Sector or **200.39 per 100,000** per WHO program data. Obstetric hemorrhage caused 35% (n=20), hypertensive disorders 33% (n=19). Seventy-five percent of deaths occurred at health facilities or during referral (MPMSR Annual Report 2023, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/2024-09/MPMSR%20Annual%20Report%202023%20Final.docx.pdf; Health Sector Bulletin Feb 2024).

- **2024:** 46 maternal deaths, MMR of **168 per 100,000 live births**, down from the prior two years. Obstetric hemorrhage caused 35% of facility-based deaths and **67% of community-based deaths**. The 2024 MPMSR report documented an average of 1 maternal death per week (MPMSR Annual Report 2024, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/2025-08/MPMSR%20Annual%20Report%202024%20Final.docx.pdf; WHO feature story Oct 2025, https://www.who.int/bangladesh/news/feature-stories/item/building-a-safer-future-for-mothers-and-newborns-in-cox-s-bazar).

**Summary for Rohingya:** MMR ranged from 179 (baseline 2017–2018) to a peak of 321 (2022), declining to 168 by 2024. The trajectory was non-linear, with a marked deterioration between 2020 and 2022 attributed to funding shortfalls and service disruptions.

### 2.2 Karen/Myanmar refugees (Thai-Myanmar border)

- **MRML and MLO camps (2004–2018):** MMR averaged **126.5 per 100,000 live births** across the 18-year study period, with wide confidence intervals due to small numbers: 10 maternal deaths documented among 12,961 live births. MMR varied between 43.2/100,000 (95% CI: 7.0–476.0) and 147.2/100,000 (95% CI: 40.4–787.5) in five-year blocks. Four deaths had unknown cause; five of six known causes were in grand multigravida women (Benner et al. 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11091483/).

- **Mae La camp (SMRU data, 2006–2010):** The Shoklo Malaria Research Unit reported an MMR of **79 per 100,000 live births** (95% CI: 40–170) in camps for displaced persons during 2006–2010, representing a six-fold decline from 499/100,000 in 1986–1990 (McGready et al., https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0040244). The broader SMRU cohort (1986–2024) reported overall MMR of 176/100,000 across 94,645 pregnancies (SMRU Cohort Profile, https://wellcomeopenresearch.org/articles/11-21).

- **Mae La camp (UNHCR HIS 2017–2018):** The UNHCR Health Information System reported 1 maternal death at Mae La in 2017 (population ~40,100) and 0 reported maternal deaths in 2018 (population ~39,061), though these figures likely reflect underreporting in a small population (UNHCR HIS 2017 and 2018 Mae La site reports).

**Summary for Karen:** MMR ranged from approximately 79 (2006–2010 in camps) to 127 (2004–2018 pooled), with a declining long-term trend. These figures are substantially lower than the Rohingya MMR in every comparable period.

---

## 3. Antenatal Care Visit Completion Rates (4+ Visits)

### 3.1 Rohingya (Cox's Bazar)

- **2022 Q2:** 90,182 ANC visits recorded; the ANC 4+ completion rate among Rohingya mothers attending facilities was approximately **75%** for all births taking place in health facilities as of December 2023 (SRH Working Group Annual Bulletin 2023, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/srh_wg_bulletin_annual_bulletin_2023_final_1.pdf). Earlier data from Q1 2023 reported ANC 4+ coverage reaching **85%** of births (SRH WG Bulletin Q1 2023, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/srh_working_group_bulletin_quarter_i_2023_2.pdf).

- **2024:** ANC4+ attendance rose to **90%** according to SRH Working Group data, up from 75% in 2023 (JEGH review article 2026, https://journals.diu.edu.bd/index.php/jegh/article/download/102/23/557).

- Of the 57 maternal deaths in 2023, 51% (29) had received at least 4 ANC visits, suggesting that ANC attendance alone is insufficient without quality of care improvements (MPMSR 2023).

- A 2025 study found the average number of ANC visits among Rohingya women was 6.9 (SD=2.6), with 19.2% delaying care until after the first trimester (Springer, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13031-025-00733-6).

### 3.2 Karen (Thai-Myanmar border)

- **MRML and MLO camps (2000–2018):** Between **93.3% and 98.8%** of pregnant women attended at least four ANC visits throughout the study period, with >90% receiving maternal tetanus vaccine. Postnatal care attendance was 96.3% per year (Benner et al. 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11091483/).

- **Mae La camp (UNHCR HIS 2017):** Antenatal care coverage was **89%** against a >90% standard. By 2018, it reached **91%** (UNHCR HIS Mae La site reports 2017 and 2018).

- The SMRU clinic at Mae La achieved >90% scores on essential elements of ANC from maternal records, including supplements, risk factor recording, and regular and correct partogram use (Stieglbauer et al., https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12884-015-0444-0).

**Comparison:** Karen camps consistently achieved ANC4+ completion rates of 90–99%, while Rohingya camps started at much lower levels and gradually improved to 75–90% by 2023–2024.

---

## 4. Skilled Birth Attendance and Facility-Based Delivery Rates

### 4.1 Rohingya (Cox's Bazar)

The trajectory of facility-based deliveries shows significant progress:
- **2018:** Home delivery rate was **88%** (only ~12% facility-based) (Health Sector Bulletin Q2 2021, https://healthcluster.who.int/docs/librariesprovider16/meeting-reports/bangladesh-health-sector-bulletin-apr-june-2021.pdf).
- **2019:** Home delivery rate dropped to **59%**; facility-based deliveries reached approximately 41%.
- **2019 (June, Camp 22):** Only **35%** of all deliveries were facility-based; MSF was the sole provider of facility-based maternity care in this isolated camp of 23,000 (Hadiuzzaman et al. MSF, https://doi.org/10.57740/qwgn-be73).
- **2020:** 17,025 facility-based deliveries reported for the full year (Health Sector Bulletin H2 2020).
- **2021:** Facility-based delivery rate reached approximately **67–70%** of total deliveries (Health Sector Strategic Plan, https://rohingyaresponse.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/Health-Sector-Strategic-Plan-2023-2024.pdf; BMJ article, https://www.bmj.com/content/375/bmj.n2722).
- **2022:** 27,240 facility-based deliveries reported; facility-based delivery rate reached **81%** (SRH WG Annual Bulletin 2023).
- **2023:** 33,854 facility deliveries; facility-based deliveries for the Rohingya response were **85%** of total deliveries. The cesarean section rate was **5.7%**, down from 7.6% in 2022 (SRH WG Annual Bulletin 2023).
- **2024:** 35,850 facility-based deliveries; 8.2% C-section rate (JEGH review, https://journals.diu.edu.bd/index.php/jegh/article/download/102/23/557). However, 3,512 babies were still delivered at home.

### 4.2 Karen (Thai-Myanmar border)

- **MRML and MLO (2002–2018):** **93%** (12,849/13,746) of deliveries occurred in the camps, with only 7% requiring emergency secondary care referral (Benner et al. 2024).

- **Mae La (UNHCR HIS 2017):** Proportion of births attended by skilled personnel was **96%** of all births. By 2018, it was **95%** (UNHCR HIS Mae La site reports).

- **Mae La (SMRU data):** The SMRU clinic delivered approximately 1,500 births annually. The C-section rate remained low at an average of **3.7%** (Benner et al. 2024) or **3.6%** across the study period. Deliveries by unskilled birth attendants at home were 20.3% in MRML and 14.7% in MLO in 2018 (Benner et al. 2024).

- SMRU trained local Karen and Burman women as skilled birth attendants through a six-month accelerated curriculum beginning in 2008, resulting in a **25% increase in clinic births**, a 16.4% drop in episiotomy use, and 99% partogram use (Oxford Tropical Medicine, https://www.tropicalmedicine.ox.ac.uk/news/birth-attendant-training-course-may-be-global-model-for-safer-birth-care-in-poor-communities).

**Comparison:** The Thai-Myanmar border camps maintained skilled birth attendance of 95–96% throughout the study period, while Rohingya camps improved from approximately 12% in 2018 to 85% by 2023—a remarkable trajectory but still lagging behind.

---

## 5. Postpartum Hemorrhage Incidence

### 5.1 Rohingya (Cox's Bazar)

Postpartum hemorrhage is consistently the leading cause of maternal death:
- **RAMOS (2017–2018):** Obstetric hemorrhage accounted for **28%** of all pregnancy-related deaths; of these, **61% were postpartum hemorrhage** and 39% antepartum hemorrhage (RAMOS Report, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/Final%20RAMOS%20Summary%20Report%20for%20circulation_0.pdf).
- **2020:** Obstetric hemorrhage was the major cause at **26.7%** of 45 maternal deaths; 8 of 12 hemorrhage deaths were PPH (MPMSR 2020).
- **2021:** Obstetric hemorrhage at **29.2%** of 96 maternal deaths (MPMSR 2021).
- **2022:** Obstetric hemorrhage at **44%** of 83 maternal deaths—the highest proportion in the series. Of facility-based deaths, 39% were due to obstetric hemorrhage (MPMSR 2022).
- **2023:** Obstetric hemorrhage at **35%** of 57 maternal deaths (n=20) (MPMSR 2023).
- **2024:** Obstetric hemorrhage at **35%** of facility deaths and **67% of community-based deaths**. Twenty-two deaths (48%) occurred within 42 days postpartum (MPMSR 2024).
- The 2021 UNICEF CER reported that the main causes of obstetric complications were postpartum hemorrhages, severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, obstructed/prolonged labor, and puerperal sepsis (https://open.unicef.org/sites/transparency/files/2022-04/Bangladesh%20CER%202021.pdf).

The MPMSR system documented an average of **1 maternal death and 15 perinatal deaths per week** in 2023, and **1 maternal death and 10 perinatal deaths per week** in 2024 (MPMSR 2023 and 2024).

### 5.2 Karen (Thai-Myanmar border)

- At MRML and MLO camps (2004–2018), the SMRU data showed that postpartum hemorrhage was the most common observed complication during labor and birth, though SBAs generally followed protocols but were "slow to recognize severity and take action" (Stieglbauer et al., https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12884-015-0444-0).

- The ALSO/BLSO training evaluation at the Thai-Myanmar border found that PPH-related MMR fell from **57.0 per 100,000** (95% CI: 30.06–108.3) in the eight years before training (2000–2007) to **25.4 per 100,000** (95% CI: 11.6–55.4) in the eight years after (2009–2016), though this reduction did not reach statistical significance (p=0.109). After adjustment, PPH-related maternal mortality was associated with birth before ALSO/BLSO implementation (Wellcome Open Research, https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:d2a1ee5a-79c4-421c-b2ae-bcddc3ab88f7/files/s4t64gq479).

- A 2016–2021 dataset from SMRU facilities showed postpartum bleeding cases ranging from 23 to 82 per year, with postpartum infections (lochiometra) ranging from 52 to 111 per year (https://html.scirp.org/file/_5-1432985_2.htm).

- PPH was a documented reason for emergency referral: pre-eclampsia, antepartum hemorrhage, and prolonged labor were the most common referral reasons from the camps to Thai hospitals (Benner et al. 2024).

**Comparison:** While PPH is the leading cause of maternal death in both settings, the proportion of deaths attributable to PPH is dramatically higher among Rohingya (28–67% of maternal deaths) than in the Thai-Myanmar border camps, where structured training programs and referral systems have reduced PPH-related mortality.

---

## 6. Neonatal Mortality (Within 28 Days)

### 6.1 Rohingya (Cox's Bazar)

- **2017–2018 (prospective surveillance):** Neonatal mortality rate was **27.0 per 1,000 live births** (95% CI: 22.3–31.8). Stillbirth rate was 15.2/1,000 total births. The majority of neonatal deaths (76.3%, n=405/531) and stillbirths (72.1%) occurred at home or in the community. Proximity to a secondary health facility was associated with lower neonatal mortality (p<0.01) (BMJ Global Health, https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjgh-2021-008110).

- **2023 (August–December):** 304 perinatal deaths reported in the first five months of perinatal surveillance. Seventy-eight percent occurred at health facilities or during referral; 22% in the community (MPMSR 2023).

- **2024:** 491 perinatal deaths reported (average 10/week). Perinatal mortality rate was **17.90 per 1,000 live births**. Key causes included birth asphyxia, preterm birth, and intrauterine growth retardation (WHO 2025, https://www.who.int/bangladesh/news/feature-stories/item/building-a-safer-future-for-mothers-and-newborns-in-cox-s-bazar; MPMSR 2024).

- WHO-trained health workers contributed to per facility perinatal death reductions: in UNFPA-supported facilities, perinatal deaths dropped from **7% to 4.8%** between June 2021 and March 2022 after midwife mentoring (UNFPA 2022, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/en/news/unfpas-midwives-mark-international-day-midwife-coxs-bazar).

### 6.2 Karen (Thai-Myanmar border)

- **Mae La (UNHCR HIS 2017):** Neonatal mortality rate was **8 per 1,000 live births**. Infant mortality rate was 19.8/1,000 live births (UNHCR HIS 2017 Mae La site report).

- **Mae La (UNHCR HIS 2018):** Neonatal mortality rate was **6 per 1,000 live births**. Infant mortality rate was 6.2/1,000 live births (UNHCR HIS 2018 Mae La site report).

- **MRML and MLO (2000–2018):** Neonatal mortality rate declined from **23.5/1,000** (2000) to **7.7/1,000** (2018)—a 62% decline over the study period. Infant mortality rate fell from 40 to 10.1/1,000 (76% decline). Perinatal mortality rate fell from 32.5 to 16.9/1,000 (48% decline). Stillbirth rate was 14/1,000 live births overall (Benner et al. 2024).

- **Mae La Special Care Baby Unit (SCBU, 2008–2011):** The introduction of a neonatal intensive care unit staffed by trained refugees resulted in a **51% decline in neonatal mortality** from 21.8 to 10.7 per 1,000 live births (p=0.04). Premature infant mortality among SCBU admissions fell from 19.3% (2008) to 4.8% (2011) (Carrara et al., https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0072721).

- **Early neonatal mortality (SMRU, 2008–2015):** Overall early neonatal mortality was 6.6/1,000 live births (95% CI: 5.40–8.06) among 15,073 singleton live births (PLOS ONE, https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0190419).

**Comparison:** Karen camp neonatal mortality (6–8/1,000 in recent years) is roughly one-quarter to one-third of the Rohingya rate (27/1,000 in 2017–2018, declining but still elevated at 17.9/1,000 by 2024). Both settings showed improvement over time, but the Thai-Myanmar border camps achieved much lower absolute levels.

## 7. Healthcare Delivery Models: NGO-Operated Field Hospitals versus Thai Ministry of Public Health Integration

### 7.1 Cox's Bazar: Fragmented NGO-Operated System

The Rohingya response operates through a **Health Sector coordination mechanism** led by WHO, with over 100 health-sector partners delivering services through:
- **90+ Health Posts**
- **44 Primary Health Centres (PHCs)**
- **4 secondary healthcare facilities** (MSF Friendship Hospital, Turkish Hospital, Hope Field Hospital, and Ramu Field Hospital) providing EmONC (Health Sector Bulletin Q1 2022).
- Only **17% of ~200 health facilities** have 24/7 access, and only **3 have surgical facilities** as of 2022 (Inspira Advisory, https://inspira-bd.com/inadequate-healthcare-services-at-the-rohingya-camp-inducing-vulnerabilities/).
- As late as August 2025, IOM launched the **first-ever CEmONC service** inside the camps at Camp 24 in Teknaf (IOM 2025, https://bangladesh.iom.int/news/iom-brings-first-ever-comprehensive-emergency-obstetric-and-newborn-care-services-coxs-bazar-rohingya-camps).
- In 2023, Teknaf Health Complex—the sole secondary hospital for the area—had **virtually no CEmONC services from April to July** due to recruitment failures, absent blood bank, and lack of specialists (SRH WG Bulletin Q1 2024, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/srh_working_group_bulletin_quarter_i_2024_2nd_june_2024.pdf).

MSF operates as a major provider, running field hospitals including a 50-bed clinic in Kutupalong (https://www.msf.org/sites/default/files/2020-10/201702_MSF_brief_on_the_situation_of_Rohingyas_fleeing_Myanmar_to_Bangladesh.pdf) and the Goyalmara hospital focusing on neonatal and pediatric care (https://www.msf.org/rohingya-refugees-saving-lives-have-just-begun-bangladesh). MSF's research in Camp 22 found it was the only provider of facility-based maternity care in a camp of 23,000, and that only 35% of deliveries were facility-based as of June 2019 (Hadiuzzaman et al., https://doi.org/10.57740/qwgn-be73).

The system is characterized by **multiple parallel service providers**, high staff turnover, and chronic funding uncertainty. The JRP health sector was only **23% funded in 2022** (receiving $25.7M of $110.8M requested) (JRP 2022 Funding Update, https://rohingyaresponse.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/2022_12_31_JRP-2022_Funding-update_FTS.pdf). By 2023, the health sector received **$48.4M of $97.3M** requested (49.7%) (JRP 2023). In 2022, a **$61 million funding gap** led to **51% of Health Posts, PHCs, and Field Hospitals being unfunded** and 3 health posts closing (Inspira Advisory).

### 7.2 Thai-Myanmar border: Integrated NGO–Government Model

Healthcare for Karen refugees operates through a fundamentally different model:

- **Malteser International (MI)** has been the main INGO responsible for preventive, promotional, and curative healthcare for over 30 years (1993–2023) in camps like MRML and MLO, implementing an integrated Primary Health Care project (Benner et al. 2024).

- The **Royal Thai Government** provides critical support: vaccines free of charge through the national EPI policy, birth certificates, phenylketonuria and hypothyroidism medication, and all national disease surveillance protocols are followed (Benner et al. 2024). The **Thai Ministry of Public Health** (MOPH) cooperates closely through the Bureau of Epidemiology and local health authorities.

- The **Shoklo Malaria Research Unit (SMRU)**, affiliated with Mahidol University and the University of Oxford, provides specialized maternal and child health services at Mae La and other camps, including a Special Care Baby Unit and systematic antenatal screening.

- **Mae La camp staffing (2017):** 3 medical doctors (1:<50,000 standard met), 2 qualified nurses, 74 community health workers, and multiple midwives. Consultations per trained clinician were 25/day (<50 standard met). The health utilization rate was 1.5 new visits/refugee/year (UNHCR HIS 2017 Mae La).

- Emergency referrals go to **Mae Sariang District Hospital** (80 km away, 3.5–7 hours depending on season) or **Chiang Mai University Hospital** for tertiary care. MI established a Memorandum of Agreement for full payment of secondary care at Thai hospitals (Benner et al. 2024). For the camps nearer to Mae Sot, emergency cases are referred to Thai hospitals in Mae Sariang or Chiang Mai (Japanese government report on Mae La, https://www.cas.go.jp/jp/seisaku/nanmin/yusikishakaigi/dai6/siryou4.pdf).

- **Cost per birth was €115 in 2018**; annual MCAH expenditure was €60,650. Per-refugee funding increased by 48% over the study period, partly due to declining population (Benner et al. 2024).

**Key structural difference:** The Thai model benefits from decades-long institutional continuity, integration with a middle-income country's public health infrastructure, a single dominant NGO provider ensuring coordination, and government provision of vaccines and emergency referral pathways. The Rohingya response is a multi-partner emergency operation in a country with a less-resourced health system, characterized by coordination challenges, service fragmentation, and donor dependency.

## 8. Midwife-to-Population Ratios

### 8.1 Rohingya (Cox's Bazar)

- UNFPA deployed **150+ licensed national midwives** by 2021, increasing to **213 midwives** in 31 UNFPA-supported health facilities and 39 Women Friendly Spaces by 2022 (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/en/news/unfpas-midwives-mark-international-day-midwife-coxs-bazar). By 2023, UNFPA supported **280+ midwives** across the camps (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/UNFPA%20Situation%20Report%20Rohingya%20crisis_Q2%202023.pdf; UNFPA Annual Report 2022, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/unfpa_annual_report_2022_01_25_05_2023.pdf).

- With a camp population of ~946,000 and 280 midwives, the approximate ratio is **1 midwife per 3,379 refugees**, far below the WHO recommended ratio. UNFPA extends support to approximately **60% of all midwives** in the Cox's Bazar humanitarian response.

- The UNFPA Midwifery Strategic Plan 2021–2023 noted the need for scaling, with midwives deployed through implementing partners to both camps and host communities (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/cxb_unfpa_midwifery_humanitarian-development_strategic_plan.pdf).

### 8.2 Karen (Thai-Myanmar border)

- MRML and MLO camps employed up to **26 midwives, 23 MCH assistants, and 4 mother support group facilitators** for a population of ~20,000, along with **110 Traditional Birth Attendants** active in both camps. The midwife-to-population ratio was approximately **1:770** (Benner et al. 2024).

- At Mae La (~40,000 population), SMRU staffed its obstetric department with local refugee women trained as SBAs through an accelerated six-month curriculum. The UNHCR HIS 2017 report does not specify exact midwife counts but notes 74 community health workers.

- Since 2010, midwives have been **fully responsible for maternal and child health care** at MRML/MLO, replacing medical assistants in this role (Benner et al. 2024).

**Comparison:** The midwife-to-population ratio at the Thai-Myanmar border (~1:770) is approximately **4.4 times better** than in the Rohingya camps (~1:3,379), contributing to substantially better outcomes.

---

## 9. Emergency Obstetric Care Availability Within 2-Hour Transport Radius

### 9.1 Rohingya (Cox's Bazar)

- The 2017–2018 prospective surveillance found that camps closer to a **secondary health facility** had significantly lower neonatal mortality than those near only a primary-level SRH unit (p<0.01) (BMJ Global Health, https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjgh-2021-008110).

- **Hope Field Hospital**, the only CEmONC and 24/7 SRHR facility in the camps, was **submerged by flooding in July 2021**, destroying medicines, equipment, and records (UNFPA flood response update, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/flood_response_update_1_week_3_august_2021_ok.pdf).

- UNFPA's Emergency Response and Transport System (ERTS) operated a 24/7 network of **8 ambulances** across all 34 camps, managing 1,670 emergency obstetric referrals in Q3 2022 (UNFPA SITREP 2022, https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/UNFPA%20Bangladesh%20Situation%20Report%20April-June%202022.pdf). Eight Referral Hubs were established in 2019, expanded to 12 by July 2020 (Springer, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13031-022-00485-7).

- Ambulances **cannot reach most camps** as they are inaccessible by road; slippery, muddy terrain makes vehicles prone to getting stuck. The journey to clinics can take up to **30 minutes by vehicle** depending on camp location (The Guardian, https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2025/jan/02/threadbare-facilities-high-mortality-cats-in-the-corridors-the-realities-of-life-for-new-rohingya-mothers-in-coxs-bazar).

- In 2023, the number of facilities providing **24/7 EmONC** was 40 out of 77 UNFPA-supported health facilities (UNFPA Q2 2023 SITREP). The first CEmONC facility capable of cesarean sections inside the camps was only opened in August 2025 (IOM 2025).

### 9.2 Karen (Thai-Myanmar border)

- For the more remote camps (MRML/MLO), the nearest Thai hospital providing emergency obstetric care is in **Mae Sariang, 80 km away**, requiring **3.5 to 7 hours** depending on season (Benner et al. 2024). This significantly exceeds a 2-hour transport radius.

- For Mae La, emergency cases are referred to Thai hospitals in **Mae Sariang or Chiang Mai** (Japanese government report on Mae La). Mae La is ~57 km from Mae Sot, which has hospital facilities, making emergency referral within a 2-hour window feasible in good conditions.

- MI maintained a **standby emergency car** at the SMRU clinic in Mae La (Stieglbauer et al. 2015). An average of **116 obstetric, neonatal, and/or infant care cases per year** required secondary emergency care from MRML/MLO (Benner et al. 2024).

- SMRU facilities were equipped with operating supplies and had **no out-of-stock or out-of-date drugs** during assessment (Stieglbauer et al. 2015). However, vacuum extraction was **not performed** in the camps, and syphilis testing was unavailable.

**Comparison:** Neither setting achieves universal CEmONC access within a 2-hour radius. The Rohingya camps face the paradox of being geographically closer to secondary facilities but having severe road/infrastructure barriers and until recently lacking any in-camp surgical capacity. The Thai-Myanmar camps are more remote from hospitals but benefit from better road infrastructure, organized referral agreements with Thai hospitals, and full payment coverage for emergency referrals.

---

## 10. Cultural Mediation Practices for Traditional Birth Attendants

### 10.1 Rohingya (Cox's Bazar)

Traditional birth attendants, known as *dai ma* or *dhorinis*, occupy a central and highly trusted role:
- Rohingya TBAs have "established positions as home-birthing assistants accepted and trusted by the community" (CPI, https://cpintl.org/impact-area/health/training-rohingya-traditional-birth-attendants-to-support-safe-births). Women reported high trust in TBAs, who provide services without monetary expectation.
- Families turn to TBAs first: women "only visit or seek healthcare at the facilities when the case cannot be managed by a traditional birth attendant... This leads to a large number of cases ending up in basic emergency obstetric and newborn care facilities with complications" (BMJ, https://www.bmj.com/content/375/bmj.n2722; UNFPA MPMSR reports).
- The MPMSR 2024 report documented an average delay of **19 hours** before arriving at a facility, largely due to home trials attended by TBAs (MPMSR 2024).
- Social Autopsies in 2024 found that preference for TBAs over medical staff was driven by "perceived gaps in respectful maternity care," nighttime security concerns, and cultural practices including use of birthing ropes and concerns about male staff and undressing (SRH WG Bulletin Q3 2024, https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/2025-01/Copy%20of%20CN_%20SRH%20Working%20Group%20Bulletin%20Quarter%20III%202024_Version%201%20%281%29_0.pdf).
- WHO has begun **engaging TBAs through orientation sessions** to encourage safer delivery practices and timely referrals (WHO 2025).
- Community Partners International trained TBAs to recognize danger signs and refer women to facilities, resulting in improved referral behavior (CPI 2023).
- Decision-making is a family process: "the women cannot make decisions themselves; they need someone—it can be the husband or imam… they are the ones who make the final decision to send a pregnant woman to a facility" (MSF medical coordinator, BMJ 2021).

### 10.2 Karen (Thai-Myanmar border)

- **110 Traditional Birth Attendants** remained active in MRML and MLO alongside 26 midwives. However, since 2010, **midwives have been fully responsible for maternal and child health care** (Benner et al. 2024).

- SMRU's strategy was to **train refugee women directly as skilled birth attendants** rather than relying on TBAs. A six-month accelerated curriculum (ICM/FIGO/WHO guidelines) was developed in 2008, training local Karen and Burman women. This resulted in no adverse perinatal outcomes and significant improvements in outcomes (Oxford Tropical Medicine, https://www.tropicalmedicine.ox.ac.uk/news/birth-attendant-training-course-may-be-global-model-for-safer-birth-care-in-poor-communities; PLOS ONE 2016).

- The relatively smaller camp populations, longer institutional history (nearly 40 years), and direct refugee involvement in service delivery created a cultural bridge that reduced the community-facility gap. The Karen community's longer exposure to Western-style healthcare within camps reduced cultural resistance over time.

**Comparison:** In the Rohingya context, TBAs remain the **primary gatekeepers** of maternity care, with cultural practices, gender norms, and distrust of facility-based services maintaining high home birth rates. In the Thai-Myanmar border context, a deliberate strategy of training refugee women as SBAs, combined with decades of institutional continuity, has effectively integrated TBAs into a formalized referral system rather than operating in competition with facility-based care.

---

## 11. Impact of 2021 UNFPA Funding Reductions on Maternal Health Services

### 11.1 Rohingya (Cox's Bazar)

The funding trajectory for the Rohingya response shows progressive deterioration:

| Year | JRP Funded ($M) | Gap ($M) | Gap % |
|------|----------------|----------|-------|
| 2019 | 692 | 228.5 | 25% |
| 2020 | 629.5 | 428.6 | 40% |
| 2021 | 689.7 | 253.5 | 27% |
| 2022 | 619.7 | 261.4 | 30% |
| 2023 | 620 | 255.9 | 29% |
| 2024 (Jan–Sep) | 455.7 | 396.7 | 47% |

(ISCG 2024 data, cited in IWA Publishing 2025, https://iwaponline.com/washdev/article/15/3/232/107532/Declining-humanitarian-funding-and-health-security)

Specific health-sector impacts:
- In **2022**, the JRP health sector received only **$25.7M of $110.8M** requested—just **23%** (JRP 2022 FTS). This led to a **$61 million funding gap** in the health sector, causing **51% of health facilities to be unfunded** and **3 health posts to close** (Inspira Advisory 2023).
- The **2019 funding gap** forced UNFPA to scale down SRHR programs, with some **family planning service sites eliminated altogether**, affecting 318,500 women and girls of reproductive age (USA for UNFPA, https://www.usaforunfpa.org/the-current-state-of-rohingya-refugees-and-reproductive-health/).
- The JRP 2023 Year-End Report stated explicitly: "Funding shortfalls worsened maternal and under-5 mortality rates" (https://rohingyaresponse.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/JRP-2023-Year-End-Report.pdf).
- The MMR rose from **179/100,000 in 2018** to **321/100,000 in 2022**, directly correlating with declining funding. The WHO/Health Sector data show the MMR peaked during the years of greatest funding shortfalls (2020–2022).

The UNFPA Supplies Partnership experienced a **52% cancellation of country workplan milestones** in 2021 due to funding cuts globally, with an estimated 240,100 women and girls not reached with family planning services (UNFPA Supplies Performance Report 2021, https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/Performance%20Measurement%20Report%202021-%20UNFPA%20Supplies%20Partnership%20.pdf). The UNFPA global funding impact was compounded by the simultaneous COVID-19 pandemic.

Conversely, the **$38.8 million World Bank grant** signed in January 2021 helped strengthen SRHR and GBV services in Cox's Bazar district, reaching over 4,500 people by June 2021 (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/en/news/strengthening-health-and-gender-services-coxs-bazar-district-us388-million-through-world-bank).

### 11.2 Karen (Thai-Myanmar border)

The Thai-Myanmar border camps experienced a different but related funding trajectory:
- Funding for MRML/MLO increased per capita (from €27.2/beneficiary in 2005 to **€52.1/beneficiary in 2018**) due to population decline, but the **absolute budget remained relatively stable** at €830,000–€1,060,000 annually (Benner et al. 2024).
- The primary donors (ECHO/EuropeAid/Global Fund) shifted focus toward voluntary repatriation and reduced engagement, with ECHO funding ending for these camps around February 2017 (Benner et al. 2024, Table 1).
- The Border Consortium reported that **funding was cut by half** even as caseloads decreased by one-third, meaning "per capita, we're getting less support now from the international community than we were 10 years ago for refugees" (PRI/Mae Tao Clinic, https://maetaoclinic.org/pri-org-with-less-foreign-aid-thai-clinic-struggles-to-serve-migrants-and-refugees-from-myanmar/).
- UNFPA Thailand's country programme document (2022–2026) noted that **"funding to refugee camps continues to decrease"** (https://www.unfpa.org/data/emergencies/thailand-humanitarian-emergency).
- In **January 2025**, the U.S. foreign aid freeze led to cuts in services including **shutdown of hospital care** in camps along the Thai-Myanmar border, affecting over 100,000 refugees (AP News, https://apnews.com/article/myanmar-refugees-camps-foreign-aid-rubio-b79eeef83a635d2b59208d8b91586b6b).

The Thai border camps' healthcare was less directly affected by the specific 2021 UNFPA funding reduction to the Rohingya response, as they operate under separate funding streams. However, the broader trend of declining international attention and donor fatigue has progressively eroded services.

**Comparison:** The Rohingya health system experienced acute, catastrophic funding cuts that directly correlated with deteriorating maternal mortality (179→321/100,000). The Thai-Myanmar border camps experienced slower erosion of funding, cushioned by per-capita increases as population declined and by the stability of the Thai government's in-kind contributions (vaccines, surveillance, emergency hospital access). The structural vulnerability of the Rohingya response to donor fluctuations is far greater due to its complete dependence on humanitarian financing.
